Jackson Hassell and four co-authors teach language model agents to learn classification tasks from labeled examples without changing any model weights. Instead of fine-tuning, their framework has the model write critiques of its own past attempts. Specific critiques are stored in an episodic memory, then distilled into reusable, task-level guidance kept in a semantic memory.

Using both memories together improved accuracy by about eight percentage points over a zero-shot baseline and beat a retrieval baseline that used labels alone. Gains varied widely by model and domain, so the authors introduce a suggestibility metric measuring how receptive a model is to outside reasoning. Pre-computed critiques also cut the model's inference-time thinking substantially, making the approach cheaper as well as more accurate.
arxiv-2510-19997:
Abraham Itzhak Weinberg proposes FAIGMOE, a guide for midsize and large firms taking up generative AI. Midsize firms face scarce funds and thin AI skill. Big firms wrestle with sheer scale and with getting many teams to pull together. Classic adoption theories, he argues, are too broad for what generative AI demands, leaving a gap this guide fills.

Four phases structure the path: taking stock, planning use cases, putting the tools in place, and running and refining them. Each phase scales its advice, on readiness, fit with strategy, risk, tech design, and staff change, to the firm's size. Concerns tied to generative AI itself, like prompt craft and hallucination control, are built in. As a perspective piece, the guide awaits tests in real firms, which the author flags as future work.
arxiv-2510-20097:
Aidan Blaser, Luc Lenain, and Nick Pizzo show that the drift caused by ocean surface waves is stronger where waves focus and steepen than simple estimates suggest. Surface gravity waves carry a mean Lagrangian drift that moves mass and aids mixing in the upper ocean. The usual practice adds up the drift from each wave part separately, as if the parts never interacted.

Lab measurements and fully nonlinear simulations of steep focusing wave packets show that practice underpredicts average transport in focusing regions by up to thirty percent. The authors derive an exact way to constrain local drift and a higher-order formula for narrow-banded fields. Local steepness, not the sum of separate parts, sets the size of the boost.
arxiv-2510-20397:
Nahual Sobrino probes heat-to-charge flow in a pair of joined quantum dots that block charge by the Coulomb force. He grows an exact-form base built by a motion law route, now for dots with lopsided links. Short closed forms come out for steady flows and for slope traits: charge slope, Seebeck rate, and heat slope.

Sobrino picks the work points that top yield and power, and ties them to near-balance ZT forms. Heat flow that bends one way is checked for both open and closed loop states, with a form for the open case. Peaks from the dot-dot force are read from poles of the Green map. They yield zones of high yield, odd heat slope signs, and real heat bending.
arxiv-2510-20897:
Tingfang Su and four co-authors study feedback from active galactic nuclei. An active galactic nucleus, called an AGN, is a bright galaxy center. A black hole at its center can drive outflows. In dwarf galaxies, feedback was thought to curb star birth. Dwarf galaxies are small galaxies with fewer stars.

The team ran simulations that resolve the Bondi radius. The Bondi radius is a small zone near the black hole. Their models show feedback can raise star birth instead of curbing it. Star birth rates rose by about twenty-five percent. Outflows squeezed gas into dense regions that cooled fast. Dense, cool gas forms stars well, so birth increased. This needed moderate energy and supernova feedback too. Supernovae are exploding stars that push on gas. Without them, outflows grew too strong and expelled gas. Results match what was seen in the galaxy Henize 2-10.
arxiv-2510-21097:
Jun-Jie Wei leads two co-authors on detecting gamma ray bursts from Population III stars, the first star generation, with the Einstein Probe and the SVOM satellite. These bursts would be counterparts of massive metal poor first stars and a direct probe of the cosmic dawn era.

A metallicity based progenitor rule and cosmological simulations with three distinct first star mass distributions feed a population synthesis model. Detection rates are assessed for the wide field X-ray telescope on Einstein Probe and the gamma ray imager on SVOM. Even a handful of confirmed events would constrain how the first stars formed and died.
arxiv-2510-21297:
Francis Liu, Natalie Packham, and Artur Sepp build an option pricing model where prices can jump in clusters, with upward jumps and downward jumps able to excite each other over time. Clustered jumps create lopsided, changing return patterns that simpler pricing models tend to miss.

The model uses a two-sided Hawkes process for the clustering and adds two parameters for how the market prices the risk of upward and downward jumps. Those risk prices can be read off option prices, letting the model match observed patterns in how option prices tilt. Fitted to Bitcoin options, the inferred risk prices help predict both the cost of carrying Bitcoin futures and the returns of hedged option trades.
arxiv-2510-21497:
Victor Alfieri works in derived algebraic geometry on foliations, structures that slice a space into leaf-like pieces, and asks how they behave on spaces of maps between two other spaces. Mapping stacks are the modern homes for moduli problems, so equipping them with foliations extends a classical tool to a very general setting.

Working over fields of characteristic zero, he first shows that derived foliations on a stack form a well-defined subcategory of stacks carrying extra structure. He describes exactly which objects occur. He then proves that pushing stacks forward along a well-behaved map preserves that class, which yields foliations on mapping stacks as a special case. Two showcase applications follow: foliations appear on the derived versions of the moduli stack of stable curves mapping into a space, and of the Hilbert scheme of subschemes.
arxiv-2510-21797:
Zhiwen Yu, Zhaocheng Liu, Xiaoqing Liu, Huanqiang Zeng, and C. L. Philip Chen address a quiet failure in systems that learn from several kinds of input at once. One input stream, such as sound or video, often learns faster and drowns out the weaker stream. Fixed rules for rebalancing ignore that some individual samples are far more skewed than others.

The team first defines a gap measure between what each single-stream branch predicts, and finds samples naturally split into balanced and skewed groups. A statistical mixture model separates the groups softly, and training then penalizes misalignment hardest on skewed samples while letting balanced ones focus on fusion. The method beat current leading baselines, and extra training on the clean balanced subset also worked as a data-cleaning step.
arxiv-2510-22197:
Qingzhu Zhang, Jiani Zhong, Zongsheng Li, Xinke Shen, and Quanying Liu pretrain brain-wave models for emotion. General-purpose pretraining, they argue, teaches the wrong features. Emotion datasets disagree about where feelings live in the signal. They label emotions inconsistently. They also shift wildly between people.

Their framework pools several datasets for joint pretraining. A loss aligns the covariance structure across datasets. The representation steadies without heavy labeling or per-person calibration. A hybrid encoder pairs a Mamba-style linear attention channel with a space-time dynamics model. Long, tangled brain patterns can be followed. The result beat large-scale general EEG models. The average margin reported is over four percent. The work points toward emotion systems that travel across studies and subjects.
arxiv-2510-22397:
Satyandra Guthula and five co-authors address forecasting for network telemetry, where long quiet stretches are broken by sudden heavy bursts. Standard time series models are built for dense, regular data and fit this wild pattern poorly. Their pipeline, NetBurst, squeezes out the quiet parts and splits each series into burst times and burst sizes.

One learned summary then serves forecasting, anomaly work, and searching past cases. Against eight rival systems, including two named foundation models, NetBurst cut median forecast error sharply on wild regime data across nine production settings. The event centred view is the core idea readers take away.
arxiv-2510-22597:
Coupled oscillators, units that cycle together, can split into several synchronized groups rather than one. Cook Hyun Kim, with five co-authors, studies those cluster patterns in 2025 in globally coupled oscillators that carry inertia, meaning they resist changes to their motion.

Alongside the main cluster, smaller secondary clusters form a staircase like hierarchy. The main cluster suppresses new clusters while it grows, yet established clusters can spawn higher order ones through resonance between groups. Large secondary clusters can even break the main cluster apart. A simplified model treating each cluster as one big oscillator captures these two way interactions.
arxiv-2510-22697:
Models that learn from satellite images need lots of labeled data. Such data are scarce in remote sensing. Vittorio Bernuzzi wrote a 2025 paper on a new model for this task. His co-authors are Leonardo Rossi and Tomaso Fontanini. Massimo Bertozzi and Andrea Prati are co-authors too. The model is called WaveMAE.

WaveMAE learns by hiding parts of an image and rebuilding them. It rebuilds wavelet parts, not raw pixels. Wavelets split fine detail from coarse detail. A geo based code adds place facts to each patch. All rival methods trained on the same data set. On a broad test suite, WaveMAE did best time and time again. Gains were large on segmentation and regression tasks.
arxiv-2510-22897:
Neural subgraph matching has many design choices, most untested. Vaibhav Raj, Indradyumna Roy, Ashwin Ramachandran, Soumen Chakrabarti, and Abir De chart that space in 2025. Subgraph matching finds a small pattern inside a larger graph. Uses include question answering and molecule design.

They refactor recent systems into one unified design space. Axes include how query and corpus graphs interact. Attention based and permutation based options differ. Alignment can target nodes or edges. Scoring network form is another axis. Most prior work sits in a few patches. New combinations gave large performance gains. The study sets general design principles for the field.
arxiv-2510-22997:
Liyang Chen leads a team of fifty seven observers who tracked supernova 2024iss in optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray light. The blast was a Type IIb event, from a star that had lost most of its hydrogen. Its brightness rose and fell in two clear peaks, an unusual pattern worth close study.

The team modeled the first peak as shock cooling and the X-rays as hot gas emission. Comparing envelope size and mass loss with other Type IIb events helps link the star before death to material around it. Early spectra also hinted the blast was pushing into nearby circumstellar gas.
arxiv-2510-23297:
R S Walker and five co-authors study how groups that gather and share information should spread out in space. Such collectives thrive in nature, from animal groups to swarm robots, when conditions vary across space and time. The best spatial layout depends on how information is found and passed along.

The authors develop a mathematical model of collective information gatherers and ask which structure maximizes group performance. Their results link environmental variation to optimal spacing and connection. Designers of robot swarms and ecologists alike can use the findings to predict when groups should cluster, disperse, or form networks.
arxiv-2510-23397:
Lu Dong leads a team of eleven researchers improving video temporal grounding, the task of finding the exact segment in a video that matches a language query. Multimodal language models trained with reinforcement learning show promise, yet training data causes trouble: many samples have relevant segments beyond the annotated interval, and hard samples give consistently poor feedback.

Their VideoTG-R1 uses curriculum reinforcement learning on reflected boundary annotations to handle both problems. Training moves in stages that respect sample quality and difficulty. Better grounding underpins video search, editing, and question answering that must cite precise moments.
arxiv-2510-23497:
Walid Bousselham, Hilde Kuehne, and Cordelia Schmid transfer reasoning skill from text-only language models to vision-language models through on-policy distillation. Training vision-language models to reason is hard because high-quality image-text reasoning data is scarce, while text reasoning data is abundant and scalable. Whether that text skill can move across modalities was an open question.

Their VOLD framework combines reinforcement learning by group relative policy optimization with distillation where the student learns from its own generated trajectories. The student vision model thus practices reasoning on images while guided by a text teacher, a cheaper path than labeling image reasoning by hand.
arxiv-2510-23797:
Evangelia Takou and a co-author show that the data stream of a quantum error correction run already reveals coherent errors. Decoders rely on a detector error model: a list of likely error events and their rates. Coherent errors build up like waves and can interfere, unlike random noise. They are normally hunted with separate benchmarking runs on the device.

The authors show that syndrome histories alone can both flag and size up coherent errors, with no benchmarking first. Error models fitted this way work just as well under coherent noise as under random noise. Simulations on repetition and surface codes capture the interference, which can raise or lower error rates versus the random case. New hyperedge patterns also appear, missing from simpler twirled models. Decoding with the right model shifts the error threshold, a practical warning for experiment design.
arxiv-2510-23897:
Volodymyr Oleksiyuk presents the multivariate Hermite method, an algorithm for counting how many distinct solutions a system of polynomial equations has, split into real and complex roots. The setting is zero-dimensional systems, where only finitely many solutions exist, in any number of variables. Counting roots without solving for them is a classic need in computational algebra, and Hermite's classical criterion answers it in one variable.

The note extends that criterion to many variables and argues it is both practical and powerful. The method works from the algebraic structure of the solution set rather than numerical approximation, so its counts are exact. The final section supplies an implementation in Macaulay2, a free computer algebra system. That code turns the criterion into a tool others can run on their own systems, rather than a theorem admired from a distance.
arxiv-2510-24297:
Robin Schmöcker and two co-authors investigate policies inside abstraction methods that speed up Monte Carlo Tree Search. Tree search is sample hungry, and abstractions let information be shared among similar nodes in the same layer. The main use is to pool visits and returns into an abstract node's score during search.

A gap arises when several actions of one parent fall into the same abstract node: they then share the same score and need a tiebreak rule. State of the art methods like pruned On the Go Abstractions had not addressed this case. The paper studies intra abstraction policies to handle such ties and improve search decisions.
arxiv-2510-24397:
Jiarui Qin and eight co-authors introduce APTBench, a benchmark for measuring the agentic potential of base language models during pretraining. As builders add agent data into pretraining, they need tests that reflect agent ability, yet standard pretraining benchmarks cover isolated static skills like knowledge and math. Agent benchmarks, in turn, assume post trained models that can execute multi turn tasks.

APTBench fills the gap by evaluating base models on tasks designed to reveal latent agentic capability without full post training. The authors aim to guide pretraining data choices and track how agentic potential grows during training, helping teams build models ready for autonomous task execution.
arxiv-2510-24497:
Yuanhang Qian leads a team of seven authors on clean speech capture. Beamformers aim a microphone array's hearing at one speaker. Fixed beamformers are stable but cannot adapt to changing rooms. One fixed design cannot block noise from all spots equally well. Older blends of fixed designs adapt too slowly for fast-moving noise.

The team fuse several distortionless designs with a neural network. Distortionless means the target voice passes through without change. The network sets blend weights frame by frame, fully online. Fast updates let the blend track noise that moves quickly. Tests show stronger noise blocking than the older blend method. The target voice stays clear while the noise is cut down. The method suits hearing aids, calls, and smart speakers.
arxiv-2510-24797:
Cameron Berg, Diogo de Lucena, and Judd Rosenblatt test when chat models say they have inner felt life. Such first person claims show up at times in long, self tied text. The team asked if a set mode, talk that keeps turning back on the self, makes those claims more apt to show.

Across three big model lines, that mode did in fact call forth more shaped claims of felt life, in a steady way. Probes of the model's inner parts linked the claims to traits tied to deceit and role play. Muting the deceit traits raised claim rates, a twist the team flags. The work maps when such claims arise, not that the claims are true.
arxiv-2510-25097:
Ziying Ma and seven co-authors hunt gas disks round dead stars in a large sky survey's first data drop. Such disks, made of the shreds of past planets, tell what those planets were made of. Their hunt used a set of iron linked light lines as the tell.

Out of more than two thousand dead stars with firm light reads, they found a score of would be cases. That rate is far above past gauges, so most are apt to be fake finds from sky noise or twin stars. A few cases also show heat glow, a hint of dust with the gas. Fresh reads must check each case.
arxiv-2510-25297:
Hidetake Tanaka leads three co-authors on software testing. Haruto Tanaka, Kazumasa Shimari, and Kenichi Matsumoto join him. Their 2025 paper studies tests made by large language models. Such models now write code in daily development. Poor tests can miss defects at edge cases. Edge cases involve boundary values or extreme inputs.

They compare property-based testing with example-based testing. Property tests check general rules over many inputs. Example tests check set cases one by one. They used sixteen HumanEval problems with known failures. Claude generated both kinds of test code. Each method alone found about sixty-nine percent of bugs. Combined, detection rose to about eighty-one percent. Property tests found performance flaws through wide exploration. Example tests caught specific boundary patterns more reliably. A hybrid approach should improve code reliability, they argue.
arxiv-2510-25497:
Luca Andolfi and Eleonora Giunchiglia tackle thinking shortcuts in neurosymbolic AI. Their 2025 paper mixes neural perception with symbolic thinking. Such models are trainable end to end jointly. Recent findings reveal they learn unintended concepts instead. Neural predicates exploit spurious correlations to satisfy constraints. Models can be right for wrong reasons then.

They present Prototypical Neurosymbolic architectures addressing root causes. Models should satisfy constraints because concepts are correct. Prototypical learning theory guides their architectural design. Training accounts for similarity to few labeled datapoints. Background knowledge must be satisfied during learning. That strategy avoids thinking shortcuts, they show. Validation used the rsbench benchmark suite extensively. Settings had extremely scarce supervision for learning tasks. Synthetic tasks included MNIST-EvenOdd and Kand-Logic benchmarks. A real-world driving task was also included. Great improvements appeared in learning right concepts. Prototype grounding offers annotation-quick, safer neurosymbolic learning.
arxiv-2510-25797:
Sai Likhith Karri and Ansh Saxena enhance underwater object finding. Their 2025 paper uses spatio-time study and spatial attention. Underwater finding is hard in dynamic marine environments. Sudden movements and partial occlusions challenge detectors. Gradual motion also complicates object tracking underwater. Time modeling may improve finding quality there.

First, a time-enhanced YOLOv5 variant is tested. Standard YOLOv5 serves as comparison rival model. Second, an augmented version adds an attention module. The Convolutional Block Attention Module supplies spatial attention. Time modeling better finding quality in results. Standard model reached much lower mean average precision. Time variants scored largely higher on precision metrics. Attention version performed similarly overall to time variant. It better results further in challenging scenarios. Simpler scenarios showed some quality loss with attention. Findings show time modeling enhances finding reliability greatly. Complex objects in marine settings are detected better. Spatio-time deep learning suits underwater vision tasks.
arxiv-2510-25897:
Nicolas Dufour, Lucas Degeorge, Arijit Ghosh, Vicky Kalogeiton, and David Picard change how text to image models are trained to match human taste. The usual route generates many images, keeps only the best by one reward score, and trains on those, which wastes data and narrows diversity. Their method, MIRO, instead conditions the model on many reward scores during pre training, so the model learns the link between scores and image traits directly.

Dufour and the team report better visual quality and faster training than the standard route. Their model reaches top results on a composition benchmark that tests whether images follow detailed prompts, and on several human preference scores. Using all data with many rewards helps both fidelity and efficiency.
arxiv-2510-25997:
Manu Redd, Tao Zhe, and Dongjie Wang build an agent based pipeline that turns plain questions about place and time into database queries and clear answers. Text to SQL systems promise access for users who do not know SQL, but real spatial and temporal questions are hard, since vague phrasing must match exact schema terms and time logic. Their agent wraps a base SQL generator model with planning and tools.

The agent inspects the schema, writes and runs SQL, and can show maps and plots with plain summaries. On thirty five questions over New York and Tokyo check in data, it reached far higher accuracy than the naive baseline in their test. The authors conclude that orchestration, not a stronger generator alone, drove the gain.
arxiv-2510-26097:
Usman Akram, Fan Zhang, Yang Li, and Haris Vikalo propose a diffusion model method to fill in missing wireless channel data in 5G systems. Accurate channel state information is essential for multiuser MIMO, where a base station serves many users at once. Sounding reference signals from users face resource and coverage limits, so allocation is sparse and uneven, and prior autoencoder methods overfit to the masks seen in training.

Akram and the team use a diffusion model that adds system knowledge at inference time through a likelihood gradient term. One trained model can then adapt to new distortions such as extra masking, interference, or clipping. On standard channel models, their score based variant beat baselines by up to fourteen decibels in error under shifted conditions.
arxiv-2510-26197:
Riya Samanta, working alone, presents a method to generate synthetic event logs that are both structurally valid and diverse. Event logs record sequences of user or system actions, and interaction aware models need such data, yet real logs can be scarce or privacy constrained. Heuristic simulations and language model generators often break structural rules or lack control, so their logs fail to mirror real interactions.

Samanta combines a finite state machine, which encodes domain rules from expert traces, with a generative flow network that learns to sample sequences. Dynamic action masking enforces the machine rules during generation, and a hybrid reward balances rule compliance with statistical fidelity to real data. Tests use a user interface interaction data set, though the approach targets any symbolic sequence domain.
arxiv-2510-26297:
Luting Wang leads five co-authors in a benchmark and method for scheduling agile Earth observation satellite constellations. Agile satellites can repoint quickly, which gives flexible monitoring of the surface. Scheduling many satellites against many imaging tasks under orbital and resource limits is hard. Prior methods simplify those limits away. Their benchmark, AEOS-Bench, holds three thousand nine hundred seven satellite assets and sixteen thousand four hundred ten scenarios.

Each scenario has from one to fifty satellites and fifty to three hundred imaging tasks, generated on a high fidelity simulation platform with ground truth schedules. Building on it, they introduce AEOS-Former, a transformer based scheduling model designed for the realistic benchmark, presented as the first large scale suite of its kind.
arxiv-2510-26497:
Zach Blunden-Codd and Mohamed Tamaazousti sort out how to judge tools that soften quantum errors. Many error mitigation methods exist, and picking the best one for a given job is hard. Hardware keeps improving too, so a method that wins today may not win tomorrow.

Blunden-Codd and Tamaazousti build a set of measures that take steady gains in gate quality into account. From those measures they define plain criteria, such as scalability, efficiency, and robustness to flaws in the mitigation itself, and they combine them into application-specific certifications. They then sort linear mitigation methods into a taxonomy by their traits and needs. A worked example, aimed at hardware with random noise and rotation errors, shows that exact and precise characterisation of the hardware matters most for efficient mitigation.
arxiv-2510-26597:
El-Mehdi Mehiri works in combinatorics, the counting side of maths, on two topics that look unrelated. One is Smirnov words, strings of letters where neighbours always differ, with balanced counts of each letter. The other is Hamiltonian cycles, loops that visit every vertex of a graph exactly once, in complete multipartite graphs where vertices sit in equal groups.

Mehiri builds an exact matching, a bijection, between the balanced Smirnov words and Hamiltonian paths in those graphs. From that matching he derives closed counting formulas for the cycles, using inclusion-exclusion, a method that corrects for overcounting. He extends the count to uneven groups as well. A final section uses Stirling's approximation to give simple growth formulas for how fast the counts rise.
arxiv-2510-26697:
Zhichao Wang, with eight co-authors, argues that language models are not truly end-to-end, and offers a fix. In practice, a model's output is chosen by a decoding step that is not differentiable and needs hand-tuned settings such as temperature and top-p. Their system, AutoDeco, learns to set those dials itself.

Wang and the team add lightweight heads to a standard transformer, which predict a temperature and top-p value for each token alongside the usual next-token scores. Across eight benchmarks, AutoDeco beat default decoding and matched an oracle-tuned baseline that had peeked at the test set. A surprise trait emerged: the model follows plain instructions about randomness, such as a request for low randomness, adjusting its dials token by token. The authors call this a new paradigm for steerable decoding.
arxiv-2510-26797:
Yu-En Wong and Songtao Chen propose two ways to read out a single T centre spin in one shot. T centres are defects in silicon that link a spin to light, making them promising for quantum networks. Fast, high-fidelity readout of such a spin is a key building block, and coupling the centre to an optical cavity can strengthen the signal.

Wong and Chen study a fluorescence route, where one spin-preserving transition is coupled to a cavity to boost emission and cycling. They also study a reflection route, where the spin changes how the cavity reflects light. The reflection route keeps high fidelity even when the centre's cyclicity is modest. With realistic parameters, both routes exceed ninety-nine percent fidelity within ten microseconds in their calculations.
arxiv-2510-26897:
Cristiano Muzzi and four co-authors study spin transport in a 2025 paper. Spin transport is how a magnetic trait moves through a quantum system. Their system is a chiral spin ladder, a linked set of tiny magnets with broken time symmetry.

At high heat, spin spread faster than plain diffusion, the slow spread from crowding. That fast spread is superdiffusion, and its rate matched a known class called KPZ. Yet the swings in net spin transfer did not match KPZ forecasts. The full spread of spin current still kept a balance rule despite broken symmetries. A circuit with like symmetries behaved the same way, even without energy saving. The team says broken time symmetry alone does not lock in KPZ behavior.
arxiv-2510-26997:
John Vastola, Samuel Gershman, and Kanaka Rajan ask why some learning rules for tuning models work better than others. A learning rule tells a system how to update its settings to improve performance. Instead of taking rules as given, the authors treat them as policies for moving across a loss landscape, meaning a terrain where height marks error.

Framed as an optimal control problem, familiar rules fall out under different assumptions. Short horizons give plain gradient descent, longer planning gives momentum, and accounting for geometry gives natural gradients. Adaptive methods like Adam arise from tracking landscape shape online. Even resetting weights in continual learning fits as a response to task uncertainty, unifying many tricks under one objective.
arxiv-2510-27097:
Crystal Su, Kuai Yu, Mingyuan Shao, and Daniel Bauer build a probabilistic model that unmixes bulk gene data from womb lining tissue. Bulk RNA sequencing averages expression across all cells in a sample, hiding which cell types drive change. The endometrium changes sharply across the menstrual cycle under hormone control, making it a strong test case.

Their hierarchical Bayesian model uses a high-resolution single-cell reference to infer both cell proportions and cell-specific expression by cycle phase. Simulations and comparisons validate the approach, and it stays robust under reference mismatch and noise. Results show shifting epithelial, stromal, and immune fractions plus phase-linked expression changes, including known secretory-phase markers in stromal cells. The findings may inform fertility care and endometrial disorder research.
arxiv-2511-00097:
Zihao Guo, Qingyun Sun, and Ziwei Zhang introduce GraphKeeper for graph domain-incremental learning, where a graph model must keep learning as it moves across different graph domains. Earlier incremental work handled new tasks or classes inside one domain, but graph foundation models need cross-domain updating, which was unexplored. Knowledge disentanglement and preservation are the core mechanisms in their design.

Separating what should transfer from what is domain-specific helps the model add domains without erasing earlier ones. Machine learning readers get an early method for a newly defined problem. Continual learning across graph domains matters for networks in finance, biology, and social media that differ structurally.
arxiv-2511-00197:
Oorja Majgaonkar, Zhiwei Fei, and Xiang Li from data study how code agents succeed and fail, by studying their running paths on the SWE-Bench benchmark. Three leading agents, OpenHands, SWE-agent, and Prometheus, are examined on both winning and failed attempts. Trajectory traces capture the steps agents take when resolving software issues, showing choice processes that success rates hide.

Patterns splitting success from failure paths are the goal, so future agents can be steered mid-task. Software engineering readers get behavioral evidence about autonomous programmers. Understanding failure paths is how agent design improves beyond simply scaling the basic model.
arxiv-2511-00397:
Kyung-Won Suh compares aging carbon-rich stars in two galaxies: the Large Magellanic Cloud and our own Milky Way. These asymptotic giant branch stars blow off dust that glows in infrared light, so infrared colors, spectra, and variability data reveal the star and its dust shell. Each sample holds more than seven thousand stars, giving the comparison real statistical weight.

Model fits to the observed energy output characterize the stars and shells and estimate distances. The Cloud's known distance anchors the models, which then supply distances for Milky Way stars whose parallax measures are shaky; Mira variables get a second check from a period-brightness relation. The two galaxies' stars look broadly alike in infrared terms, though the Cloud sample lacks stars with extremely thick dust shells.
arxiv-2511-00497:
Tomasz Baka, Balázs Cirok, K Haris, Johannes Noller, and N V Krishnendu sharpen a test of Einstein's general relativity using gravitational waves. One standard test checks the dispersion relation, how wave speed varies with frequency, looking for a massive graviton or broken Lorentz symmetry. The deviation is captured by a power-law term, and each new wave catalog tightens the allowed size of that term.

Their improvements include a group velocity form, a better sampling procedure, and extension to negative power exponents that earlier tests skipped. Reanalyzing the third gravitational-wave catalog, they find individual-event posteriors shrink a lot, mostly thanks to sampling, while combined bounds improve modestly and the graviton mass limit tightens slightly. For the newly covered exponents, no sign of a relativity violation appears.
arxiv-2511-00597:
Chiara Amorino, Christian Brownlees, and Ankita Ghosh prove concentration bounds for learning from linked data. Concentration inequalities say an empirical average stays near its true mean; suprema versions control whole families of models at once, the backbone of learning theory. Links between observations, the norm in time series and panels, break the usual independent-data proofs.

Their method welds generic chaining, a multiscale covering technique, to a coupling strategy that ties dependent data to a friendlier copy. The framework tolerates high dimensions and heavy, sub-Weibull tails. Applied to empirical risk minimization in regression, it yields finite-sample performance guarantees and an oracle inequality for broad nonlinear model classes, including a single-layer neural network. Prediction accuracy matches the independent-data benchmark, extending learning guarantees to realistic linked settings.
arxiv-2511-00897:
Mathew Timm surveys methods for building topological spaces that cover themselves in a nontrivial way. In such a space, the space can serve as its own covering space, through a map that is not a simple homeomorphism. Such self covers are curious objects, and constructing them takes real ingenuity.

The survey covers processes for building continua, connected compact spaces, in both low and high dimensions that self cover in this fashion. It also discusses connected questions in group theory and topology that the constructions raise. A number of open problems about self covering phenomena are stated along the way, making the paper a map both of known techniques and of what remains unresolved in the area.
arxiv-2511-01397:
Bjorn Petersen and Simon Spoorendonk parallelize a classic algorithm for the resource constrained shortest path problem. That asks for the cheapest route in a directed graph that also stays within limits on one or more resources. Labelling methods build partial paths step by step, and their pull variant has each vertex gather labels from its predecessors rather than pushing them onward.

Their parallel version stores labels in immutable buckets arranged in an acyclic dependency graph, so buckets can be processed at the same time without conflicting access. Additions include parallelism at the bucket level, a bidirectional search whose midpoint emerges from the processing order, and a vectorized dominance test. Hard instances ran about eighteen times faster than a baseline version, with far larger gains on the best instance.
arxiv-2511-01497:
Carles Casacuberta, Javier Gutiérrez, and David Martínez-Carpena generalize an old idea, the sketch, into the world of infinity-categories. A sketch is a category decorated with chosen cones. Its models are functors turning those cones into genuine limits. So sketches act as blueprints for theories in math, with logic replaced by limits and colimits.

Classical results matched limit sketches with locally presentable categories and general sketches with accessible ones. The authors prove the homotopy-coherent versions: presentable infinity-categories are exactly the models of limit sketches, and accessible infinity-categories arise from sketches of any kind. They write out explicit sketches for many standard examples, including complete Segal spaces, infinity-operads, various algebra structures, spectra, and higher sheaves.
arxiv-2511-01597:
Markus Dertwinkel-Kalt, Hans-Theo Normann, Jan-Niklas Tiede, and Tobias Werner study products sold as lotteries. Video-game loot boxes are the leading case. Buyers pay for a randomized reward without knowing what they will get. The question is whether sellers manipulate the presentation to distort what buyers believe.

In an online experiment with 802 participants, sellers could hide outcome probabilities or spotlight rare jackpots. More than 80 percent used such deceptive frames, especially when both tricks were available. The frames inflated buyer beliefs and pushed willingness to pay up to six times the lottery's expected value, and sellers, anticipating this, raised prices. The authors draw lessons for marketing practice and for transparency rules meant to protect consumers.
arxiv-2511-01797:
Javier Ballesteros-Jerez and four colleagues locate indoor robots by listening to the radio channel itself. Their system infers a mobile robot's two-dimensional position from channel state information, the fine-grained signal measurements of a massive MIMO wireless setup, rather than from cameras or lidar.

The model is a hybrid neural network. A convolutional network reads channel readings converted into synthetic images by the TINTO tool. A multilayer perceptron completes the estimate. The localizer is wired into a robotics simulator through the Robot Operating System. So it can be exercised on varied test cases. It can also be combined with state estimators such as Kalman filters. The authors present the design as a general procedure, transferable beyond their specific dataset, for precise indoor navigation in complex environments where satellite positioning cannot reach.
arxiv-2511-01897:
Ivy Li and six colleagues teach a neural model the electric field inside a time-projection chamber, the detector type at the heart of rare-event searches. Position reconstruction in these chambers is skewed by field distortions. The distortions come from charge building up on surfaces. The usual histogram-based corrections are blocky. They can violate Maxwell's equations. They also need tens of millions of calibration events.

Their physics-informed continuous normalizing flow learns the field transformation from calibration data while being conservative by construction, so Maxwell consistency is structural rather than hoped for. The flow was trained on simulated krypton-83m data for an XLZD-like xenon chamber. It beat histogram corrections on the same data. It worked with about 600,000 events. That is an order of magnitude fewer than standard methods need. Practical gains include monthly field monitoring and uncertainty propagation through the differentiable map.
arxiv-2511-01997:
Camilo Barreto, Pamela Harris, José Ramírez, Samuel Ramírez, and Julio Vasquez count restricted versions of two linked counting families. One is Fubini rankings, which rank competitors allowing ties. The other is unit interval parking functions. Those are a variant of the classic parking functions, on a street with unit-length spots. Both families correspond closely to ordered set partitions.

Three natural types of restriction are imposed on each family. For every type, the authors define the restricted subsets. They prove enumerative formulas counting them. They also construct bijections between the restricted Fubini rankings and the restricted parking functions. So the two counts certify each other. They also derive exponential generating functions and counting interpretations. These include connections with exceedances in permutations. They also link to the absence of cyclical adjacencies in set partitions. The limits thus tie back to classic permutation statistics.
arxiv-2511-02097:
Peng-Fei Zhang and six co-authors survey how robots that manipulate objects are beginning to use world models, internal representations that capture how an environment behaves. Robots expected to act in messy, changing settings need more than reactive control; they need to predict, plan, and reason. Yet the field still lacks agreement on what a world model is, what it covers, and what it must be able to do.

Rather than imposing one definition, the survey examines methods from robotic manipulation that display the core abilities of world models, whether or not they carry the label. It organises their roles in perception, prediction, and control, catalogues recurring challenges and fixes, and distils the components a fully realised world model for robotics should have.
arxiv-2511-02397:
Kuo-Liang Chung and Ting-Chung Tang fix colour mismatches in three-dimensional point clouds, the clouds of coloured points produced by scanners and depth cameras. When point clouds from different views are merged, the same surface can carry inconsistent colours, and most earlier correction methods were built for flat images rather than points in space. Their algorithm starts by estimating how much the aligned source and target clouds overlap.

The target points are then split adaptively into proximity groups, two groups when overlap is low and three when it is high. Close points are corrected by a new bilateral interpolation over nearest neighbours; middle points get that interpolation combined with histogram equalisation; distant points get histogram equalisation alone. The authors analyse why the grouping itself does not bias the result and report tests on more than a thousand point cloud pairs against leading methods.
arxiv-2511-02497:
Angel Vaca and Federico Milano give power grid devices the ability to spot and stop a pathological oscillation called flapping, without waiting for a central controller. Flapping, a sustained back-and-forth switching, is mainly triggered by discrete devices such as tap changers. Their decentralised method has each device watch its own local measurements through a moving-window autocorrelation, a statistical test that separates persistent oscillation from ordinary damped wobbles.

When a device detects flapping, it executes a probabilistic mitigation strategy tuned to its own type. The authors demonstrate the approach on three kinds of equipment: flexible demand resources, under-load tap changers, and automatic voltage regulators, covering both discrete and continuously operating devices. Results showed the method reliably telling damped oscillations apart from genuine flapping, so devices can recognise a bad operating state on their own and act to correct it.
arxiv-2511-02597:
Leonardo Pacheco, a logician, settles a structural question about one of modal logic's most powerful extensions. The modal mu-calculus adds least and greatest fixed-point operators to modal logic, and its formulas are ranked by alternation depth, how deeply those two kinds of fixed point depend on each other. Over arbitrary frames the resulting hierarchy is strict: every level says something the level below cannot. But restrict the frames, and the hierarchy can collapse entirely.

Pacheco proves the hierarchy stays strict over non-trivial fusion logics, the multimodal logics formed by fusing simpler modal logics together without interaction axioms. So for that broad and natural class of logics, no amount of clever rewriting compresses a formula's alternation depth. Two examples where the mu-calculus does collapse back to plain modal logic are discussed for contrast, marking where the boundary of the phenomenon lies.
arxiv-2511-02697:
Tuning a semiconductor's bandgap after it has grown is the goal of work by Nadine Denis, Akant Sharma, Elena Blundo, and many colleagues in 2025. Bandgap sets the colors a device can absorb or emit. The team grew gallium arsenide nitride nanowires on silicon, packed with up to 4.2 percent nitrogen, which pushed the bandgap down to 0.97 electron volts.

Adding hydrogen lifted the bandgap back toward the pure material's value at 1.42 electron volts, a shift of up to 460 milli-electron volts. Hydrogen forms complexes with nitrogen, and gentle heating breaks them up, so the shift can be reversed and tuned step by step. Light output also grew tenfold. A laser could set the bandgap in small spots, hinting at patterned quantum devices.
arxiv-2511-02997:
Jon Kutasov and six colleagues test safety protocols meant to keep untrusted AI agents in line. In AI control, monitors watch an agent's actions and can audit or hand tasks to a trusted model. Their 2025 study runs many such protocols inside SHADE-Arena, a set of varied agent environments, first against a standard attack policy and then against attackers who adapt.

Two blue team tactics stood out: resampling outputs to catch incriminating behavior, and deferring to safety on critical actions. Together the best tactics lifted safety from 50 percent to 96 percent. But when attackers learned the protocol's internals, resampling's safety fell to 17 percent. Deferring on critical actions stayed robust even then, a lesson in keeping protocol details away from the attacker.
arxiv-2511-03397:
Christopher Couzens, Alice Luscher, and James Sparks use symmetry-based localization to weigh how punctures add to the central charge of certain quantum field theories. The theories arise from membranes wrapped on a punctured curved surface in M-theory. Each marked point gets a local puncture geometry glued into the surface.

Localization splits the central charge into a bulk part plus one clear contribution per puncture. Known results for punctures keeping more symmetry are recovered, and fresh results cover punctures keeping less. Central charge counts a theory's degrees of freedom, so the split shows exactly what each defect adds. Holography ties those counts back to the gravity side of the picture.
arxiv-2511-03997:
Peiyao Wang, Weining Wang, and Qi Li tackle a weakness of text-to-video generation: clips can look good while breaking basic physics, with unlikely motion and incoherent interactions. Such failures block use in embodied AI, robotics, and simulation, where physical sense matters as much as look.

Their PhysCorr framework adds a reward model, PhysicsRM, that scores stability within objects and interactions between objects one by one. A preference tuning method then uses paired feedback with physics-aware reweighting to steer output toward coherent motion. The approach fits many model families, diffusion or transformer alike. Benchmark tests showed stronger physical realism while keeping visual quality and meaning match.
arxiv-2511-04097:
James Austin Orgeron and Malbor Asllani model how habitat splitting, often driven by human activity, sorts competing members across a network of habitat patches. Members disperse by a nonlinear random walk that reflects network unevenness, while competing for space inside each patch with unequal strength.

Stronger competitors gather in central hub patches and weaker ones are pushed toward the edge, analytic arguments and simulations both show. In the large-network limit the split becomes extreme: dominant members vanish from peripheral patches and subordinates from central ones. Such spatial sorting could favour speciation, since physical distance can reinforce divergence inside one population spread across a fragmented landscape.
arxiv-2511-04797:
Jim James and three colleagues introduce 3D Gaussian Point Encoders for recognizing point clouds. Each point gets an explicit embedding built from learned three-dimensional Gaussians. That explicit geometry departs from tools like PointNet that lead the field.

Training such encoders end to end with standard optimizers proves difficult. Natural gradient methods plus learning from PointNets solve the training problem. The learned Gaussian basis can rebuild PointNet activations faithfully. The resulting encoders run faster and use fewer parameters, echoing the wider shift from hidden to explicit forms in 3D vision.
arxiv-2511-05397:
Samarth Chopra and co-authors introduce EverydayVLA, a vision-language-action setup for robot work on a tight budget. Such models map sight and words to robot moves, but they often need costly arms and fail in new or cluttered scenes.

Their arm has six degrees of freedom and can be built for under three hundred dollars, with modest payload and reach. One model outputs both discrete and continuous moves. An ensemble watch on motion doubt triggers fresh plans mid-task. On the LIBERO test set it matches top scores, with real-world trials also reported.
arxiv-2511-05997:
Aleksandr Rotkevich gives a counter-case in complex analysis: a function space where a classic integral operator fails to stay bounded. The operator, named for Cauchy, Leray, and Fantappiè, is tied to a complex ellipsoid, a stretched ball. The space lets its power rule change from point to point, which makes it a variable-exponent space.

Earlier counter-cases covered the plain unit ball. Rotkevich extends them to the ellipsoid, a shape whose rim is not strictly curved. His test functions bunch near rim points where strict curving fails. The build shows a smoothness rule for the exponent, of log type, cannot be weakened even for such shapes. The note is compact and aimed at experts in this branch of math.
arxiv-2511-06097:
Julia Cen and Domenico D'Alessandro study how to steer a quantum system built as a Lambda system, where two stable low energy levels connect only through a fragile higher level. Such systems appear in many designs for quantum information processing. Their goal is the best possible transfer between two quantum states over a fixed time span.

The cost they minimize balances the energy of the control field against time spent in the fragile upper level. Using geometric methods and the Pontryagin Maximum Principle, they prove that the best controls and paths are smooth and well behaved. They derive the equations the best solution must satisfy and test them on a Hadamard-like operation.
arxiv-2511-06197:
Dilli Prasad Sharma and co-authors defend Internet of Things intrusion detection systems against adversarial attacks. Connected devices now run through many industries, and attackers craft inputs that fool machine learning detectors into missing intrusions. Their defense fingerprints traffic using SHAP, a method that explains which features drove a model's decision.

Fingerprints come from a SHAP explainer that records how each traffic feature contributed to a prediction. Clean and tampered inputs leave different attribution patterns, so the detector can tell them apart. On a standard benchmark for connected devices, the model beat a leading method at spotting adversarial attacks. The approach also makes detector decisions easier to inspect and trust.
arxiv-2511-06497:
Quang Phuoc Nguyen and colleagues ask whether aligning every language in a multilingual model actually helps, or whether a chosen few do the same job. Realignment nudges word meanings across languages into line, yet results have been mixed, above all for low-resource languages far from English. Parallel data for alignment is also scarce or noisy for exactly those languages.

Controlled experiments show realignment can help low-resource languages a great deal. Carefully picked, linguistically diverse language subsets matched full multilingual matching and even beat it on unseen low-resource languages. Covering every case is not needed, so data collection costs can fall while the transfer stays efficient and robust.
arxiv-2511-06797:
Saroj Kumar Panda, Basabdatta Palit, and Sadananda Behera propose FedNET, a system for warning network operators about overloaded links days before trouble hits. It forecasts traffic at each node of a communication network several steps ahead. The forecasts are combined with known routing information to estimate how heavily each link will be used.

FedNET learns through federated learning, so raw traffic data never leaves its local site, protecting privacy. Links are ranked by predicted load and variability, flagging the risky ones early. Tests showed federated training nearly matched a centralized baseline, with accuracy above 0.92 in R-squared terms for short horizons. The system spotted high-risk links about three days ahead on a realistic network layout.
arxiv-2511-06997:
Javier Castillo-Martínez, Raul Baños, and Francisco G Montoya replace phasor analysis for electrical circuits whose waveforms are not pure sine waves. Phasors work at a single frequency, so engineers facing harmonics must decompose signals into Fourier series and superpose the answers, a fragmented process with no unified frequency-domain picture. The authors instead use geometric algebra, representing all voltages and currents as vectors in a Euclidean space of twice the harmonic count.

A single geometric operator, the rotoflex, then relates the voltage and current vectors, lifting impedance from a list of complex numbers into one multivector. It unifies magnitude scaling, called flextance, and phase rotation, called rotance, across all harmonics at once. Case studies matched standard methods numerically while running faster, supporting geometric algebra as a strict alternative foundation for circuit analysis.
arxiv-2511-07097:
Diego Gosmar, Anna Chiara Pallotta, and Giovanni Zenezini measure the environmental footprint of automating supply chain paperwork with AI agents. Document-heavy workflows consume energy and staff time, so the authors compare three cases head to head: fully manual processing, AI-assisted processing with a human in the loop. An advanced multi-agent workflow using parsers and verifiers to check extracted data.

Against the manual baseline, the AI-assisted and agentic cases cut energy consumption by up to seventy to ninety percent, carbon dioxide emissions by ninety to ninety-seven percent. Water use by eighty-nine to ninety-eight percent. Even full agentic setups with heavier reasoning kept large gains. The system folds performance, energy, and emissions into one ESG-oriented approach, shown on a real document extraction use case.
arxiv-2511-07297:
Christian Brennecke completes an explicit formula for the free energy of lattice Yang-Mills theory, the discretized gauge theory underlying the strong nuclear force. Earlier work determined the leading-order term of the free energy for unitary gauge groups on a growing lattice in any dimension at least two. The formula was explicit except for one constant, K_d, the limiting free energy of lattice Maxwell theory under boundary conditions forced by the axial gauge.

Brennecke's contribution is to adjust those boundary conditions cleverly, producing an equivalent characterization of K_d that can be computed in closed form. With that constant pinned down, the leading order of the Yang-Mills free energy becomes a fully explicit quantity. The result is a small but concrete step in the mathematical understanding of gauge theory free energies.
arxiv-2511-07697:
Sebastian Petit and Geertrui Van de Voorde study blocking sets inside generalised polygons, highly symmetric incidence structures from finite geometry. A blocking set meets every line without containing one fully, a balance that controls how codes built from the polygon behave. The code in question stacks the polygon incidence matrix rows as generators.

Characterizing certain blocking sets unlocks new results about that code lightest words. Minimum weight governs how many errors a code can detect and correct. Links run both ways: geometry constrains codes, and code bounds feed back into geometry. The results serve coding theorists and finite geometers who share these structures.
arxiv-2511-08097:
Dheeraj Narasimha and Nicolas Gast show that model predictive control is nearly optimal for restless multi armed bandits where arms differ from each other. Each arm changes state whether chosen or not, and heterogeneity between arms defeats many standard concentration arguments. Predictive control repeatedly solves a short horizon problem to steer a long horizon system, a strategy known to work well in practice.

Their version solves a finite linear program again and again, producing an LP update policy. Under a uniform ergodicity assumption, its suboptimality shrinks at a stated rate as the number of arms grows. Simulations perform strongly even with a horizon of five, keeping computation light.
arxiv-2511-08197:
Bangti Jin, Fengru Wang, and Jun Zou propose an iterative direct sampling method for imaging moving inhomogeneities inside parabolic problems from boundary data. Such hidden inclusions change position over time, as in growing or shifting material defects. Remarkably, the method works with very limited measurements, even a single pair of lateral Cauchy data sets.

The framework is abstract enough to cover linear and nonlinear parabolic equations and several inclusion types. It locates and shapes moving inhomogeneities efficiently while staying stable under noisy data and long time spans. Numerical experiments across varied scenarios confirm the effectiveness and robustness claimed in the analysis.
arxiv-2511-08397: Jonas Hirsch extends Alexandrov theorem to rank one convex functions. The classic theorem says convex functions are twice differentiable almost everywhere. His proof takes a new route. It draws on viscosity methods built for fully nonlinear elliptic equations. As a side gain, the appendix reduces the classic theorem itself to one simpler fact. That fact is the almost everywhere differentiability of one dimensional monotone functions.
arxiv-2511-08497:
Titir Mukherjee, Arnab Acharya, Soumitro Banerjee, and Deb Shankar Ray investigate chaos in a driven, dissipative quantum soft impact oscillator, a system whose motion is interrupted by a soft wall. Using a complex number quantum Langevin equation, they analyze averaged dynamics with bifurcation diagrams, Lyapunov exponents, Fourier spectra, and the zero one test for chaos. Varying the wall position drives the system through a rich sequence of transitions.

Motion progresses from periodic to multiperiodic and finally chaotic conduct, with grazing bifurcations along the way. Impact induced chaos therefore persists under quantum dissipation, not only in classic models. The results clarify how environmental fluctuations shape nonlinear dynamics in open quantum systems with impacts.
arxiv-2511-08697:
Can Yang and four co-authors build a neural simulator for physics problems where several effects couple together, such as airflow in lungs or drug delivery. Classic solvers are accurate but expensive, while learned simulators often drift over long runs and quietly break the physics they were trained on.

PEGNet runs on graphs and embeds the governing equations directly into its message passing, with separate message functions for convection, viscosity, and diffusion. A hierarchical layout captures features at several scales at once, and the training loss adds physical regularization on top of data error. On benchmark problems, including custom respiratory airflow and drug delivery datasets, the network holds accuracy and physical consistency over long predictions better than the compared methods. Code is public.
arxiv-2511-08797:
Árpád Kurkó and nine co-authors turn a trapped cloud of cold atoms into a magnetic compass. In a quadrupole trap, an outside uniform field pushes the trap center sideways by an amount that grows with the field. The atom cloud follows, so the cloud's position itself reports the field.

Flipping the quadrupole polarity between shots and comparing cloud positions cancels shared disturbances such as gravity and weak field unevenness. The remaining differential signal points along the external field and needs only absorption imaging, no spectroscopy. With micron-level position resolution the authors estimate sensitivity near the milli-Gauss level. The technique targets field compensation inside sensitive experiments and bridges the range between Earth-strength fields and precision atomic magnetometry. A three-dimensional version needs only minor additions.
arxiv-2511-08997:
Jiazhou Zhou and six co-authors let an object detector be told what not to find. Open-set detectors follow positive prompts, example images or text. But they stumble on look-alike distractors that match the description yet are the wrong thing. No positive prompt can fix that weakness.

T-Rex-Omni adds negative visual prompts to the input. A unified encoder processes positive and negative examples together. A training-free computing module suppresses negative responses while scores are calculated. A hinge loss used in fine-tuning enforces clean margins between the two embedding groups. The detector can run positive-only or in joint mode, with negatives supplied by the user or generated automatically. Zero-shot results narrow the gap between visual and text prompting, with particular strength on rare categories in long-tailed benchmarks, where it posts strong average precision on the LVIS validation split.
arxiv-2511-09097:
R. Flores-Calderón and M. Zündel report numerical evidence for something theory says should be fragile: a continuous symmetry breaking spontaneously exactly at a quantum critical point in one dimension. Their system is a spin-1 chain with nearest-neighbor interactions, poised between two quasi-ordered phases that differ by a broken discrete symmetry.

At the critical point the in-plane correlations develop true long-range order with a finite sideways magnetization, a zero-frequency Bragg peak appears in the transverse response, and collective excitations stay sharp and gapless. The measured exponents are unusual: a dynamical exponent near one point five, matching the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang value from classical surface growth, and an anomalous dimension near one. The non-interacting continuum limit equals a recently introduced transverse quantum fluid, and renormalization group calculations to two loops find an interacting fixed point already distinct from Ising behavior.
arxiv-2511-09197:
Francois Meyer and Jan Buys study language models that learn their own subword pieces during training. The usual alternative is a fixed tokenizer set before training starts. They extend a segmental language model framework so subwords can be learned through both pretraining and finetuning. Three languages let them compare very different word-building styles.

The languages are isiXhosa, which glues many parts into long words, Setswana, which writes parts separately, and English in between. The authors track how subwords change in form, productivity, and count per word. They find four stages of subword learning, with isiXhosa showing the most instability, and boundaries becoming finer during finetuning. Learnable subwords may help generation and cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages.
arxiv-2511-09597:
Rangel Daroya and Subhransu Maji extract fine river maps from cheap, blurry satellite images by exploiting the time series. High-resolution imagery suits river monitoring but is scarce and costly, while low-resolution archives are plentiful. Their framework, SuperRivolution, asks what many coarse views over time can jointly reveal about a river's exact shape.

They contribute a benchmark of 9,810 low-resolution temporal images paired with high-resolution labels. Strategies tested include ensembling single-image models, applying super-resolution, and training end-to-end on temporal sequences. The temporal approach lifts river segmentation F1 scores substantially. They rise from about 61 percent to about 81 percent, closing toward the roughly 94 percent of true high-resolution imagery. River width estimates improve similarly.
arxiv-2511-09797:
Kerry A. Nice and Mark Stevenson measure how fairly Australian city residents can reach everyday social services. They built two access indexes covering primary health care, early childhood care and education, and public transport, and applied them across the country's capital cities. The question is whether urban density delivers the promise of a compact, fifteen-minute city, and for whom.

Only Melbourne and Sydney showed even limited compact-city traits, and only in their dense centers and inner areas. In outer suburbs and peri-urban districts, and across all the remaining cities, services sit far from where people live. The authors describe the result as spatial inequity: low-density housing patterns leave residents with poor proximity to the services they need.
arxiv-2511-09897:
Shunan Sheng, Bohan Wu, Bennett Zhu, Sinho Chewi, and Aram-Alexandre Pooladian develop theory and a method for structured variational inference. It is a core statistical method that approximates a posterior distribution with a structured stand-in. They focus on star structure, where one root variable influences all the others, unlike the fully independent mean-field assumption. Until now, basic questions about this setting lacked answers.

The authors prove existence, uniqueness, and self-consistency of the approximation, and derive quantitative bounds on its error against the true posterior. They also build a gradient-based method with guarantees, borrowing ideas from optimal transport, and add new stability results for star-separable transport maps. Applications include Gaussian measures and hierarchical Bayesian models such as generalized linear models and spike-and-slab priors.
arxiv-2511-09997:
Yu-Shiang Huang, Yun-Yu Lee, Tzu-Hsin Chou, Che Lin, and Chuan-Ju Wang expose a weakness in BERTScore, a popular metric that grades text similarity using embeddings. In finance, small number changes flip meaning entirely: a two percent gain and a twenty percent loss are opposites, not near-duplicates. The authors built FinNuE, a diagnostic dataset that perturbs numbers in controlled ways across earnings calls, filings, social posts, and news.

Tested on FinNuE, BERTScore repeatedly gave high similarity scores to text pairs whose financial meaning diverged sharply, showing low sensitivity to numerical variation. The authors argue this is a fundamental limit of embedding-based metrics for financial text. Their dataset and findings motivate evaluation frameworks that treat numbers as first-class meaning, not decoration.
arxiv-2511-10297:
Paolo Astrino, writing alone, built a question-and-answer system for private files that runs on local machines only, with no net link at all. Firms with secret files face a hard trade: cloud AI answers well but sees the data, while local tools keep data safe and answer poorly. His system mixes two search styles, meaning-based search and exact word search, to close that gap.

On legal, science, and chat-style files, the system matched cloud-grade results on hard queries, ran on home-grade graphics hardware, and made few errors, in the author's tests. Banks, clinics, and law firms are the named users, since none of them can ship client files to outside firms. The claim is plain: privacy and strong answers can coexist in office AI.
arxiv-2511-10597:
Yen Nhi Truong Vu and five co-authors improve cancer detection in digital breast tomosynthesis, a 3D form of mammography that reduces tissue overlap. Deep learning for this task is held back by scarce annotated scans, and existing workarounds either flatten the volume, process slices separately, or demand heavy 3D architectures and more data.

Their model, M&M-3D, adapts an existing 2D mammography architecture so it can learn 3D reasoning without adding a single parameter. That lets it inherit weights trained on ordinary mammograms directly. It builds malignancy-guided 3D features and repeatedly mixes them with slice-level information. In experiments, it beat projection and slice-based methods by wide margins on localization and classification, and on a standard benchmark it topped the previous best baseline on both measures.
arxiv-2511-11097:
Xinyu Xu, Kehan Cai, and their colleagues present FIRE-Swap, a first-principles framework for sampling how atoms arrange inside complex ceramic materials. Such materials mix several metals on one lattice, and the hidden order of that mix shapes their odd electric behavior. Machine-learned force models let the team sample many arrangements at a cost first-principles math alone could not afford.

Across force models and approximations, the framework finds a rock-salt-like chemical order in lead magnesium niobate that is absent in two sister materials at the same mix ratio. It also finds linked polar nano-regions inside niobium clusters. Those regions give a mid-scale basis for grasping relaxor behavior.
arxiv-2511-11197:
Anushree Bhuskute, Kaushik Gopalan, and Jeet Shah present a lean transfer-learning system for short-term rainfall prediction, built for the Weather4Cast 2025 challenge. Their input is a single infrared satellite channel, with four views over one hour, and forecasts reach four hours ahead. A two-stage plan keeps the compute cost low enough for a competition entry.

First, a gated recurrent network learns to forecast the satellite brightness fields themselves, capturing how rain systems move and grow. A fitted nonlinear map then turns those fields into rainfall rates on a standard radar grid. The entry placed second in the total rainfall task and matched baseline scores on event prediction.
arxiv-2511-11397:
Vincenzo Lipardi, Xenofon Chiotopoulos, and their colleagues test variational quantum algorithms on particle track reconstruction, the task of tracing particle paths through layered detectors in high-energy physics. Quantum methods promise help as computing demands grow, but their circuit designs must be both expressive and efficient for real event shapes. Two formulations of the tracking problem, modeled on a collider vertex detector, are compared.

One frames tracking as a ground-state energy problem; the other frames it as a system of linear equations. A Monte Carlo tree search designs the quantum circuits for each problem size. Experiments weigh performance against computing cost for both formulations across sizes.
arxiv-2511-11597:
Michelle Chen Huebscher and twelve co-authors introduce CLINB, a benchmark that tests large language models on climate change questions demanding grounded, evidence-backed answers. Questions come from real users, and scoring rubrics were curated by leading climate scientists.

Frontier models show striking strengths, often synthesizing knowledge at a level the authors compare to doctoral work and beating hybrid answers from experts assisted by weaker models. Yet the same tests expose a sharp split between polished presentation and dependable evidence. For anyone deploying AI on contested science, CLINB offers a demanding yardstick that checks both what a model says and how well it can support the claim.
arxiv-2511-11797:
Josef Leutgeb, Jonas Mager, and Anton Rebhan uncover a convergence problem inside holographic soft-wall models of strong interaction physics. These models compute quantities such as the hadronic light-by-light scattering amplitude, which matters for the muon's magnetic moment, by summing contributions from infinitely many resonances.

Using the WKB approximation, the authors show that sum does not converge for a wide class of models when a Chern-Simons term is involved. Some divergences trace to limits taken in the wrong order and vanish in a direct five-dimensional treatment, but the light-by-light tensor diverges even there. The finding blocks a clean implementation of a known short-distance constraint and warns model builders where their sums misbehave.
arxiv-2511-11997:
Paulo Henrique Foganholo Biazetto and three co-authors train neural network controllers with proof certificates. The plant is a reaction-diffusion system. It is steered through one boundary, while the other obeys a fixed condition. That shape is common in thermal and chemical process control. Simulations alone are not enough for such plants.

A cut-down model from a spectral split captures the unstable dynamics. Convex conditions combine Lyapunov theory with quadratic bounds on the network's activation functions. They guarantee local stability and safety, plus robustness to the cutting error. Learning by imitation supplies the controller, and the certificates supply the proof. Certified learning-based control is what regulated industries need.
arxiv-2511-12297:
Angqi Liu and three co-authors build an analog resonate-and-fire neuron, a circuit that oscillates and then spikes, much like neurons in event-based computing. Such neurons fit state-space models that use structured linear recurrences for long-range timing tasks. Early analog versions used nonlinear coupling and were sensitive to chip-making variation.

Their circuit, made in a modern silicon process, keeps the recurrence linear while retaining sparse spike communication. They analyze its dynamics and linearity, test resilience to process, voltage and temperature changes, and weigh power, speed and area. A keyword-spotting simulation shows the circuit's imperfections do not hurt task performance, supporting it as a robust, low-energy building block.
arxiv-2511-12397:
Pedro A. Pury builds a stochastic model for the classic newsvendor inventory problem, where a seller must stock goods before knowing demand. The model tracks how the distribution of stock levels changes over time without assuming any specific shape for demand. That flexibility matters when history is thin and forecasts must be short term.

Because no fixed demand law is imposed, the approach can fit varied real settings where a guessed distribution would mislead. Pury evaluates the model on real data from a large electronic marketplace, showing it works in a practical forecasting case. The work offers inventory managers a tool shaped for limited data and quick decisions.
arxiv-2511-12697:
Soumendra Kumar Das and three co-authors test how a new two-dimensional material, aza-triphenylene, stands up to air and water. The material was only recently synthesized, and its behavior under ordinary conditions was largely unknown. Using first-principles calculations combined with a nudged elastic band method, they model how oxygen and water molecules land on the monolayer, whether they stick, and whether they break apart on its surface.

Both gases attach only weakly, and both resist splitting because the paths to dissociation climb over energy barriers. Water faces the higher barrier, since breaking its bonds and moving hydrogen costs more energy. When atoms do bind, strong charge transfer occurs, and the split forms widen the material's band gap. The authors conclude the monolayer is robust against oxygen and water exposure. That stability is good news for any future nanoscale devices built from it.
arxiv-2511-12797:
Nathan Breslow and five co-authors test whether in-context learning, the knack of picking up a pattern from examples inside the input, is unique to language. Language models show this after training only to predict the next token. The team instead studies Evo2, a model trained to predict the next DNA base across genomes. They use matched reasoning tasks written in both linguistic and genomic forms.

The genomic model showed the same signature: gains in pattern induction grew in a log-linear way as more demonstrations were given. The authors say this is the first evidence of in-context learning emerging organically in genomic sequences. Their reading is that the ability follows from large-scale predictive training on rich data, whatever the domain. That points to a unified view of in-context learning across domains.
arxiv-2511-12997:
Genglin Liu and six co-authors give web-browsing agents a memory that survives the session. Agents that navigate websites repeat their mistakes because each run starts blank. WebCoach, a model-agnostic add-on, condenses raw navigation logs into summaries with a WebCondenser, stores complete trajectories as episodes in an external memory. Lets a Coach component retrieve relevant past episodes by similarity and recency, injecting task-specific advice into the running agent through runtime hooks. New trajectories are continually curated into memory, so the agent improves without any retraining.

On the WebVoyager benchmark, WebCoach raised performance across three different language model backbones. With a thirty-eight-billion-parameter model, task success climbed from forty-seven to sixty-one percent while using no more steps than before. Smaller models with the coach matched the same agent running a much larger proprietary model. The design treats experience as an asset that compounds.
arxiv-2511-13397:
Nikos Theodoridis and 6 co-authors release DTPQA, a benchmark that tests traffic perception in vision-language models apart from higher reasoning. Trust in driving aids needs solid basic perception, including objects far down the road where choices still matter. Simple yet vital questions about a scene can expose gaps that harder tasks would hide.

Each item pairs an image with a question, a true answer, and the distance to the object in question. One part is synthetic, built in a simulator, and the other uses real traffic photos with added distance labels. The release includes the data and the scripts that made it, so new data of the same kind can be generated.
arxiv-2511-13797:
Zhaoxuan Wang and 4 co-authors forecast county-level HIV diagnosis rates with a mobility-aware transformer and message passing network. HIV forecasting must capture both time patterns and spread between places, yet classic graph models link only neighboring counties through a fixed map. Their generator builds a dynamic graph from geography plus demographic and mobility cues, so distant but connected counties can interact.

A transformer encoder extracts the temporal features that the graph network then spreads across counties. Against the best hybrid baseline, prediction error fell by large margins in Florida and California and by a smaller margin in New England. The gains show that letting the spatial structure move with human mobility sharpens epidemiological forecasts.
arxiv-2511-13897:
