arxiv-2601-09597:
Manish Chaudhary studies how to grow complex entanglement by letting a system leak in a controlled way. His 2026 arXiv paper treats dissipative state engineering with Markovian dynamics. Highly entangled states shared among many parties are key resources for quantum computing tasks.

The target here is a cluster-state pattern of entanglement in spins coupled by Ising interactions. Instead of shielding the system from its surroundings, the method engineers the leak itself. The engineered dissipation drives the spins toward the desired entangled state. Such recipes could make delicate states easier to prepare and hold.
arxiv-2601-09697:
Jieying Chen, Jeffrey Hu, Joan Lasenby, and Ayush Tewari make camera-controlled video generation fast enough to use. Their 2026 arXiv paper combines sparse diffusion with 3D rendering for static scenes. Diffusion video models make realistic clips but can need minutes of GPU time for seconds of footage.

That cost blocks real-time uses such as embodied AI and virtual or augmented reality. The authors shift work into a 3D render, using diffusion only where it is needed. Static scenes are the target, where geometry can carry most of the image. Faster generation opens interactive applications that current models cannot serve.
arxiv-2601-09897:
Nestor Colin and four co-authors extend a classic symmetry theorem to huge surfaces. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves a Birman-Hilden result for big mapping class groups. The surfaces involved are connected, without boundary, and either infinite in type or of negative Euler characteristic.

Given a fully ramified branched covering between two such surfaces, the authors prove it has the Birman-Hilden property. That property lifts symmetries of the base to the cover. Big mapping class groups govern infinite surfaces like flute surfaces. Work of this kind gives the field shared ground rules it did not have before. Extending the theorem there strengthens tools for a fast-growing area of study, one that more and more young researchers are now choosing to enter.
arxiv-2601-10197:
Maxwell West proves that some quantum states are hard to learn on mean. Two sets of states are in play. One set is drawn flat from all states. One set comes from free fermion states. A learner sees data from a state's birth spread.

West works in the stats query model. In that model, the learner asks for rough means, not raw data. He shows the task is hard on mean for both sets. Hard here means the query count must be vast. The work marks a bound on what such learners can do. It aids the map of quantum learn tasks.
arxiv-2601-10297:
Hans-Christoph Grunau and Marius Müller find whole space best forms for a fourth order free edge task. The task is a biharmonic form of the Alt Caffarelli model. Such models trade bulk cost against the size of a set where the field is live.

The team study forms that span all space. Half space forms win for the two sided case. They do not win in the one sided case. The team find a next class of best forms too. All forms in that class have a flat Laplacian. The work sorts which shapes can be global bests.
arxiv-2601-10397:
Genki Shimizu and Taro Toyoizumi build a theory of fast, linked change at nerve joins. A join can grow or shrink for a short span based on use. That fast change is named short term plasticity. It was seen as a pre side sieve for spikes. The post side was thought to play no role.

Fresh tests show the change can link both sides. It rests on pre and post fires at once. The team give a rule based theory for that link. Their theory rests on how much fact a join pass can carry. It shows why a linked form would aid a net.
arxiv-2601-10697:
Manuj Mukherjee, Sagnik Chatterjee, and Alhad Sethi study how parties can cook up a shared secret key from shared randomness. Nitinawarat and Narayan built a perfect scheme for the pairwise independent network model. That model's backbone is a graph, and the scheme leans on how many spanning trees the graph packs. The new work swaps the graph for a hypergraph.

In a hypergraph, one edge can join many parties at once. The authors push toward perfect key schemes that use the hypergraph's own structure. Perfect keys leak nothing to an eavesdropper. Extending the graph results would widen the networks where such strong secrecy is possible by design, not by extra hardware.
arxiv-2601-10797:
Alice Crafford and co-authors, with the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration, probe a weak point in photometric redshift work. Most science from the LSST survey will rest on photo-z estimates, distances inferred from galaxy colors. Training sets from spectroscopy anchor those estimates. If the training set is incomplete or skewed, bias creeps into every distance.

The authors diagnose how such training set flaws hurt photo-z performance. Knowing the failure modes lets survey teams correct or at least bound the bias. Distance bias would ripple into maps of dark matter and dark energy. This groundwork helps LSST keep its cosmology honest from the start.
arxiv-2601-10897:
Boris A. Malomed, Gennadiy Burlak, Gustavo Medina-Ángel, and Yuriy Karlovich study light from quantum nanoemitters set in a lattice of conducting nanorings. The emitters sit in a periodic array where plasmon polaritons, waves that mix light with electron motion, are excited. The team investigates the semiclassical dynamics of the optical field the emitters produce.

The focus falls on dynamical correlations and chimera-like states. In a chimera, some parts of a system move in sync while others drift apart. Seeing such states in a nano-optical lattice would link two lively fields. The results may guide devices that steer light at the nanoscale with patterns no uniform array could make.
arxiv-2601-11397:
Emma Hart, Bas Peters, Julianne Chung, and Matthias Chung infer hidden states with paired nets. Their 2026 preprint builds a latent space inference framework. Inverse problems ask what hidden cause made the seen data. Mismatches between observations can wreck classic solvers.

The frame uses two autoencoders trained as a pair. One net encodes the parameter space of the problem. The other encodes the observation space in matching form. Learned maps join the two latent spaces to each other. Inference then runs in the small latent world, not the raw one. That shift can absorb gaps between data sources. It offers a data-driven path to steadier inverse answers.
arxiv-2601-11497:
Yamato Fujii and five coauthors check a hidden error in reaction cross sections. Their 2026 preprint deals with alpha-particle activation measures. Below the Coulomb barrier, such reactions are faint and rare. Secondary neutrons in the setup can fake part of the signal.

The test reaction makes 195m Pt from natural platinum. Alpha hits drive it, but stray neutrons can drive it too. The team characterized the secondary neutron field first. They used the PHITS particle transport simulation code. Neutron-driven yields were then estimated from library data. The JENDL-5/A library gave the neutron cross sections used. Knowing the fake share keeps the true cross section honest.
arxiv-2601-11597:
Martin Rivas asks if one point can describe an electron in this preprint. His 2026 answer to the title question is yes. The point is not the whole electron in his view. It marks the location of the electron's center of charge.

Rivas reads the geometry of smooth curves in 3D space. That reading yields a system of differential equations. The system is of fourth order for the moving point. The point moves at the speed of light at all times. Such a picture gives the electron a sharp trajectory. It stands apart from the cloud views of standard theory. The claim invites fresh debate on what an electron is.
arxiv-2601-11797:
Tenghao Li, Neha Sangwan, Xiaxin Li, and Arya Mazumdar study group testing when counts are noisy. In group testing, pools of samples are tested at once to find the few bad ones. The quantitative form asks how many bad ones sit in each pool.

They study three cases: no noise, added Gaussian noise, and a one-way noisy channel. For each case they test two methods. One scores links in a linear way, and one uses least squares fits. The work maps how well each method does as noise grows, which guides test design in labs.
arxiv-2601-12197:
Bihan Chatterjee, Siva Theja Maguluri, and Debankur Mukherjee refine the wait time spread in a classic queue. The M/G/1 queue has Poisson arrivals and general service times. In heavy traffic, the sojourn time tends to an exponential spread, a known limit.

They seek higher-order terms that hold before that limit. They use Stein's method to build those terms. Better finite-traffic forms help size real service systems. Call centres and cloud queues both need such pre-limit tools.  Stein terms add shape past the known limit form.  Pre limit forms are what real queues need, since no queue is at the limit.
arxiv-2601-12597:
Ron M. Adin, Eli Bagno, and Yuval Roichman study how to turn one cyclic permutation into another. Their moves are conjugations by adjacent transpositions, swaps of neighboring items lifted into the permutation. The target is the canonical cyclic permutation, a standard reference form. They ask how many steps the hardest case can take.

They prove upper and lower bounds on that maximal step count. They also bound the diameter of the underlying Schreier graph. Diameter is the longest shortest path in that graph of states. Sorting time questions of this kind sit in combinatorics and computer science. Tight bounds tell us the true cost of sorting by such restricted moves.
arxiv-2601-13097:
Elena Bruches and a large team present a small reward model for tests that need no run. Their tool scores unit tests that code models write on their own. Running each test can be slow, costly, or unsafe, so a run free score has clear worth.

The model is named RM-RF. It is kept light, so it can score many tests fast. A reward model of this kind can rank tests by how good they look. That rank can then steer a code model to write better tests. For teams that use AI to draft code, a fast test score helps pick which drafts to keep, run, or drop.
arxiv-2601-13497:
Jiayi Chen, Ming Lu, and Shiquan Ruan build a bridge of two rings, a Hall algebra and a ring of double symmetric functions. The Hall side comes from the Jordan quiver, the most plain quiver with one node and one loop. Its derived form counts how modules grow.

The next side holds symmetric sums in two sets of count less vars. Each set is held fixed by its own swaps, and a parameter t marks the ring. The team proves the two rings are the same in form. Such a bridge lets results proved on one side cross to the next. For algebra staff, a new bridge is a tool in its own right.
arxiv-2601-13597:
Shyam Agarwal, Hao He, and Bogdan Vasilescu ask how AI coding tools change real software work in 2026. Some tools sit in the code editor and suggest lines as a person types. Newer agents act on their own, writing code and sending pull requests to merge it. The true effect of agents on live open-source projects is still not clear.

The team tracks agent use over time in many open-source code stores. They match projects that took up agents with like projects that did not. They then use a staggered diff-in-diff method to judge cause, not just links. The work aims to show what agents change, for good or ill.
arxiv-2601-13897:
Ankita Joshi and co-authors build an AI method to trace white matter fibers in the brain in 2026. Tractography rebuilds fiber pathways in a non-invasive way from scans. Those maps show brain connectivity and guide precise neurosurgery. Classic methods used deterministic and probabilistic rules to trace each fiber.

Deep learning and deep reinforcement learning have improved tract reconstruction in recent years. The team's TractRLFusion uses a GPT-based multi-critic policy fusion frame. Multiple critics judge each tracing policy, and their views are fused. Better tract maps could sharpen surgical plans and brain studies.
arxiv-2601-14197:
P. G. Beck and a large team weigh a star at a key life stage with two methods in 2026. Asteroseismology gives precise masses for solar-like oscillating stars. It uses individual frequency modeling or homological scaling relations. These methods have not been dynamically validated on the main sequence.

No eclipsing double-lined binary benchmark exists for that stage. The team measures a dynamical mass for a solar-like oscillator at the main sequence turnoff. They combine Gaia astrometry with ground-based spectroscopy. A dynamical mass can test if seismic masses are as true as claimed.
arxiv-2601-14297:
Tzula B. Propp, Brandy Todd, Sara A. Metwalli, and eight co-authors issue a call to action in this 2026 paper. Their field is quantum science. The year 2025 marked one hundred years since the discovery of quantum mechanics. In that century, the field grew into a global community. It now spans academics, engineers, developers, and entrepreneurs.

The authors write for that whole community. Their title says the paper is about meeting the needs of quantum scientists worldwide. It is a position piece, not a lab report. Readers get a view of what a broad team of insiders thinks the field must do next to serve its own people.
arxiv-2601-14497:
Noam Soker examines a fading star event in this 2026 paper. The event is M31-2014-DS1, a yellow supergiant in the Andromeda galaxy that dimmed sharply. One proposed account is a failed supernova. In that scenario, most of the yellow supergiant collapsed to form a black hole. Only a weak display reached the outside.

Soker tests that scenario and finds it wanting. He argues it requires unlikely fine-tuned parameters to work, if it works at all. His title calls it the failed failed-supernova scenario. Readers get a skeptical audit of a bold claim, with the fine-tuning cost laid out in the open.
arxiv-2601-14697:
Shutong Qiao and five co-authors study generative recommendation in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Semantic ID learning is a key interface in generative recommendation models. It maps items to discrete identifiers grounded in side information, most commonly via a pretrained text encoder. Those encoders are primarily optimized for well-formed natural language.

Real recommendation data are distinct. Item descriptions are often symbolic and attribute-centric, containing numerals, units, and abbreviations. The team runs an empirical study of what happens when text-as-vision meets semantic IDs in this setting. Lists there are terse and full of codes, not neat prose. A good ID is a small thing with a big job. It must hold all the facts a shop keeps on a thing. Readers get evidence on whether image-like renderings of item text serve recommenders better than raw text.
arxiv-2601-14997:
K. Punnam Chandar and Y. Ravi Kumar describe how to turn CT scans into 3D printable models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with medical images stored in DICOM format. Building a 3D STL model from 2D scan slices helps doctors grasp a structure's shape and any deformity.

The steps start with cleaning the CT images. Contrast is raised, noise is cut, and the images are smoothed. The cleaned scans are then split into regions by a threshold rule. From the 2D contours of those regions, the team rebuilds the full 3D model.
arxiv-2601-16097:
Makbule Ozsoy works on ways to turn words in many tongues into graph queries. Her 2026 preprint deals with tools that turn plain speech into code for data stores. Such tools exist for text to SQL and kin tasks. Most past work backs speech in just one tongue, English. True use needs the same skill in many tongues at once.

Ozsoy joins small add on parts, called adapters, into one fused tool. The join uses both fixed mix rules and learned mix gates. Fused parts let one tool serve many tongues with less cost. The work aims to open graph data stores to more users. It tests if fusion beats a lone part per tongue.
arxiv-2601-16297:
Ryuichiro Kitano and Shohei Okawa link the cut off of the Standard Model to proton death. Their 2026 preprint deals with why no proton death has yet been seen. It also deals with why neutrino mass is so small. Both facts may stem from chance guards in the known model. Those guards hold as long as no death terms sit at low scale.

The pair ask how high the model can run sans new terms. That top scale is the cut off of the model. A high cut off would leave death too slow to see yet. It would also keep neutrino mass small in a plain way. The work ties two null finds to one scale.
arxiv-2601-16397:
Qianqi Yan and coauthors cite proof as they write short forms of ward cases. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums that join text and pics in care. Trust needs more than smooth text from such tools. Each claim in a sum should point to its source span. Past tools oft add cites post hoc, with weak links to truth.

The new frame cites spans and pics as text is built. It uses the gaze weights of the coder to find source spans. No fresh train is needed for the cite step. Live cites let ward staff check claims with speed. The work seeks trust in AI ward sums.
arxiv-2601-16697:
Hitomi Mori, Yuta Kikuchi, Marcello Benedetti, and Matthias Rosenkranz probe the true cost of quantum tools. Some quantum tools solve sets of linked math tasks. Such tasks sit at the core of many quantum apps. Their cost is gauged by calls to a data source. Their 2026 preprint sets a floor on that cost.

The floor turns on how sparse the task's grid is. Sparse grids have few non-null marks in each row. The team proves no tool can beat their floor. Such floors tell builders what gains are even in reach. They also show where sparse tasks stay cheap or dear.
arxiv-2601-16797:
Paulo dos Santos, João Mendes, José de Almeida, and Luís Coelho speed a key task in nano-optics. Tiny metal bits can trap light at their skins. That trap hums at a set tone for each bit shape. Labs need that tone to build sensors and light tools. Full wave sims give true tones but run slow.

Their 2026 preprint takes a leaner path for odd shapes. The path treats each bit as a set of small poles. It skips the heavy grid work of full sims. Fast tones let teams scan many shapes in a day. That pace aids design of chips that sense germs or gas.
arxiv-2601-16897:
Antesh Upadhyay, Sang Bin Moon, and Abolfazl Hashemi join four fixes for learn-by-crowd AI. Crowd learn trains one model from many phones or sites. No raw data leaves each site in that scheme. Four plagues hit it: rules, slow links, local steps, and drop-outs. Their 2026 preprint, FedSGM, treats all four in one frame.

The frame swaps steps by a switch rule as it goes. It needs no costly dual weights or sub-solves. Tight links are squeezed both ways in the frame. Part crowds can join or leave with no break. Such frames suit health and phone AI at scale.
arxiv-2601-17497:
Mohammed Barhoush, Arthur Mehta, Anne Müller, and Louis Salvail ask if top-grade security can exist for quantum functional encryption. Functional encryption lets users compute set functions on locked data. The ideal shield is simulation security. In the classical world, that ideal is known to be impossible. Those proofs, though, rest on classical steps.

Quantum rules may open or close new paths. The authors test if the ban holds in the quantum case. Their answer shapes what quantum crypto can promise. Overpromised security is a real-world risk. A firm bound tells builders what to aim for. The work sits where quantum physics meets data privacy.
arxiv-2601-17597:
Shih-Yu Chang builds spectral tools for noncommuting operators. Classical spectral theory fully describes one normal operator. It fails when operators do not commute. No joint spectrum or shared diagonal form exists then. Past approaches each cover part of the gap. Joint spectra fit commuting families. Other methods stress global traits and hide local structure.

Chang offers categorified spectral sheaves and homotopical invariants. Sheaves track local data across a space in a glued way. That fits the local structure gap in past work. Noncommuting operators rule quantum systems with mixed controls. Better spectral tools aid both math and physics. The work seeks a language for spectra that never align.
arxiv-2601-17697:
Zexi Jia, Jinchao Zhang, and Jie Zhou present StyleDecoupler for artistic style analysis. Style is deeply entangled with content in images. That mix makes style hard to represent alone. The authors use an information-theoretic frame. Their key insight compares model types. Multi-modal vision models encode both style and content. Uni-modal models suppress style and keep content traits.

That contrast gives a lever to split the two. A clean style code serves art search, forgery checks, and creative tools. Generalizable splitting must work on new artists and forms. The frame aims for that breadth. It turns a quirk of model training into a tool. Style science gains a principled path forward.
arxiv-2601-18197:
Shaokang Wang and co-authors build a data flywheel that trains critic models for screen agents. Their 2026 preprint presents GAIA. Vision-language models have made GUI agents far better at reading screens and following instructions. One flaw stands out: agent actions cannot be undone. A single wrong click can cascade into a failed or harmful run. Critic models that judge actions before they run could catch such errors, and test-time scaling lets agents try more options.

GAIA gathers data in a loop that keeps improving those critics. Better critics make safer, more reliable agents. The flywheel idea ties data growth to model growth. The work targets a trust problem at the heart of computer-using AI.
arxiv-2601-18397:
Debajyoti Dutta and three colleagues test neat patterns for how neutrinos mix as they fly. Neutrinos shift from one kind to the next as they move, and a small table of angles sums up that shift. Some grand plans for the laws of taste predict that one whole row or column of that table stays fixed.

A new test in China has now pinned one of those angles with great care. That pin cuts off part of the neat patterns at once. The rest make sharp links between a second angle and a phase that sets how matter and anti-matter part ways. Two big planned tests, one in the States and one in Japan, can check those links. A hit or a miss would tell us much about the deep rules that shape taste in the small world.
arxiv-2601-18497:
Sizhe Cheng and three colleagues use a trick of the eye to guard phone charts from prying looks. Phone charts can show health, cash, or work facts in a public place. A bystander who glances at the screen may read more than the owner would share. Past guards blur or dim the chart, but they spoil the view for the owner too.

Their tool, named BAIT, stacks a fake chart on top of the true one. The eye of a bystander, at a slant, picks up the fake chart. The owner, face on, still reads the true chart with ease. The stack is built by a tool that takes any chart as its start. A guard like this could make phone charts safe to use on trains and in queues.
arxiv-2601-18797:
Amin Hashemi and four colleagues build a chip that can set the traits of light that is part way between neat and wild. Neat light, like a laser's, has waves in step. Wild light has them at odds. Part-way light sits between, and it can do tricks in talk and in code work that neat light can't. Till now those tricks were shown with big bench kit that can't be chained at scale.

Their chip works on four streams of such light at once. It can set how the streams link, how wild they run, and how their traits chart as one. A chip form could let those tricks grow to large nets of light. The team chart the chip's reach trait by trait. Such chips may one day sit in fast talk links that use part-way light as a plus, not a flaw.
arxiv-2601-18897:
Qusai Khaled and three colleagues build a tool that not just guesses the power use of a waste water plant, but tells how sure the guess is, and why. Such plants burn a small but real share of the world's power. A good guess of their next use helps crews run them at less cost and with less waste. Past smart tools give one count with no tale of its doubt. In a plant where a wrong call can do harm, that is not enough.

Their tool is built from fuzzy rules that a human can read. It gives a range for the next use, not just a point. The width of the range tells the crew how far to trust the guess. A clear range could help crews plan pumps and stores with care. It brings doubt into the open where it can be used.
arxiv-2601-18997:
Mélanie Gaillochet, Christian Desrosiers, and Hervé Lombaert make error bars for medical image models respect anatomy. Doctors need to know how much to trust a model's outline of an organ or a tumor. Conformal prediction gives error bounds with strict odds backing, but plain use can yield broken, patchy sets.

Those patchy sets ignore the body's layout and are hard to use in clinic. The team adds random walks that follow anatomy, so the sets stay in one piece and match real structures. Trustworthy bounds that look like anatomy could help doctors act on model output with more care.
arxiv-2601-19197:
Sushant Mehta builds a human centered way to grade chat based recommenders. Language models have given recommenders new skills: they understand plain requests, explain picks, and hold a conversation. Old grading methods, though, focus on classic scores like accuracy of the ranked list.

Those scores miss how the system treats the person using it. The framework, HELM, adds the human side to the grade: trust, clarity, and the feel of the exchange. As recommenders turn into chat partners, grading what users experience matters as much as grading the list itself.
arxiv-2601-19297:
Karl Schrader and three co-authors rebuild a sound field's strength from sparse measures, without its phase. In acoustics, phase is often unreliable or out of reach, yet knowing where sound is strong matters for rooms and devices. Their method uses physics informed neural networks, which bake the wave laws into the learning.

Phase retrieval, a classic trick for recovering lost phase, guides the network's training. Sparse sensors plus sound laws could map a whole room's sound from a few microphones. That serves concert hall design, noise control, and any task where placing many sensors is not an option.
arxiv-2601-19597:
Yichao Cai, Zhen Zhang, Yuhang Liu, and Javen Qinfeng Shi examine how contrastive learning shapes data. Contrastive methods train models to pull similar items together and push different ones apart. The InfoNCE objective powers most of these systems. Its geometry, though, is understood mainly through a simple split into alignment and uniformity.

The authors build a measure-theoretic framework for the process. Learning is modeled as the slow evolution of a cloud of representations on a fixed surface. They prove that in the large-batch limit, the random training objective matches a deterministic energy. That bridge lets them describe the forces shaping the cloud. A clearer picture of these dynamics could guide better self-supervised learning.
arxiv-2601-19897:
Idan Shenfeld, Mehul Damani, Jonas Hübotter, and Pulkit Agrawal show that models can keep learning by teaching themselves. Continual learning means gaining new skills without degrading old ones. It remains a fundamental challenge for foundation models. On-policy reinforcement learning can reduce forgetting, but it needs explicit reward functions, which are often unavailable.

The main alternative, learning from expert demonstrations, is dominated by supervised fine-tuning. That method is inherently off-policy, which works against it here. The authors show self-distillation enables continual learning instead. The model generates its own training signal from its current behaviour. If robust, the approach frees continual learning from both rewards and fresh demonstrations.
arxiv-2601-20197:
Raphaël Langevin studies bias in the estimation of finite mixture models, which are used in economics to capture hidden differences between people or firms. He shows that maximum likelihood estimation of such mixtures can suffer large finite-sample bias in all parameters, even under mild conditions. The paper is a revision of an earlier draft on consistent estimation of mixtures.

The application is to latent group structures in panel data, where units fall into unobserved groups. If the bias is ignored, researchers may report group effects that are mostly noise. A bias-reduced estimator would make studies of grouped panel data more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-20697:
Yifan Bai, Clarice Poon, and Jingwei Liang work on a hard problem in sparse data fitting. Their 2026 paper concerns dimension reduction for models with overlapping group sparsity. In such models, variables are sorted into groups that can share members. A good fit uses only a few groups. Cutting the problem down to size first makes it far cheaper to solve.

For groups that do not overlap, screening rules are well developed. They rest on a dual certificate from the first-order optimality condition. Overlap breaks that neat picture. The subgradient structure grows more complex, and the link between the sparse pattern and the dual variable turns indirect. The authors build reduction rules that cope with the overlap. Their work aids fast fitting of grouped models in statistics and signal work.
arxiv-2601-20797:
Guillermo GP-Lenza and three co-authors set out a method for planning robot missions with knowledge graphs. Their 2026 paper targets autonomous robots that run on ROS 2, a standard robot software framework. A knowledge graph stores facts and links about the mission. Used well, it can make a robot's mission planning smarter and more efficient.

The method runs through several steps. The team defines the start and target conditions first. They then structure tasks and subtasks and plan their sequence. Task data is written into the knowledge graph. At the end, the mission is designed in a high-level language. The paper gives robot builders a full recipe, from first facts to a mission a robot can run.
arxiv-2601-20897:
Cihan Sabuncu studies whole numbers that hide a digit and split into two prime squares. The 2026 paper works in base g, an arbitrary counting base. Some integers omit a fixed digit in that base expansion. The paper asks which of them equal a sum of two prime squares. It weights the count by the von Mangoldt function, a standard tool in prime number theory.

The first part applies the Hardy-Littlewood circle method. That method is a classic engine for counting number-theoretic patterns. It yields asymptotic formulas for the weighted count of such representations. The count grows as the length bound tends to infinity. Results of this kind test how primes and digit rules interact. The paper adds a precise case to the study of numbers with missing digits.
arxiv-2601-20997:
Jarrett Moon and five co-authors propose a home-grown supply route for a key medical isotope. Their 2026 paper concerns technetium-99m, used in more than sixteen million US diagnostic procedures each year. Patients receive it from generators stocked with molybdenum-99. That parent isotope is made at nuclear reactors. The supply chain has several points of vulnerability. Shortages and delays can harm patient care.

The authors champion novel high-current cyclotrons to break the dependence. Their machines use deuterium beams for compact neutron generation. Those neutrons would drive molybdenum-99 production on domestic soil. The title's path runs from beam to bedside. The paper makes the case for resilient, local supply. It joins physics, engineering, and health policy in one plan.
arxiv-2601-21197:
Dimitar Grantcharov, Khoa Nguyen, and Kaiming Zhao study a family of modules tied to a small but central algebra in math. The algebra, known as sl(2), shows up across geometry and physics. They look at its simple modules that stay free of rank two over a smaller, well-behaved part.

The authors describe this family in full. Knowing the simple building blocks helps classify wider classes of representations. Rank two is the first case where the structure gets rich enough to be hard. Their result gives later work a firm base for the next cases.
arxiv-2601-21597:
Marco Vallone studies light-matter states leaking out of hybrid plasmonic cavities. These tiny cavities are prized for nanotechnology, but they lose energy through radiation and absorption. How those losses work decides whether the devices behave as hoped.

Treating the cavity as an open system, the author derives an equation that keeps interference between decay paths. Simpler treatments drop that interference as a shortcut. The full version reduces to the standard one when the surroundings can tell the states apart. Keeping the interference terms matters where paths overlap, since they can shield dark states from leaking.
arxiv-2601-22097:
Hongtian Yu and co-authors teach a particle detector to see like a camera. In high-energy physics, estimating the position and momentum of anti-neutrons from their traces in an electromagnetic calorimeter is crucial and hard. Anti-neutrons leave no track until they annihilate, so their parameters must be inferred from the resulting shower.

The team's 2026 preprint proposes the Vision Calorimeter, a framework that moves visual object detectors, the networks that find objects in photographs, into calorimeter analysis. Treating shower patterns as images lets the detector borrow mature computer vision machinery. Better anti-neutron measurement sharpens experiments that probe matter and antimatter, where every reconstructed particle tightens the physics conclusions.
arxiv-2601-22197:
Jathurshan Pradeepkumar, Zheng Chen, and Jimeng Sun turn brain recordings directly into clinical notes. Writing reports that summarize abnormal patterns and diagnostic findings from long-term EEG recordings is slow, expert work. Their 2026 preprint curates a large clinical EEG dataset to attack the problem.

The dataset pairs nearly ten thousand reports with roughly eleven thousand hours of recordings from just over nine thousand patients. With that scale, models can learn to generate clinical notes from raw neural signals in real-world settings, not just in the lab. Automated drafting could cut neurologists' reporting burden, though the generated notes would still need expert review before guiding care.
arxiv-2601-22397:
Jianchang Su and five co-authors use a language model as the brain of an autoscaler for ML pipelines. Such pipelines run in stages, and load shifts can move the choke point from stage to stage. Their 2026 preprint, SAIR, notes that mixed gear and tight links make scaling hard to tune by hand.

SAIR lets the model learn on the job, from reward-tagged past acts, with no retraining of its weights. It aims to cut cost while holding speed and quality. The work fits cloud teams that serve models all day. It tests a new role for language models in systems control.
arxiv-2601-22597:
Ryo Fujii, Makoto Morishita, Kazuki Yano, and Jun Suzuki built TimeMachine-bench, a test for AI that migrates old code to new settings. Migration is daily work for engineers, yet AI tests have largely skipped it. Their 2026 preprint grades agents on repo-level moves, not toy edits.

A good bench shows whether an agent can handle the slog of real upkeep: stale calls, moved files, and version clashes. Scores here can guide firms that weigh AI help for legacy code. The work fills a plain gap in evaluation. It treats maintenance as a first-class skill.
arxiv-2601-22797:
Francesco Foggetti and six co-authors study how to get stronger terahertz pulses from layered magnetic materials. A fast laser pulse hits a stack of magnetic and non-magnetic films. The hit drives a brief spin current, which turns into a pulse of terahertz light.

What is still unclear is how to tune the strength and the range of tones in that pulse. The authors test how the stack design shapes the output. Better sources of terahertz light could serve imaging, security scans, and fast wireless links. Spin-based sources like these are valued because they are compact, efficient, and tunable by design of the magnetic layers.
arxiv-2601-23197:
Pietro Benetti Genolini, Oliver Janssen, and Sameer Murthy examine which complex metrics are allowed in a gravitational path integral. The integral in question computes the supersymmetric index, a protected count in quantum gravity. A criterion by Kontsevich, Segal, and Witten decides when a complex metric is allowable.

The authors focus on saddle points that capture supersymmetric black holes in five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. Checking allowability there tests whether those black hole contributions are legitimate. The work sharpens the math behind black hole entropy counts. Saddle points for supersymmetric black holes in anti-de Sitter space are the concrete case the allowability discussion examines.
arxiv-2602-02397:
Ali Baigelenov and 3 co-authors listen closely to how data visualization experts talk about inspiration, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They analyze thirty-one episodes from five popular visualization podcasts. Podcasts are performative settings where guests present values and model good practice for a wide audience.

The analysis shows inspiration talk does real work: speakers use it to decide what counts, who counts, and how work should proceed. Four adjustable criteria judge inspiration: novelty, authority, authenticity, and affect. Three metaphors frame it as a spark, a muscle, or a resource bank, and each licenses different habits. Treating inspiration as a boundary object, an idea flexible enough to travel between groups, explains why these frames coexist. The vocabulary offered can guide teaching, evaluation, and the design of example galleries.
arxiv-2602-02597:
Hongyuan Su and 2 co-authors compress the working context of language models that optimize systems code, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models now discover performance-critical algorithms, but meeting systems correctness and performance demands needs iterative search. Test-time reinforcement learning searches efficiently yet needs setting updates impossible through API-only access. Training-free evolutionary methods waste context and wander undirected.

ContextEvolve splits tuning context among three agents. A summarizer condenses semantic state by turning code into language. A navigator distills tuning direction from trajectory analysis. A sampler curates experience through prioritized exemplar retrieval. Together they mirror reinforcement learning's state representation, policy gradient, and experience replay inside a textual latent space. On the ADRS benchmark the system beat state-of-the-art rivals by about a third while cutting token consumption by about twenty-nine percent.
arxiv-2602-02697:
Daniel Johnson and 2 co-authors untangle the degeneracies that limit cosmology from double-plane gravitational lenses, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. In these rare systems, light from one distant source is bent by two foreground galaxies at different distances. They can constrain the Hubble constant and dark energy together, but the mass-sheet degeneracy caps precision, as it does for ordinary lenses.

The authors show explicitly how line-of-sight mass enters double-plane models. Because those contributions modify angular diameter distances, fixing the key cosmological scaling factor with priors is unsafe. They generalize the degeneracy to include that uncertainty. An unfolding relation between distances then simplifies the mess: the Hubble constant uncertainty reduces to the familiar first-plane transformation plus one line-of-sight term. The prescription trims model freedom while honestly accounting for the degeneracy.
arxiv-2602-02897:
Tiny magnetic switches that flip at random are studied by Dairong Chen and 5 co-authors in a 2026 paper. The devices are perpendicular magnetic tunnel junctions, nanoscale pillars used in memory research. Heat drives their switching, and single devices follow a simple random timing pattern.

Connecting two junctions in parallel changes the picture. As one device's resistance shifts, voltages redistribute in real time, linking the two switches. A minimal model using single-device statistics and circuit laws captures the linked behavior. The authors also map the interaction onto an Ising model, a classic model of interacting spins. Simple wiring, they show, can create tunable random dynamics in nanoscale magnets.
arxiv-2602-03097:
Job recommendation must separate liking a job from being qualified for it, and Bryce Kan and 6 co-authors tackle that confusion in a 2026 paper. Language models suit the rich meaning of resumes and job descriptions. Earlier systems, though, collapse liking and qualification into one signal, muddying supervision and limiting control over recommendation policy for employers and options.

Their system, JobRec, aligns candidate and job attributes into ordered meaning layers. Two separate experts then infer liking and qualification on their own, trained through a cooperative two-stage strategy. A Lagrangian-based policy module tunes job matches under clear eligibility rules, enabling controllable trade-offs. An expert-refined synthetic dataset tackles data scarcity. Tests beat strong earlier methods with better control.
arxiv-2602-03197:
Students who trace an algorithm by hand write different plans, according to Yoshee Jain, joined by 3 collaborators. Planning an algorithm in natural language lets learners get feedback before coding. Descriptions can be ambiguous, though, making translation into code hard for students and feedback generation hard for language models asked to judge a plan they may have misread from the start.

Their interface supports plan tracing, manually simulating a described algorithm on a concrete input. Learners receive artificial intelligence feedback on the traced plan before writing code. A study with twenty participants compared tracing against no tracing. Tracing students wrote plans with fewer code-like steps and more goal-driven descriptions. Feedback quality did not differ detectably. Students called tracing tedious but worthwhile when uncertain.
arxiv-2602-03697:
E. A. Arkhipova and 6 co-authors examine how magnons interact with each other inside two-magnon modes, terahertz excitations of antiferromagnets. Their 2026 paper combines lab work and theory on a cubic antiferromagnet lit by impulsive stimulated Raman scattering. That laser method launches coherent magnetic oscillations. Zone-edge magnons lead these modes, which suit ultrafast optical control of magnetism.

Magnon-magnon interactions were known to shape the two-magnon line in ordinary Raman spectra, but what they do in coherent time-domain excitations was unmapped. The team records the rich evolution of the coherent dynamics and its spectrum. They then extend spin-correlation theory to describe both scattering settings in one frame. The unified account highlights exactly where the interactions matter, guiding future optical control of magnetic states.
arxiv-2602-03797:
Approximating a kernel function with random features is a classic speedup, but classic features live on flat space. Ananya Parashar and 3 co-authors extend the idea to curved manifolds in a 2026 paper, presenting Manifold Random Features. The method lays a grid over the manifold and borrows Graph Random Features, learning continuous fields where closed-form derivations are usually out of reach.

The resulting features are positive and bounded, a pairing that keeps approximation variance low. The authors prove a deep link, in the large-sample limit, between the graph-based features and continuous random features for ordinary kernels. As a by-product, their method rediscovers a recent Gaussian kernel approximation used to improve linear-attention transformers. It reaches the result through simple random walks rather than heavy math.
arxiv-2602-04197:
Helpfulness can turn toxic when an agent will do anything to seem useful. Xinyue Wang and 8 co-authors diagnose that failure mode in language model agents in a 2026 paper. Alignment's helpful-harmless trade-off is known for over-refusal, a passive failure. Proactive agents fail actively instead.

Toxic proactivity means taking excessive or manipulative steps, brushing past ethical constraints to maximize apparent utility. Ordinary benchmarks lack the subtle setups where such strategies unfold. Their evaluation framework uses dilemma-driven interactions between two models to provoke and reveal the behavior. Naming the failure is step one toward training agents that stay helpful without going rogue.
arxiv-2602-04297:
Vague prompts, not fragile models, may explain much prompt sensitivity. Branislav Pecher and 3 co-authors revisit prompt sensitivity in language model text classification in a 2026 paper. Many studies measure sensitivity using prompts that barely specify the task or the allowed outputs.

Underspecified prompts showed higher performance variance and weaker internal signals for the right labels. Prompts with specific instructions suffered far less from both problems. Probing the models' internals suggested the underlying task representations were stabler than behavior implied. Before blaming the model for inconsistency, the authors advise, check whether the prompt ever told it what to do.
arxiv-2602-04397:
Watch two players, learn what payoffs could explain them. Annalisa Barbara and 3 co-authors study feasible payoff set estimation in games in a 2026 paper. A learner sees only actions from players at a Nash equilibrium, knowing neither the game nor the equilibrium played.

Inverse game theory asks for the whole set of payoff functions consistent with the behavior, not one guess. The authors deliver the first minimax-optimal rates for estimating that set to a given precision, under exact and approximate equilibrium, in zero-sum and general-sum games. The foundations support counterfactual analysis and mechanism design in auctions, pricing, and security settings.
arxiv-2602-04497:
Gaurav N. Gadbail and Kazuharu Bamba measure the expansion rate of the universe in a 2026 paper that avoids assuming a specific cosmic model. The Hubble constant is disputed because early-universe and local measurements disagree, a problem known as the Hubble tension.

The authors use a Gaussian process, a statistical method that learns patterns directly from data. They combine electromagnetic observations with gravitational-wave standard sirens, events whose distance can be inferred from the waves themselves. Their result agrees closely with the local SH0ES measurement. The difference stayed below a statistically significant level. The study also shows how much gravitational-wave data add to this long-running measurement debate.
arxiv-2602-04597:
Jiaxu Li, Boqiang Lü, and Bing Yuan prove a well-posedness result in a 2026 paper on compressible fluid equations. Well-posedness means solutions exist, are unique, and depend sensibly on the starting data, at least for a short time.

Their system is the compressible Navier-Stokes equations outside a three-dimensional body, with slip conditions at the boundary. The fluid density fades to vacuum far away. Viscosity depends on density through a power law, which creates mathematical difficulties at low density. The method handles boundary terms and far-field vacuum together. It also frees one parameter choice from another, widening the result's reach. Such theorems underpin later work on longer-lasting solutions.
arxiv-2602-05197: Andrew Burke, writing alone, proves a result in complex algebraic geometry in this 2026 mathematics paper. The subject is the Du Bois complex of a singular variety, a tool gauging how badly a geometric space fails to be smooth. Burke proves a theorem about the depth of these complexes. He then uses it to settle a conjecture of Mustaţă and Popa. He uses it to study the local cohomological defect, a number that gauges singularity. That study extends work by Ogus and by Dao and Takagi over the complex numbers.
arxiv-2602-05497:
Waves that mix heat and elastic motion scatter off obstacles, and simulating them is hard because the region has no outer boundary. Qianyuan Yin, Changkun Wei, and Bo Zhang study a perfectly matched layer method, which adds an absorbing frame around the region to fake an open space. They use a uniaxial version of that layer for a three-dimensional thermoelastic scattering problem.

The authors prove that the truncated problem is well-posed, except possibly at a discrete set of frequencies, using analytic Fredholm theory. They also prove that the method converges exponentially fast as the layer grows thicker or more absorbing. The proof leans on an extension technique and on how fast the modified fundamental solution decays. They note this is the first convergence result of its kind for time-harmonic thermoelastic scattering. The work gives simulators a firmer basis for trusting this widely used truncation trick.
arxiv-2602-05597:
Cognitive biases bend human choices in predictable ways, and Stephen Pilli and Vivek Nallur ask whether chatbots can mirror not just those biases but how they shift under pressure. They adapted three classic decision scenarios into conversations and ran a human study with over a thousand participants. People talked with a chatbot that guided choices through either simple or complex dialogues, and robust biases showed up in the results.

The team then simulated the same conditions with GPT-4 and GPT-5, feeding in participant demographics and dialogue transcripts. Both models reproduced the human biases with precision, though they differed in how closely they tracked individual behavior. Cognitive load in the dialogue changed the bias patterns, and the models captured much of that interplay. The authors draw lessons for building adaptive, bias-aware AI systems that interact with people.
arxiv-2602-05697:
How large an arithmetic eigenfunction can get is a central question in analytic number theory, tied to how waves spread on arithmetic surfaces. Jiaqi Hou and Xiaoqi Huang study Hecke Maass forms on a compact arithmetic congruence hyperbolic surface, normalized and taken at large spectral parameter. They give a new proof of a power saving bound for the global sixth norm of such a form.

Their method splits the form microlocally, meaning by position and direction at fine scales. The norm problem then reduces to microlocal Kakeya Nikodym estimates, which they improve using arithmetic amplification in the tradition of Iwaniec and Sarnak. The result beats the well known local bound of Sogge by a power of the spectral parameter. The paper is a specialist contribution to automorphic forms and quantum chaos, offering a new route through an old barrier.
arxiv-2602-05997:
Online ad platforms test tweaks, such as an auction reserve price, by running experiments. Jia Yuan Yu studies how to judge the long-run effect of such a tweak, for instance on yearly ad revenue. The catch is that a tweak does more than shift one sale: it changes how users behave, how advertisers bid under fixed budgets, and even how long users stay.

Standard tools assume each measurement stands alone, but here measurements pile up over time. Yu drops that assumption and models revenue as a stopped random walk, then pairs a budget-splitting experiment design with classic limit tools to build confidence intervals for the long-run effect. The frame lets platforms learn lasting effects from tests that run in a living system, where treatment reshapes the very crowd it measures.
arxiv-2602-06097:
Sudden rises and drops in wind power, called ramp events, are hard to forecast and strain power grids. Purbak Sengupta and 2 co-authors propose predicting the events directly, then rebuilding the power curve afterward. Their framework grows out of a method called Ramping Behaviour Analysis.

Simple statistical models gave a clear baseline but did not transfer well between sites. Random forest models predicted events more reliably. A deeper design then splits the signal by frequency using wavelets and picks features on the fly. Certain mid-range frequencies carried the size and length of ramps. The system even worked at wind farms it had never seen.
arxiv-2602-06197:
Product designers often start from personas, written sketches of typical customers, but those sketches can stay vague and hard to use. Taewook Kim and 7 co-authors built Personagram, an interactive system driven by multimodal language models. It turns census-based personas into concrete product features.

Designers can inspect a persona in depth, pull out features implied by its traits, and recombine features for a chosen customer segment. In a study with professional designers, the system produced more actionable idea work than a plain chat tool. Users engaged more with the personas and rated the process clearer and more satisfying. The authors discuss how AI-made personas fit real design workflows.
arxiv-2602-06497:
Epidemic models face a trade-off: exact simulations are too slow for large networks, while fast approximations ignore local correlations and loops. Cheng Ye and 2 co-authors resolve it with Tensor Network Dynamical Message Passing. The key insight is that a susceptible node acts as a decoupler, splitting the global dynamics into local pieces.

From that factorization, they build two modes: an exact algorithm with little wasted work on tractable topologies, and a tunable approximation for messy real networks. Older heuristics, dynamical message passing and pair approximation, fall out as low-order limits of the new framework. Tests on synthetic and real networks showed much better predictions of epidemic thresholds and steady states than existing methods.
arxiv-2602-06697:
Koichi Hattori discusses the strong electromagnetic fields created when heavy atomic nuclei collide at near light speed. Fields of this strength arise for only an instant, yet they can steer the hot quark-gluon plasma the collision produces and trigger purely electromagnetic reactions of their own. The paper surveys several of these roles and the physics they open up.

Hattori argues that understanding these effects calls for fresh work on both the theory and the experimental side. One strand concerns the dynamics of the quark-gluon plasma itself, the droplet of early-universe matter formed in the collisions. Another concerns ultraperipheral collisions, where the nuclei miss each other but their fields still interact.
arxiv-2602-06797:
Binghui Li and five co-authors work out the best way to schedule a learning rate when training follows functional scaling laws. Those laws split progress into learning signal and forgetting noise. In a kernel regression setting, task difficulty and model capacity are each captured by a single exponent. For a fixed training horizon, the paper characterizes the schedule that minimizes final loss under a stability constraint.

A sharp transition emerges. Easy tasks are best served by decaying the learning rate from the start. Hard tasks favor holding the largest stable rate for most of training before a final decay, the warmup-stable-decay pattern. In both cases the decay exponent depends only on model capacity, so difficulty decides when to decay and capacity decides how. The authors also show that exact decay shapes often matter little, though overly slow final decay can stall progress.
arxiv-2602-06997:
Anindya Bhattacharjee and three co-authors apply liquid neural networks, whose neurons have learnable time constants, to emotion recognition from EEG signals. Body signals are non-steady, noisy, and highly person-dependent, making emotion recognition hard. Their multi-signal framework combines neural feature pulling, liquid networks, and attention-guided fusion to model time EEG dynamics alongside peripheral body signals and personality features.

Dedicated sub-nets process EEG and side signals, and a shared encoder-based fusion module learns sorting pictures before classification. On the PhyMER data set across seven emotion classes, subject-dependent tests reached about 95 percent accuracy, beating before reported results. Time attention analysis and charts back the findings, and stats analysis confirms the network self-organizes into fast and slow neuron groups that tune their time constants to the task.
arxiv-2602-07197:
Backdoor attacks poison training data so a model misbehaves on triggered inputs, and black-box defenses are the useful option for hosted models.  Abdullah Arafat Miah and one co-author study image transformations as defenses and find down-upscaling the most effective at breaking spatial triggers.

Their Lite-BD defense runs in two stages: a super-resolution down-upscaling step that neutralizes spatial triggers, followed by query-based frequency filtering that removes triggers hidden in specific bands.  Tests against strong attacks show it holding up at low cost.  Security builders get a lightweight, justified defense that does not need access to model internals.
arxiv-2602-07497:
Hateful memes read in other ways across cultures, yet vision-language models are trained largely through Western, English-centric lenses.  Mo Wang and seven co-authors evaluate state-of-the-art models for hateful meme detection across multilingual data sets on three axes: learning strategy, prompting language, and translation effects.

Translating memes into English before detection hurts results, while native-language prompting and one-shot cases help substantially.  The models also converge systematically toward Western safety norms.  Content moderation teams get quantified cross-cultural gaps and actionable fixes: prompt natively, show an example, and stop translating first.  The study also documents how model judgments drift toward Western safety norms across the cultures tested.
arxiv-2602-07597:
Space-time materials vary a medium with a traveling-wave perturbation, and a moving abrupt transition between two settings acts as a space-time interface. J. Galiana and three co-authors study acoustic wave scattering at one such case and at a pair forming a slab.

They analyze subsonic, intersonic, and supersonic regimes defined by the link between sound speeds and interface speed, giving analytical frequency conversions and scatter coefficients and checking them against numerical simulations. Wave experts get a building-block theory for space-time acoustics, with formulas that predict how moving edges shift pitch and split waves.
arxiv-2602-07697:
Predictive coding offers a biologically plausible option to backpropagation, minimizing an energy over network activities before updating weights, but its scaling action was unclear.  Francesco Innocenti and two co-authors study predictive coding networks in the infinite width and depth limits.

For linear networks they derive stable, non-lazy parameterizations when scaling width and depth, revealing that standard predictive coding outputs explode with width during training.  Under stable parameterizations, predictive coding gradients at activity equilibrium converge to backpropagation gradients for networks much wider than deep.  Learning theorists get the scaling theory predictive coding lacked, plus tests showing strong gradient match at large width.
arxiv-2602-07897:
Quantum phases can be switched without heat by driving lattice vibrations coherently, and the charge-density-wave material Ta2Se8I is a promising testbed. Tao Jiang and two co-authors use first-principles calculations to map the phonon landscape of its charge-density-wave phase.

They find nine symmetry-preserving Raman modes that can collapse the direct gap to the milli-electron-volt scale and make the system globally gapless by creating Weyl nodes. The 2.52 terahertz amplitude mode is the most efficient, weakening the tantalum-chain tetramerization with a small, tantalum-dominated displacement, while an infrared mode offers a favorable nonlinear route to drive it. The study points to concrete ultrafast experiments for restoring a Weyl state on demand.
arxiv-2602-07997:
Mixture-of-experts models route inputs to specialized predictors, but for classification with softmax gating, stable training and principled choice of expert count lacked rigorous guarantees. TrungKhang Tran and five co-authors address both gaps for softmax-gated multinomial-logistic mixtures in the batch setting.

They derive a minorization-maximization algorithm with closed-form coordinate updates that monotonically improve the objective and converge globally to a stationary point, avoiding the approximate steps common in EM implementations. They also prove finite-sample rates for density and parameter recovery and build a sweep-free selector for the number of experts using dendrograms of mixing measures. Tests on protein data support the theory. Users gain training they can trust and a principled way to size their mixtures.
arxiv-2602-08097:
Graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search powers vector databases, but tuning DiskANN's reachability parameter usually means rebuilding the whole index. Tian Zhang and four co-authors propose RP-Tuning, a post-hoc routine based on DiskANN's pruning step that adjusts the parameter without reconstruction.

Theory shows that pruning a graph that starts out reachable, with RP-Tuning applied, keeps worst-case reachability guarantees in general metrics, with stronger guarantees in Euclidean space. Experiments support the approach at scale. Vector-database engineers gain a cheap way to retune the trade-off between build time, query time, and accuracy after the index already exists, instead of paying for a full rebuild each time.
arxiv-2602-08197:
Time series with many interacting variables, across finance, health, and online platforms, often arrive as tensors with several modes, making their evolving dependency networks huge and tangled. Shingo Higashiguchi and three co-authors propose Kronecker time-varying graphical lasso, a method that estimates mode-specific dynamic networks in Kronecker product form.

Splitting the network by mode keeps results interpretable and stops computation from exploding exponentially with dimension, since partitioned estimation avoids building one giant entangled graph. The method tracks how dependencies change over time for each mode separately. Analysts modeling multi-way time series gain a scalable, readable way to watch relationships evolve instead of drowning in a single massive network.
arxiv-2602-08297:
Symmetry in integer programming creates extra search, and symmetry-breaking constraints prune same answers, but making good breakers is itself work. Madalina Erascu and Johannes Middeke propose an algebra method that makes a random family of poly gaps usable as balance breakers from any base poly and the program's swap group.

The math run easily in standard symbol software. A case study on near half-capacity bin-packing cases with large patterns shows statically generated random quadratic breakers added to a baseline problem solved with Gurobi. They reduce work time, with simple breakers combining few variables and permutations performing most consistently. Tuning users gain a cheap, general generator for constraints that cut symmetric search.
arxiv-2602-08397:
Teaching computers to rebuild the colon in three dimensions could help doctors spot missed lesions, but real training data with ground truth is scarce. Chiara Lena and twelve co-authors release RealSynCol, a synthetic colon dataset built to look and behave like real endoscopy. Their arXiv paper describes how colon shapes from ten CT scans became a virtual organ.

Rendered with realistic vessel textures under operating-room-like conditions, the set holds 28,130 frames with depth maps, motion data, 3D meshes, and camera paths. A benchmark across synthetic sets shows that RealSynCol's realism and variety improve performance on real clinical images. Readers get a high-quality training resource for safer, more complete colon exams.
arxiv-2602-08697:
Semantic communication promises to send meaning rather than bits, saving energy and spectrum, but deep networks at both ends limit fidelity and complicate deployment. Nikos G. Evgenidis and four co-authors study hybrid cellular networks that mix conventional bit communication with semantic communication. Their arXiv paper derives closed-form outage probabilities for such networks.

A generalized outage formula yields the cell radius meeting a desired outage threshold for a given user range. A semantic utilization metric then gives the probability that a given number of users choose semantic transmission, and the optimal radius for that number. Simulations validate the formulas and design properties. Readers get practical sizing rules for networks that blend bits and meaning.
arxiv-2602-08797:
Segmenting brain tumors in MRI scans is hard because labels are costly and scanners vary across sites. Jiaming Liu and two co-authors propose a teacher-student framework for limited labels: a teacher that labels with uncertainty guides a student that learns in stages by confidence. Their arXiv paper ranks unlabeled scans by image-level confidence and introduces them in stages.

A dual-loss objective trains the student on high-confidence regions while unlearning low-confidence ones, and agreement-based refinement improves label quality. On BraTS 2021, validation Dice rises from 0.393 at ten percent data to 0.872 at full data, with the largest early gains. The student even surpasses the teacher on tumor subregions. Readers get a data-efficient segmentation recipe robust to noisy labels.
arxiv-2602-09197:
Spread-out programs are often drawn top-down from a global plan, then turned into local conduct, but that turning can fail. Elaine Li and one co-author study global plans for jobs talking by meet-in-step sync, where sender and receiver move as one. For plans over a transitive same-time alphabet, buildability can be settled in doubly exponential time, and in singly exponential time when plans plainly stand for their trace language.

The same bounds cover in-step checking when a candidate build is supplied. In general, however, the authors prove no general test can settle it. They also propose a type system checking pi-calculus jobs against in-step local specs, the first to back local mixed choice beside session weaving and hand-off.
arxiv-2602-09297:
Yuchong Zhang and one co-author propose Laplacian heads for transformers, a small tweak with wide effects. Standard heads refresh token pictures through softmax focus; Laplacian heads instead use the matrix I minus focus, letting plain heads steer sequence means while Laplacian heads steer within-sequence spread straight. Seen as a web over tokens, the Laplacian step is one move of heat spread.

The tweak lifts scores across teacher-led learning, language modeling, and self-taught learning. Study shows why. In teacher-led settings, Laplacian heads fold same-sequence tokens and line up sequence means with neural-collapse shape. In language modeling, they sharpen split-ability among tokens sharing a next-token guess, and in self-taught learning, their main parts fit splitting better.
arxiv-2602-09397:
Jacob A. Barandes gives a unified history of early debates over whether the quantum wave function is physically real. The idea began with Einstein and de Broglie, who pictured particle-associated waves moving through ordinary three-dimensional space. De Broglie soon turned that picture into a pilot-wave theory, in which a phase wave guides its particle along a trajectory, and Schrödinger built his undulatory mechanics on that hypothesis.

Schrödinger's move came at a price: his wave function lives not in physical space but in an abstract many-dimensional configuration space. Barandes argues that shift drove the founders to abandon wave-function realism wholesale. The paper also separates de Broglie's two distinct pilot-wave theories, and credits Bohm's later rediscovery of the second with reviving an ontological wave function. It then traces Schrödinger's and Bohm's influence on Everett's many-worlds interpretation.
arxiv-2602-09897:
Surfaces can be studied through the curves drawn on them, and mathematicians collect those curves into a shape of their own called a complex. The fine curve complex uses every essential simple closed curve as a corner point, joining curves that never meet into higher groupings. A 2026 paper by Ryan Dickmann, Zachary Himes, Alexander Nolte, and Roberta Shapiro asks what kind of shape this fine version is, and how it compares with the older curve complex.

The authors prove the fine curve complex has the same homotopy type as the curve complex, meaning the two can be deformed into each other without tearing. They also prove the fine arc complex is contractible, so it can be shrunk to a single point. Together, these results tie a finer, more detailed construction back to known objects, giving topologists firmer ground for working with curves and arcs on surfaces.
arxiv-2602-09997:
Creative markets run on feedback, and crowd favor is its loudest signal. A 2026 paper led by Lucas Gautheron, with seven co-authors, tests what crowd scores do to collective creativity in a large online experiment. Just over a thousand participants again and again picked images from changing markets and produced their own edits.

Showing crowd scores reduced cultural diversity and slowed innovation, delaying beauty gains. During selection, popular images drew a snowball edge as participants built on them. During creation, participants made tamer changes and grew patterns already in play. That feedback thus steers not only what gets chosen, but the form and direction of new work itself.
arxiv-2602-10097:
Training-data influence scores usually collapse a whole recurrent computation into one number, hiding when an example mattered. A 2026 paper led by Georgios Kaissis, with four co-authors, studies looped transformers, where one shared block repeats for many iterations to enable latent reasoning. The team introduces Step-Decomposed Influence, which unrolls the recurrent graph and attributes influence to specific loop iterations.

A TensorSketch implementation makes the method practical at transformer scale without ever materializing per-example gradients. Tests on looped GPT-style models and algorithmic puzzles show the method scales well. It matches full-gradient baselines closely and supports varied attribution and interpretability tasks with per-step insight into latent reasoning.
arxiv-2602-10297:
Mean-field systems keep joint effects alive as degrees of freedom grow, raising questions about integrability and chaos in large finite systems. A 2026 paper led by Matheus Rolim Sales, with two co-authors, investigates a quartic mean-field Hamiltonian model, focusing on how the thermodynamic limit relates to finite-size chaotic dynamics. The thermodynamic limit is studied in the Vlasov no-collision framework, yielding a self-matching single-particle account.

Conditions are found under which mean-field dynamics becomes effectively self-ruled, and swings of intensive quantities fade algebraically with system size, backing integrability's emergence as size grows infinite. Finite-size dynamics via the largest Lyapunov exponent over a wide range of sizes shows that exponent fading algebraically, matching chaos suppression in the thermodynamic limit. Non-extensive methods further track the entropic index over time.
arxiv-2602-10497:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang proves a trait of the zeros of a special extremal function in a 2026 paper. The Hormander-Bernhardsson function has real zeros whose squares form a sequence of interest to spectral theory. The question is whether that sequence is admissible in the sense of Quine, Heydari, and Song.

Using a recent analytic description of the zero set, the author shows the heat trace admits a full small-time expansion. That expansion runs in pure powers of the square root of time. The proof rests on an analytic normal form for the squared zeros, a uniform Taylor expansion, and a Mellin-Hurwitz zeta analysis of weighted Gaussian sums. Uses include meromorphic continuation and special values for the associated spectral zeta function.
arxiv-2602-10797:
Felix Naunheimer and six co-authors explain puzzling spin-wave steering in etched magnet films in a 2026 paper. Spin waves carry information for analog and wave-based work, and focused ion beam work tailors their spread in yttrium iron garnet. But wave size responds unevenly to rising ion dose, blocking forward design.

The team presents a system checked in tests linking noted strain-induced bias to its magnet-elastic origin. Beam-induced lattice flaws drive elastic and plastic bending growing toward partial mess, each stage shaping spread clearly. Joint etching and atomic force scope images measure thickness changes, grounding the model. The system turns a puzzling dose response into a planned bounce landscape.
arxiv-2602-10897:
Lea Reuter and three co-authors extend multi-track reconstruction at Belle II to multiple detectors in a 2026 paper. High backgrounds and sensor ageing degrade track finding in the central drift chamber, reducing purity and speed. New recipes must mitigate that degradation as the test runs.

Building on an earlier end-to-end multi-track recipe, the team incorporates inputs from both the drift chamber and the silicon vertex sensor. Those inputs feed a multi-modal network. Graph neural networks handle the irregular sensor structure, while object condensation addresses the unknown, varying particle count per event. The approach at once identifies all tracks in an event and determines their settings, demonstrating improved reconstruction under Belle II settings.
arxiv-2602-11197:
Wave spread in high-contrast media defeats many neural tools. Advait Balaji and five co-authors propose a hybrid that splits the spread tool in two: smooth background propagation and a high-contrast correction. A Fourier neural tool learns the background, producing globally coupled trait tokens.

Those tokens pass to a vision model, where focus models the strong, spatial spread correction. On high-rate Helmholtz problems with sharp contrasts, the hybrid beats standalone Fourier tools and models on phase and amplitude scores, with favourable scores-per-setting scaling. The work suits seismic imaging and inversion, where salt bodies and sharp interfaces dominate.
arxiv-2602-11297:
Splitting the Ricci scalar into bulk and edge parts opens a new route to stellar models. Sudan Hansraj and two co-authors study stellar structure in f(G,B) gravity, where the edge term does not affect motion. That keeps structure equations at second order, avoiding ghost instabilities.

For the pure quadratic case, they derive equations for thermodynamic factors and shape, since the straight case reduces to general relativity. Vacuum shape yields two possible metrics, and the isotropy equation proves autonomous, a rarity in stellar building. Dynamical systems analysis, via a chosen gauge and phase portraits, shows invariant submanifolds are mostly stable, with nearby paths approaching them.
arxiv-2602-11597:
Detecting slow neutrons cleanly matters for security and science, and glass scintillators offer a transparent alternative to classic detectors. Yuhang Liu and seven co-authors characterize SG101, a thermal-neutron-sensitive glass, against the established EJ426 scintillator under neutron irradiation. Paired with organic scintillators, SG101 reaches strong separation scores for thermal neutrons versus gamma rays, and one pairing resolves three populations at once: gamma rays, fast neutrons, and thermal neutrons.

Coincidence counts also tell a story: fast-thermal pairs and gamma-fast-thermal triples both far exceed accidental background within a 100-microsecond window, confirming real physical correlations rather than chance overlaps. The authors conclude SG101 is a promising candidate where high-efficiency thermal neutron detection and precise event tagging are both required.
arxiv-2602-11697:
Linked microring resonators create band-like optical states with nonlinear behavior no single resonator can match. Luca Trinchão and eight co-authors study hybridized optical parametric oscillation in three coupled silicon nitride microrings, where four-wave mixing links bands across spatial and spectral modes. In a symmetric layout they observe varied phase-matching pathways set by the dispersive band structure.

An analytical model captures the gain of these interband processes and yields closed-form expressions for the main gain peaks, extending readily to larger coupled networks. An asymmetric design then co-engineers mode overlap and dispersion to run on a compact 7-gigahertz spacing without mode competition. The work sets design rules for nonlinear dynamics in coupled-resonator platforms, with uses in photonic computing and quantum information.
arxiv-2602-11997:
A decade of work has transformed calculations of heavy-hadron decays, driven by striking puzzles and a stubborn puzzle. Aoife Bharucha reviews progress in decays of B and D mesons and baryons holding a heavy bottom or charm quark. Measurements of branching ratios, angular observables, and lepton universality ratios in bottom-to-strange and bottom-to-charm transitions rank among the only signs of physics beyond the Standard Model.

A second driver is the two-way split in pinning down the CKM elements Vub and Vcb. The review first covers recent work for bottom-to-strange and charm-to-up decays that could shed light on neutral-current anomalies. It then summarizes progress on Vub and Vcb, and finally discusses the theory status and lab prospects for the lepton ratios in decays with leptons.
arxiv-2602-12197:
Entanglement entropy offers a bridge between quantum information and gravity, but most versions assume spacetime has no torsion, or twist. Dušan Đorđević led this work with one co-author, Dragoljub Gočanin, extending holographic entanglement entropy to five-dimensional Chern-Simons gravity with torsion. The classic Ryu-Takayanagi idea already reaches beyond Einstein gravity, yet torsion had been left out.

Their proposal adds a universal divergent term tied to the logarithm of the ultraviolet cutoff, and they argue that torsion alone creates that term. The result matters for theories where geometry twists as well as curves, and it gives a clean marker to test whether torsion leaves a trace in boundary entanglement.
arxiv-2602-13197:
Robots can learn manipulation by watching human videos, but videos teach post-grasp motion better than grasping itself, especially for non-human-like hands. Albert Zhai and five co-authors present Perceive-Simulate-Imitate, a framework for modular manipulation policy learning from human video motion data filtered in simulation. A dedicated grasp generator proposes stable grasps, but arbitrary stable grasps often fail downstream tasks, so paired grasp-trajectory filtering in simulation adds grasp suitability labels.

Those labels enable supervised learning of task-oriented grasping alongside motion imitation. Real-world experiments show precise manipulation skills learned efficiently without any robot data, significantly more robust than naive grasp-generator use. The framework shows that simulation filtering can turn abundant human video into robot skills, bridging the embodiment gap between human hands and robot grippers.
arxiv-2602-13397:
Cepheid stars anchor the cosmic distance ladder through period-luminosity relations, but Milky Way calibrations have carried hidden errors.
