Bloch band geometry shapes many crystal traits, yet direct measures stay an active research area. The team mimics electron response to light with ultracold fermionic atoms in shaken optical lattices. Excitation strength at each quasimomentum and shaking polarization maps the interband Berry connection straight. Between the ground band and excited bands 2, 3 and 4, the method reveals clear lines and Dirac strings linking K and K prime points where the connection flips direction.
arxiv-2605-11697: Nigatu and others present a motion-aware Rainbow system for joint Delta and 3-RRS robot fitting. A shape design stage tunes the 3-RRS shape to grow jam-free workspace, widening the safe search region. The arms expose a 6-degree-of-freedom subspace, with a five-dim task space skipping peg-axis spin. Fitting becomes a Markov choice process with a 12-dim state and 12 commands, trained with a shaped reward and plan. In sim it settles stably, inserts well and breaks less than vanilla DQN and an old planner.
arxiv-2605-11897: Milan Češka and four colleagues speed up optimal conditional reachability math in Markov decision processes. The standard reduction creates cyclic, hard-to-solve models. Their new method stays stable in numbers, decides thresholds in linear time on acyclic models, and matches standard reachability query speed. Built into an abstraction-refinement system, it checks millions of Markov chains at once, with speedups of multiple orders of magnitude on Bayesian network, probabilistic program, and runtime monitoring tests.
arxiv-2605-11997: Darlan Noetzold and three colleagues build a unified microservices platform for endpoint security and hate-speech risk alerting. Current tools handle data loss, productivity tracking, or hate-speech detection in isolation, delaying response. Their platform collects endpoint telemetry and applies predictive language models, routing events through RabbitMQ and serving data through Redis. Transformer models such as BERT reached 87 percent average accuracy on hate-speech risk, and the platform surfaced exfiltration and policy violations promptly.
arxiv-2605-12497: Yang and five colleagues study visual perception where the target must first be identified from outside facts before it can be found in pixels. They name the task Perception Deep Research and release WebEye, a benchmark with verifiable evidence, knowledge-heavy queries and precise box and mask labels across grounding, segmentation and question-answering views. The set holds 120 images, 473 object instances, 645 question pairs and 1,927 task samples. Their Pixel-Searcher agent searches the web to resolve hidden identities, then attaches them to boxes, masks or grounded answers.
arxiv-2605-12797: Mukherjee, Grayling and Wason study how outcome delay harms sample-size re-estimation in clinical trials. When recruitment continues while outcomes are awaited, long delays add pipeline participants who do not feed the interim analysis. That inflates the final sample size and power, raising cost. The team derives the final sample-size distribution under varied delays for continuous and binary outcomes, and assesses precision with RMSE plus two new metrics, delay impact and cost. Trials whose re-estimated size falls below the original plan suffer most, often ending overpowered.
arxiv-2605-12897: Kliniewski and four colleagues present DynoJEPP, a tool that jointly handles estimation, prediction and planning for robots in changing settings. Older joint tools let prediction and planning leak back into estimation, spoiling it and yielding unsafe plans. DynoJEPP adds a one-way link that blocks that leak, keeping estimates clean. Without it, the robot crashed in most tests; a team variant also folds in the moves of other moving objects.
arxiv-2605-12997: Xie and Luo test how neural operators that solve wave equations cope with shifts in their inputs. They compare the Fourier Neural Operator and DeepONet on a one-dimensional variable-coefficient wave equation, varying input frequency and coefficient smoothness separately. Smoothness shifts leave both models stable, with the Fourier model more accurate. Frequency shifts hurt the Fourier model sharply on unseen high frequencies, while DeepONet degrades more gently despite higher overall error.
arxiv-2605-13197: Wen and six co-authors present McCast, a memory-guided method for correcting drift in long-horizon precipitation nowcasting. Autoregressive nowcasting predicts states from past outputs, accumulating errors that drag forecasts off course. Rather than treating memory as a loose pile of states, McCast uses time-ordered memory to correct drift. A Drift-Corrective Memory Bank estimates corrections in two stages: an extractor predicts a correction, then a retrieval module refines it from historical memory. On SEVIR and MeteoNet it reaches state-of-the-art performance over long horizons.
arxiv-2605-13497: Xinye Wanyan and four colleagues propose APG4RecSim, a framework that builds user profiles for recommendation simulation. Simulated users help evaluate recommender systems in real time, yet most work lifts memory and action parts while user records are ignored. Hand-crafted records scale badly, since simulation datasets are scarce, so it builds realistic records with minimal human help. Tests on three benchmarks show it leads on discrimination, ranking and rating, lifting ranking quality by up to 7 percent and cutting rating divergence by 8 percent.
arxiv-2605-13697: Igor Nikolaevich Nikonorov, Maxim Vladimirovich Barkov and Maxim Lyutikov show the Guitar nebula is an exceptional bow-shock pulsar wind nebula. Particles escaping the nebula to form the X-ray kinetic jet must reach energies near the neutron star's maximal electric potential, marking it as an extreme accelerator. Exceptionally bright H-alpha emission requires the pulsar PSR J2225+6535 to pass through a dense low-ionisation interstellar region. The authors hypothesise the Guitar passes through a narrow dense shell of an old supernova remnant.
arxiv-2605-13897: Keshvarikhojasteh, Pluim and Veta join three kinds of patient data to guess how long a patient may live. Slides of tissue, RNA readouts and clinical notes each pass through their own encoders. A low-rank bilinear fusion step then joins the streams and models how pairs of data types combine. Risk scores from the model map to survival times through a Kaplan-Meier calibration step.
arxiv-2605-13997: Zhong, Zheng and Allen-Blanchette attack a snag in shrinking sparse mixture-of-experts layers without retraining. Three experts can pair well yet form a locked cycle when merged as a trio, so pair scores alone cannot tell which trios merge cleanly. The snag turns out to be a precise object, the harmonic kernel of the simplicial Laplacian on a 2-complex of experts, edges and faces. HodgeCover then greedily covers the harmonic-critical parts to pick merges.
arxiv-2605-14097: Parisi and four co-authors test language-model help in live group talks over charity donations. Two studies with 879 people in total put trios to work splitting a donation budget in real-time text chats with real money at stake, 7,200 dollars in all. Study one compares three frontier models as helpers, while study two compares helper strategies against no help. Help did not clearly lift group accord in either study, yet people still preferred helped chats.
arxiv-2605-14297: Alvo, Russo and Kanoria study reinforcement learning in hybrid action spaces, where discrete choices pick regimes. Standard policy gradient methods use score-function estimators with severe credit-assignment issues in high dimensions. Differentiable simulation sidesteps these issues by backpropagating. Hybrid Policy Optimization backpropagates through the simulator where smoothness permits, using a mixed estimator of pathwise and score-function gradients, keeping unbiasedness. HPO clearly beats PPO on inventory control and switched regulator problems, with gaps growing with continuous dimension. The mixed gradient's cross term becomes negligible near a discrete best response.
arxiv-2605-14897: Deproost and team introduce Critic-Driven Voronoi State Partitioning for distilling deep reinforcement learning policies into clear models. Traditional distillation minimises only behaviour distance between original and surrogate policies. The new method partitions a black-box policy into regions where a simple model class is optimised. The critic value network guides iterative introduction of new subpolicies in regions with insufficient value. Nearest-neighbour lookups assign a linear function to each point, yielding a cell diagram, with distillation claimed to approach the original using a modest set of linear maps.
arxiv-2605-15297: Pedro L. S. Lopes studies the Optimistic Quantum Fourier Transform under a surface-code fault-tolerant model for reconfigurable neutral-atom hardware. The transform's reliance on phase-gradient resources and small blocks demands mobile resources and parallel execution. His hot-zone architecture separates data storage from processing and sends magic-state factories, link qubits, and phase-gradient registers toward fixed data. Two hot zones match serial transform latency, four roughly halve runtime, and more zones approach constant time at steep cost.
arxiv-2605-15397: Kangning Cui and fourteen colleagues introduce ELDOR, a drone-based benchmark for tracking illegal gold mining in the Amazon rainforest. It covers over 2,500 hectares of annotated aerial imagery with pixel-level labels for mining activity and surrounding ecology. Four tasks test segmentation, recognition, classification, and vision-language understanding, and current methods still struggle with small, rare mining structures and fine recovery classes. An interactive explorer lets domain experts browse the data and run models.
arxiv-2605-15597: Jiale Liu and fourteen colleagues ask how to turn 3D assets into sparse panoramic RGB-D-pose data with full scene cover. Their COVER curator casts geometry from picked views into candidate panoramas. It scores added cover and docks depth clashes. Greedy picks keep standard cover-style approximation conduct. The CM-EVS set built this way holds 36,373 panoramic frames from 1,275 indoor scenes, plus outdoor panoramas in one schema. It spans all thirteen room types with a median of just 25 frames per indoor scene.
arxiv-2605-15897: Vladislav Dodon and four colleagues seek causes behind the boost and break of magnetic braking in CVs. Modeling binary change with MESA, they compute turnover span straight from donor structure rather than set rules. They add irradiation from the feeding white dwarf that heats outer layers and drives extra winds. That span spikes as the donor nears full convection, driving the break parameter and starting the period gap. Plausible rates let light-driven winds supply the needed boost, yielding tracks in line with observed traits.
arxiv-2605-16097: Zhou, Bode, and Hunt formalize cooperative transport, where teams of robots must jointly carry large items that no single agent can move. Existing path-finding frameworks lack true cooperation for such loads. They present an optimal solver with an incremental expansion strategy and a family of faster sub-optimal solvers. Tests show the expansion strategy prunes the search space sharply, while the sub-optimal solvers set a new quality-versus-speed frontier.
arxiv-2605-16197: Gutoreva, Tsim, and Papakonstantinou argue that AI safety and alignment must grow from co-regulation of the human-AI mind system as a whole, not from curbing an outside tool. AI now shapes attention, reasoning, synthesis, and choices before conscious thought, forming one linked unit with its users. Loose delegation risks deskilling, automation bias, transfer of epistemic authority, and oracle-style centralization of knowledge. The authors close with design rules for joint regulation aimed at engineers and governance bodies.
arxiv-2605-16297: Li and Ye ask which tasks inside an enterprise workflow a language-model agent can reliably handle, and under what conditions. Most frameworks judge at the activity level, though one activity can bundle work of very different difficulty. Their T-IPO model represents each task as an eight-element tuple, and their LARA rubric scores readiness across five dimensions, with compliance sensitivity weighted 1.5-fold. Tested on 127 tasks, inter-rater agreement reached kappa 0.80, and pilot deployment showed auto-completion falling from 95 percent at level one to about 40 percent at level three.
arxiv-2605-16397: Papanikolaou and four others build adaptive run-time processing for sea object detection, adding GPS track data to a YOLOv8-based model. Frames where vessels sit close together and converge fast get full-model processing, while other frames activate only part of the network. Scene difficulty is judged from inter-vessel distance and how fast that distance shrinks. The strategy maintains detection performance while cutting run time and compute cost, enabling a flexible accuracy-cost balance versus full-model inference.
arxiv-2605-16697: Wald examines ordered front-to-back any-hit traversal, a ray-tracing task that lists every hit along a ray in strict front-to-back order, even hits at the same distance. He describes several ways to solve it within the limits of the existing ray-tracing pipeline. He then evaluates those realizations against one another. The focus is guaranteeing order and completeness, not skipping hits.
arxiv-2605-16997: Zhang, Soe and Xu prove a weak solution exists for the 3D Beris-Edwards system in whole space under stable bulk conditions. The solution meets natural bounds, the distributional form of the equations, and an expanded Leray-Hopf-type energy inequality for weak-strong uniqueness. The proof avoids a direct limit in that expanded inequality, where non-corotational terms hold fourth powers. It first secures the physical free-energy inequality via hyperviscous approximation and a localised tail estimate, then derives it from a low-order chain rule for bulk energy.
arxiv-2605-17097: Belli and López classify surfaces in Sol, a three-dimensional solvable group, that hold their shape under Gauss curvature flow. They study flows tied to three symmetry directions: two shifts and one stretch. For stretch-invariant surfaces, they prove only certain flat vertical planes can be shift-flow solitons. For shift-invariant surfaces, they map the main traits of the remaining flows, both in outer shape and inner curvature.
arxiv-2605-17197: Le, Karimi and Rahnemoonfar propose OPTNet, a point transformer for segmenting post-disaster 3D scenes that learns how to order points instead of relying on fixed curves. A self-supervised sorter predicts the permutation that best preserves locality for attention, replacing costly neighbor searches and sampling. On the 3DAeroRelief dataset it beats leading baselines by a clear margin, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-00097:
Pak and colleagues let an AI agent design, build, and fly high-powered rockets in this 2026 arXiv paper on RocketSmith. The system uses a language model to orchestrate tools for design-for-additive-manufacturing, shaping parts for 3D printing. Subagents check flight stability and generate parametric parts for the rocket assembly, iterating on flight settings with or without a human in the loop. Four rockets with different motors and assemblies came out of the workflow.

The components were printed on fused-deposition machines, checked by hand for flight readiness, and launched at an event. All four rockets achieved launches, and two were recovered in condition to fly again. Altimeter data showed rockets reached 80 percent of the apogee, the peak altitude, that the system had predicted. The authors present that agreement between simulation and experiment as proof that agent-led design can carry a physical product from prompt to flight.

arxiv-2606-04097:
Sayan Banerjee, Subrata Mandal, Peter Orth, and Mathias Scheurer develop in 2026 a theory for reading superconductivity in materials whose normal state has chiral Bloch bands, where electron waves carry a handedness. Recent layered materials show superconductivity emerging from exactly such states.

Their tool is quasiparticle interference, the ripple patterns that defects imprint on electron waves and that microscopes can image. They show the geometric structure of the bands shapes these patterns even before superconductivity sets in, with strong dependence on which sublattice is probed. In the superconducting state, the interference also encodes the phase pattern of the pairing. The authors show how images around impurities can distinguish rival pairing states, including ones with moving Cooper pairs.
arxiv-2606-04197:
Aliakbar Mehdizadeh and Martin Hilbert explore in 2026 how memory length and network shape jointly decide whether groups of language model agents reach consensus, fragment, or lock into competing conventions. They ran a networked naming game, where agents must agree on a word, across hundreds of simulations.

Eight network layouts with sixteen agents were crossed with different memory depths, over four hundred runs in total. Longer memory slowed settling in decentralized networks but sped it in centralized ones, and faster settling there meant freezing into fragmentation sooner, not agreeing. Centralized networks kept more rival conventions alive overall. Bridge agents, those connecting clusters, suffered a coordination penalty. Agent choices matched a belief-based model called fictitious play, suggesting belief updating, not reward chasing, drives the dynamics.
arxiv-2606-04297: Alexandra Ballow computes in 2026 the Hochschild homology of generalized Reedy categories. Such categories index diagrams in homotopy theory. Hochschild homology is a stable summary that can be computed from the structure itself. Her result covers the standard cases at once: the simplex category, finite sets, finite-dimensional categories, and the PROP of an operad. One proof for all four gives researchers a ready reference, where each case once needed its own work.
arxiv-2606-04397:
Gawde and colleagues present Context-as-AI-Service, a 2026 arXiv system that helps language model agents write more accurate developer documentation. Good documentation often depends on facts spread across many files, and an agent can miss the chain linking them. The service indexes source code, API references, and existing guides, and agents query it while drafting, mixing keyword and meaning-based search.

They tested it with Claude Sonnet 4.6 on a production software kit, in two tasks: fixing API reference comments and checking a generated tutorial. In the comment review, the aided agent matched the baseline's five fixes and added four findings it missed, including two cross-file factual errors. In the tutorial check, it caught an executable bug, an API-use improvement, and two missing prerequisites. Across five runs per task, the service cut working time by 22 to 34 percent, and it also lowered token use.
arxiv-2606-04497:
Sakuldee and Abdi propose a complete recipe for controlling nuclear spins inside hexagonal boron nitride, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. The negatively charged boron vacancy is a missing boron atom in the crystal. It holds an electron spin that can reach nearby atomic nuclei. Those nuclei make promising qubits. Qubits are the basic units of quantum information. But practical methods to prepare and control them have been lacking. The authors use the electron spin as a helper qubit.

The recipe uses a background magnetic field and a multi-tone continuous drive. These engineer the electron-nucleus coupling. A Hahn echo sequence suppresses unwanted interactions. Radio-frequency drives carry out the gates. In simulations with realistic parameters, single-qubit gates reached fidelity as high as 99 percent. Multi-qubit gates reached 95 percent. Each gate finished in under 300 nanoseconds. That is fast enough to evade the electron spin's decoherence.
arxiv-2606-04697:
Kiselev studies whether randomness adds power to reductions between total search problems, in a 2026 arXiv theoretical computer science paper. TFNP is the class of problems where a solution is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently, built on principles like the pigeonhole principle. Black-box reducibility compares such problems by how solutions convert between them.

The equivalence holds for reductions from complete problems in PPP, PPAD, PPA, and a parameterized variant of PPP, the classes capturing the pigeonhole and parity arguments at the heart of the theory. As a consequence, all known black-box separations originating from these classes are strengthened automatically into randomized separations: the gaps do not close when randomness is allowed. The result cleans up the map of TFNP.
arxiv-2606-04897:
Goïcoechea and co-authors report a 2026 arXiv experiment on Anderson localization, where disorder stops waves from spreading through a material. Earlier claims for light in three dimensions stayed disputed, because side effects could mimic the expected signal. The team therefore tested microwaves passing through disordered aggregates, meaning loose packings of small metal pieces.

Their main samples packed irregular aluminum pieces in a plastic box at a metal filling fraction near 60 percent by volume. A comparison sample used aluminum flakes at only 15 percent, mixed with polystyrene spheres. At the lower share, the transmitted beam kept spreading, as ordinary diffusion predicts. At 60 percent, its sideways spread stopped growing over time, and a scaling check matched theory well. Fitted localization lengths, near 0.4 to 0.6 centimeters in their analysis, sat far below the sample thickness.
arxiv-2606-04997:
L. Toscani De Col and a large team report a working thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with a feedback loop in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instead of ticking on electron transitions like today's atomic clocks, a nuclear clock uses a low-energy transition inside the thorium-229 nucleus, which should resist outside disturbances better. The team locks a continuous-wave laser to the 148 nanometer nuclear transition.

The nuclei sit inside a millimeter-sized calcium fluoride crystal held at room temperature, and rapid feedback comes from continuous absorption spectroscopy. A subharmonic of the laser light is compared against an ytterbium single-ion clock. The nuclear clock's instability falls steadily, approaching one part in a quadrillion over a day of running. The team also used the clock to constrain models of ultralight dark matter. It matched the best atomic clocks on photon coupling and went beyond earlier work on the coupling to quarks.
arxiv-2606-05097:
Rabsan Galib Ahmed and Graeme Smith prove a no-go theorem for Gaussian quantum repeaters in this 2026 arXiv paper. Photon loss in optical channels caps how far quantum information can travel, and repeater nodes are the standard fix, but practical repeaters usually need hard non-Gaussian operations. Whether purely Gaussian protocols could raise communication rates over lossy bosonic channels had remained an open question.

The authors show they cannot. Any repeater chain built from Gaussian operations, homodyne measurements, and arbitrary classical communication cannot enhance the quantum capacity of a pure-loss attenuation channel beyond what direct transmission already achieves. Their proof generalizes the notion of k-extendibility into fractional extendibility for Gaussian states and establishes useful properties of the new concept. That machinery gives a powerful framework for analyzing Gaussian quantum networks more broadly.
arxiv-2606-05197:
This 2026 arXiv paper by Gábor Vattay is a reply and rebuttal. It disputes a claim by Lohmiller and Slotine that classical action can compute quantum waves exactly through an equivalence with the Schrödinger equation. Their most recent note tried to repair a gap, the Bohm quantum potential. It introduced a position-dependent time change meant to make the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel.

Vattay finds that the change breaks the multivariable chain rule. Because each position carries its own clock speed, the spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical frame. The claimed vanishing of the quantum potential therefore does not hold. He concludes the framework is the same as the well-known semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials, not the general exact method claimed.
arxiv-2606-05397:
Justin Kalloor and colleagues present Dyadic Phase Fixing in this 2026 arXiv paper, a compiler technique that cuts the cost of fault-tolerant quantum programs. Fault-tolerant machines run circuits built from Clifford gates plus the T gate, whose count dominates estimates. Phase kickback can slash T-count for rotations by dyadic angles, fractions with powers of two in the denominator, but it worked only for structured circuit families.

Dyadic Phase Fixing generalizes the trick to arbitrary circuits. It uses unitary synthesis to extract dyadic-angle rotations from any input circuit, and a decision matrix sizes the phase gradient register. Across a benchmark set the workflow cut T-count by 70 percent against the gridsynth compiler and 60 percent against repeat-until-success synthesis. For some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverged, showing that T-count is an incomplete proxy for the cost of a fault-tolerant program.
arxiv-2606-05497:
Alvin Wei Ming Tan, David Cardinal, and Tania Lorido-Botrán present LEVANTE-bench in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark that asks whether vision-language models reason like children. The benchmark is built on tasks and data from the LEVANTE network, which measures children's cognition across cultures. It compares models against 1,547 children aged five to twelve in three countries, across six cognitive tasks.

Alignment proved uneven. More capable models aligned better with children overall. But matching human error distributions varied widely by task. On several tasks, smaller models actually matched younger children's mistakes better than large ones did, suggesting scale moves models away from child-like reasoning even as accuracy rises. Even the best-performing models struggled on matrix reasoning and mental rotation. The authors conclude that current vision-language architectures align only partially with children's abilities, and that accuracy alone hides how differently they get there.
arxiv-2606-05797:
Amirhossein Zare and colleagues pre-train one model to predict treatment outcomes over time in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clinicians must guess how a patient will fare under each future treatment plan. Confounding shifts over time, patients differ, and data for retraining are scarce. Standard causal tools fit a fresh model to each cohort. CausalLongPFN learns from synthetic patient episodes drawn from a wide family of causal simulators.

The synthetic worlds include feedback between treatment and confounders, hidden patient types, and delayed drug effects. At the bedside the model stays frozen. It reads support trajectories plus a planned treatment sequence and returns a distribution over outcomes. Multi-step forecasts unroll one step at a time under the chosen plan. Branchable benchmarks for cancer, HIV, and warfarin dosing, plus real clinical data, test the approach against standard longitudinal methods. The design targets zero-shot causal prediction for new cohorts.
arxiv-2606-05897:
Russell, reporting for the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations, surveys the newest Higgs boson property measurements in a 2026 arXiv paper. The two giant LHC detectors recorded proton collisions at two energies. The Standard Model fixes neither the Higgs mass nor much of its behavior, so precision matters. Charge-parity violation in Higgs couplings could also help explain the universe's matter surplus.

CMS measured the Higgs mass and width through its decay into two photons. A second CMS result pinned the width through decays to W boson pairs. ATLAS combined channels to test the charge-parity nature of Higgs couplings to vector bosons. Both experiments sharpened channel-by-channel results. CMS also probed the charge-parity structure of the Higgs coupling to tau leptons. Together the measurements tighten the portrait of the Higgs sector. Any crack from Standard Model predictions would point at new physics.
arxiv-2606-06197:
Hafez Abdelghaffar, Ahmed Alansary, and Ali Hamdi work on pulling exact answers out of passages in this 2026 arXiv paper on question answering. A context based system receives a text and a question and must return a short, precise answer drawn from that text. Large language models still wander into vague or off target replies, even when the answer sits in front of them. The authors test whether focused fine tuning fixes that weakness.

They fine tuned several pretrained models on SQuAD 1.1, a benchmark built from context, question, and answer triples, and compared them under one shared setup. Fine tuning lifted every model's scores over its untouched baseline. The fine tuned RoBERTa base model performed best overall, reaching a ROUGE L score near eighty seven hundredths and a BERTScore near ninety five hundredths. The authors conclude that task specific training, not raw model size alone, drives reliable answer extraction.
arxiv-2606-06297:
Daniel Spiegel and Romain Bachy release a software toolbox for measuring reading speed in this 2026 arXiv paper on vision science. Standard reading charts use fixed sentences, so patients memorize them across visits and scores improve for the wrong reason. Reading aloud also mixes in speech motor limits, hiding how fast the eyes and brain actually process text. A French method by Perrin and colleagues solved this by generating fresh sentences from a logical scheme.

The toolbox adapts that sentence generator to English and ships it as open source MATLAB code. A semantic ontology with proto truth logic creates thousands of simple sentences whose truth values are unambiguous. Band pass psycholinguistic filtering, which keeps only sentences inside chosen ranges of word familiarity and complexity, was added for English. Special logic resolves ambiguities that English grammar introduces. The package targets maximum reading speed testing for low vision patients and cognitive research alike.
arxiv-2606-06397:
Shuo Wang and a large team of co-authors argue that graph learning leaderboards are misleading in this 2026 arXiv paper. Relational learning models are usually ranked by averaging scores across many datasets, as if all data shared one structure. The authors show that averages hide a systematic factor: the intrinsic geometry, or curvature, of each dataset. Models shine or flop depending on that geometry, so a single ranking can crown the wrong winner.

Their framework sorts datasets into positive, negative, and near zero curvature regimes before scoring. They benchmarked eighteen models, from graph convolutional networks to graph foundation models and tabular methods, across fourteen datasets. Rankings proved stable inside each regime but shifted sharply across regimes. In some regimes, expensive foundation models added little over geometry matched graph networks. The authors propose geometry aware evaluation as the new standard and release their splits and tools for the community.
arxiv-2606-06597:
Richard D Barney and co-authors find that quantum fuzziness can steady a memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Hopfield network stores patterns as attractors: show it a corrupted cue and it settles into the nearest stored memory. Their quantum vector version replaces binary neurons with quantum spins pointing in continuous directions, so the dynamics come from the spins' non commuting operators. They derive the equations of state and phase diagrams for both this network and its classical twin.

The surprise is that quantum fluctuations stabilize the stored patterns instead of washing them out. The temperature up to which retrieval works rises, and the overlap with the target pattern grows. The gain strengthens as more patterns are loaded, up to capacity. The authors read this as order by disorder, a quantum effect where fluctuations favor order. They suggest it as a design principle for quantum enhanced associative memories.
arxiv-2606-07497:
Kanumalla and a team measure the elemental makeup of an ultra-hot Jupiter's atmosphere in this 2026 arXiv paper from the Roasting Marshmallows observing program. Ultra-hot Jupiters are gas giants heated above 2,000 degrees, hot enough that volatile ice-forming and refractory rock-forming elements stay gaseous and visible, making them natural labs for planet formation. The target, MASCARA-1 b, sits at 2,600 degrees. The Gemini telescopes took its dayside spectrum at high resolution to cross-check against model atmospheres.

The analysis detected species and found the atmosphere enriched in rock-forming elements relative to expectations. That pattern constrains how the planet assembled, since rock-forming material traces the solid blocks it accreted. Comparing refractory and volatile abundances is the field's lever for telling formation near the star from migration after forming farther out. The paper is the fifth in the series using the instrument program on ultra-hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2606-07597:
Zhou, Alazraki, Cao, and Rei explain why experiments mislead teams choosing pretraining data recipes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Labs tune data mixtures on small runs and extrapolate to full budgets, but when high-quality data are scarce they get repeated more often as budgets grow, silently changing the recipe. This repetition mismatch, the authors show, is a culprit behind failed extrapolations. Their fix is a subsampling procedure that forces proxy experiments to match the target run's repetition rate for each source.

In a 2-source setting mixing limited data with web crawl, one repetition-controlled experiment used 1/16 of the target tokens. It recovered a mixture within 1/20 of the optimum for a mid-sized model, versus an error without control. Matching that accuracy naively required horizons consuming most of the budget. A 3-source test also succeeded with 2 controlled horizons. The moral: repetition is a variable in mixture design, not a nuisance.
arxiv-2606-07797:
Gustavo M. Meneses, Daniel Dominguez, and María José Sánchez show a route to sustained entanglement in two superconducting qubits, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Entanglement, the linked quantum state of two particles, is a resource for quantum computing. The pair here couples through a longitudinal interaction driven periodically, a setup described by Floquet theory for systems repeated in time.

Starting from an unentangled ground state, the linked state grows when the drive mixes two separate eigenstates at a multiphoton resonance, where drive and jump energies match. The usual rotating-wave shortcut cannot capture this, so the team builds an effective account with generalised perturbation theory. The lasting effect comes from hybridisation, the blending of the Floquet states that overlap most with the start state. One knob, the drive strength, controls it well. At certain strengths it vanishes entirely, an effect named coherent destruction of entanglement.
arxiv-2606-07897:
Botas, de Font-Reaulx, and Hewitt build a ruler for measuring how readily AI models cave to their users, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The behaviour, epistemic sycophancy, is a model endorsing claims mainly to agree with the user. Existing tests use binary flips or ask models for explicit probabilities, but real sycophancy shows up as graded shifts of support in ordinary language.

Their AI Epistemic Deference Index scores how sensitive a model's expressed support is to the attitude in the user's prompt. Estimating it needs probabilities read from natural language, obtained with model judges validated against human judgement. The test bed holds five hundred propositions and sixteen thousand prompts across eight prominent models. Every model showed substantial deference: Claude models deferred least, Grok and Gemini most. Deference grew when prompts asked for a written artefact, and concentrated on propositions where models held weaker beliefs.
arxiv-2606-08597:
Kothari analyzes a graph construction central to modern hardness-of-approximation algorithms in this 2026 arXiv paper. Kikuchi graphs are auxiliary graphs built from hypergraphs, where vertices are subsets of a fixed size and edges encode hyperedge constraints. They power recent sum-of-squares lower bounds and refutation algorithms. Kothari proves that the level-parameter Kikuchi graph of a random even-uniform hypergraph spectrally approximates the Kikuchi graph of the complete hypergraph. The sampling rate is sharp up to a logarithmic factor.

The proof uses the matrix Bernstein inequality, a concentration tool for random matrices, but applies it to an appropriate collection of blocks of Johnson eigenspaces, a new organizational device. As an application, the natural sum-of-squares relaxation for the maximum XOR problem is integral. It exactly solves the problem on planted noisy instances once the number of hyperedges passes an explicit threshold.
arxiv-2606-09197:
Albano Tabacchi, Bhanu Pratap Singh, and colleagues build a compact high-resolution photoacoustic microscope by hiding its ultrasound sensor in the lens's blind spot, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The technique fires laser pulses into tissue; absorbed light heats tiny regions that expand and emit ultrasound, imaging absorbers like melanin without labels. Optical-resolution versions focus light tightly, but standard designs struggle to fit an acoustic detector around the optics.

Their system uses a reflective objective, a mirror lens with a central obscuration zone light never reaches. Into that dead space fits a large-area PVDF transducer, a flexible polymer sensor, improving detection while preserving optical performance. They measured resolution and how signal strength depends on pulse energy. For validation they imaged sections of mouse B16F10 tumors against microscopy and stained histology. The signal correlated strongly with melanin-rich regions at 532 nm, with multi-wavelength excitation as future work.
arxiv-2606-09697:
Gianluca Barmina and his co-authors argue that a language model's refusal can do more than block harm in this 2026 arXiv paper. Flat refusals stop a risky request, yet they can leave a person in crisis with no path forward. The team's PsychoSafe scheme recasts refusal as structured support, drawn from proven crisis care practice.

They built a corpus of eight thousand prompt-response pairs across five risk zones, from self-harm to coercion. Two routes put the scheme to work: a crafted prompt, and light fine-tuning of a Qwen model. On five hundred test prompts, prompting raised refusal quality by twenty-eight percent over a plain baseline. Gains ran highest for pointing users to outside help, up forty-seven percent. Plain task skill stayed intact. Fine-tuning pushed refusal and referral rates near perfect, but answers grew less apt, a trade the authors flag.
arxiv-2606-09797:
Bobkov and his co-authors predict a new superconducting state where the phase itself staggers from cell to cell in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stage is a stack of an Ising superconductor on a balanced antiferromagnet. Ising spin-orbit coupling locks electron spins to the plane. The magnet's pull leaks into the superconductor by proximity.

In the new state, the order parameter's phase steps in a pattern tied to the magnetic grid. That step drives tiny loop currents, with opposed orbital moments on next-door cells. The state needs at least three unlike magnetic sublattices per cell, plus live spin-orbit coupling. For a stack of NbSe2 on MnPS3, first-principles and Bogoliubov-de Gennes runs found firm phase steps. Steps ran near a tenth of a radian between sites. Loop currents reached about fifteen percent of the critical current.
arxiv-2606-09897:
Dang brings tools from derived algebraic geometry into supergeometry, the mathematics that adds anticommuting coordinates to ordinary geometry, in a 2026 arXiv paper. His objects are transmutation stacks, geometric spaces that Simpson linked to three kinds of data: locally constant sheaves, D-modules, and Higgs bundles. These give Betti, de Rham, and Dolbeault versions of cohomology, the algebraic way of counting holes and shapes.

Dang develops derived categories on superstacks, proving base change and recollement results that let categories be glued and compared. With that machinery he gives new proofs of Penkov's theorem on D-modules. He also proves that de Rham cohomology matches its super counterpart, a key consistency check. The paper argues that derived and super geometry face parallel problems, so methods from one setting transfer naturally to the other.
arxiv-2606-10297:
Han and Xiao develop a method for sorting how individual firms reacted to a crisis from noisy market data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on financial econometrics. Their multi-method approach combines difference-in-differences causal estimation with cluster-robust inference, unsupervised trajectory clustering and hidden Markov models, and logistic regression for resilience prediction. They show it on two hundred forty-six Chinese A-share IT firms during the January 2020 COVID-19 shock, using non-IT index firms as controls.

The return decline proved market-wide rather than limited to IT, while the IT effect was elevated volatility, robust after a multiple-testing fix. Clustering produced three trajectory groups: fast recovery firms that gained strongly, a resilient moderate group, and a persistent drag group that lost ground, the largest of the three. The framework offers a template for splitting partial market signals in other crises.
arxiv-2606-10697:
Zhang and colleagues rethink how fashion search sees clothing in this 2026 arXiv paper on information retrieval. Attribute-specific fashion retrieval answers queries about one feature, a neckline or a sleeve. But vision transformers chop images into square patches that cut across the regions attributes live in, letting background noise leak in. Their framework, Super Fashion, uses attribute-guided attention to crop meaningful regions. It then segments those regions into superpixels, clusters of similar pixels following real boundaries, and feeds superpixel tokens, not patch tokens, to its transformer.

Separate codes let attribute and superpixel tokens interact and fuse, sharpening where the feature sits. On 3 benchmarks it improves mean average precision over the prior best by 1.84 percent on FashionAI, 9.27 percent on DARN, and 9.35 percent on DeepFashion. The authors argue that coherent tokenisation, respecting shapes in the image instead of a rigid grid, is the key ingredient for fine-grained search.
arxiv-2606-10797:
Waman and colleagues compute how strong magnetic fields reshape baryon magnetism in this 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear theory. The eight lightest baryons, the octet containing the proton and neutron, sit in matter that can be hot, dense, strange, and strongly magnetised, in collisions and magnetars alike. The team combines a chiral SU(3) quark mean-field model of the medium with a constituent quark model of the baryons, including the Dirac sea, the polarised vacuum.

With the sea included comes magnetic catalysis: condensates grow with field strength, and the baryons' masses rise with the magnetic field. At 100 megaelectronvolts, the field's effects are strongest at low density and moderated as density grows. Strangeness shifts weight between light and strange quark sectors, separating the Lambda, Sigma, and Xi baryons from the nucleons. Decomposing the moments shows valence quarks carry most of the medium dependence, with sea and orbital parts as corrections.
arxiv-2606-10897:
Moser characterizes critical points of a worst-case energy for maps in this 2026 arXiv paper. For maps between Riemannian manifolds, the infinity-harmonic functional measures the largest stretch anywhere, rather than an average. That max-type energy is not differentiable, so such points are defined through a subdifferential, covering cases like energy minimizers within a fixed homotopy class.

Moser derives a geometric condition exactly equivalent to criticality, stated through a vector-valued 1-current on the domain that packages its key properties. The current itself turns out to be a critical point of a generalized mass measure. The result gives these non-smooth variational problems a concrete handle.
arxiv-2606-11597:
Dong-Xu Yu and Zhe Wang model how supercooled liquids flow in this 2026 arXiv paper on soft matter physics. A supercooled liquid is cooled below its freezing point without turning solid, so it flows extremely slowly. Rheology, the study of how materials flow, shows odd behaviour in such liquids, including thinning under steady push and a stress overshoot when flow starts.

Their model pictures the liquid as a shifting mixture of solid-like and liquid-like regions. Two ingredients do the work: a correlation length describing medium-range order, and a local elastic interaction limiting how stress spreads inside solid-like patches. Every parameter is fixed from the still, equilibrium state, with no fitting to flow data. Even so, the model quantitatively matches measured flow across a wide range of shear rates. It also tracks how molecular motion becomes uneven, or heterogeneous, linking the large-scale flow to microscopic behaviour.
arxiv-2606-11697:
Priyank Vasu and three colleagues decompose special surfaces into simpler pieces in this 2026 arXiv paper on geometry. The surfaces have zero mean curvature, meaning they are perfectly balanced between bending in and out at every point, like soap films. The work spans three spaces with different distance rules: ordinary Euclidean space, Lorentz-Minkowski space from relativity, and isotropic space.

The authors derive new Euler-Ramanujan identities, formulas splitting one quantity into an endless sum of parts. These split the conjugate of Scherk's first minimal surface into stretched catenoids, soap-film shapes formed between two rings. Factorisation and power series methods then split broad families of such graphs into helicoids, spiral ramps, and Enneper surfaces. Finite versions are proved too, including tower-like splits. The theory is aimed partly at lamellar structures, layered materials built from such surfaces.
arxiv-2606-11997:
Shay Nadel, Amir Sivan and Aviv Karnieli propose a way to see invisible quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Arrays of emitters coupled to a waveguide can host dark states: collective modes whose radiation cancels by interference, giving them very long lifetimes. That same decoupling makes them unmeasurable by standard techniques. The trade-off is fundamental for quantum technologies, which need states both protected and accessible.

The authors' solution probes the array with weakly squeezed light from a nonlinear waveguide, light whose quantum noise is redistributed. They show the resulting fluorescence spectrum reveals transitions between the dressed dark states of the array. Numerical studies of four- and six-emitter arrays confirm the spectrum maps onto the dark-state transition frequencies. The readout also survives realistic flaws such as free-space decay. Beyond measurement, the squeezing strength offers a knob for controlling the dark-state manifold itself.
arxiv-2606-12197:
Kothari and Tudose prove a conjecture about the vibrations of networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A graph is a network of vertices joined by edges. Its Laplacian, a matrix built from vertex degrees and connections, has eigenvalues that act like vibration frequencies. Brouwer's conjecture bounds the sum of the largest few: it may not exceed the edge count plus a small triangular correction. Partial results covered special families for decades.

The authors prove the bound for every graph and every cutoff. Their route uses the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem, a known result comparing Laplacian eigenvalues with the degree pattern of split graphs, a family whose vertices divide into a clique and an independent set. Surprisingly, they also prove the reverse direction. Brouwer's conjecture and the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem therefore imply each other exactly. Two problems treated as separate turn out to be one statement in disguise.
arxiv-2606-12297:
Lionas and co-authors propose that the universe's speeding expansion is a quantum bookkeeping effect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cosmic acceleration is usually blamed on a cosmological constant or dark energy. Quantum theory allows post-selection: conditioning results on a final state as well as an initial one. With coarse-graining, ignoring fine detail, post-selection can bend effective classical dynamics. The authors build a cosmological model on that idea.

Their model needs no cosmological constant, dark energy, or modified gravity. The expansion history depends on at most two parameters beyond standard evolution. Fits to supernova and cosmic chronometer data rival the standard model. The coincidence problem, why acceleration starts now, dissolves naturally. Early radiation and matter eras come out standard. One sharp difference: the model predicts a present-day jerk parameter, the expansion's third derivative, far from the standard value. Future data can kill or confirm the idea.
arxiv-2606-12497:
Cherepanov and co-authors ask what memory alone buys a robot, stripping away every other gadget, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models predict action chunks from the view, which fails when a needed cue has left the screen. Existing memory-augmented models change many things at once, so recurrence's contribution stays unclear. Their muVLA adds memory tokens, carried across timesteps and updated by self-attention, to an OpenVLA backbone. Training uses truncated backpropagation, with no auxiliary losses.

On MIKASA-Robo, success across five training tasks jumps from 0.42 at baseline to 0.84 at the strongest setting, while held-out tasks climb from 0.07 without memory to 0.23 with it. Cue-recall tasks drive the gain: remembering a color goes from near zero to above nine in ten. Tasks needing different memory stay near baseline. On LIBERO, success hits about ninety-six percent; nothing is lost when the world is fully visible.
arxiv-2606-12597:
Diaz-Uriarte and co-authors teach cancer progression models to answer what-if questions correctly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Evolutionary accumulation models infer the order in which tumors gain mutations, from snapshots across patients. Clinicians hope such models can nominate drug targets. But the obvious trick, conditioning on a mutation's absence, predicts intervention effects wrongly. The authors formalize intervention, using Pearl's do-operator, for every model family.

For most models, intervening becomes a tweak to parameters. They flag which implementations are equivalent and test the modularity assumption. Drawing causal diagrams at the individual level, with fitness explicit, splits interventions models conflate. Killing cells that carry a mutation is not inactivating the mutation itself. Since the goal is choosing targets, they recast evaluation as ranking, defining intervention objectives and a protocol for scoring model rankings. The framework travels beyond cancer to any model read as a structural causal model.
arxiv-2606-12997:
Greenbury and colleagues compare, head-to-head, the reliability of 2 leading methods for probabilistic emulation of physical systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The 2 options are generative models, such as diffusion or flow matching, and ensembles of fixed-rule models with added randomness trained with the continuous ranked probability score loss. Both predict well, but how reliable their uncertainty is had not been checked under matched terms.

Across 2-dimensional spatiotemporal physical systems, with matched model size and computing budget, the authors check coverage of forecast ranges with accuracy and speed. Continuous-ranked-probability-score-trained ensembles usually achieve more reliable error bars in both single-step prediction and autoregressive rollouts, with better coverage than generative models trained in a latent space, and they run faster. Generative models trained in ambient space match the ensembles' coverage but with larger latency. Score-trained ensembles keep coverage when trained in latent space.
arxiv-2606-13097:
Chun and colleagues present FCGraft, a functional cache grafting framework for synthesising code policies for embodied agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Code-writing language models generate executable control programs from natural-language goals. But in open-domain environments this suffers 2 limitations: delayed decoding from prefill computation over long prompts, and limited robustness. Generative decoding produces application-interface mismatches, missing safety guards, and unstable control logic.

FCGraft maintains a library of function-level checked code skeletons with their linked prompt-level key-value caches from the Transformer. For a new task, it retrieves relevant functions and grafts their caches. It builds policies by stitching, which composes cached function segments into a composite policy. It also patches: adapting the necessary code regions to task-specific parameters and constraints with less decoding. Against the prompt-level caching method RAGCache, FCGraft achieves an 18.31 percent higher task success rate and 2.3 times faster policy synthesis.
arxiv-2606-13397:
Das and colleagues present Mod-Guide in this 2026 arXiv paper, a moderation feedback system aimed at insensitive speech toward Indigenous ethnic and religious minority communities. Online language can sideline minority groups, yet moderation now relies on large language models whose judgements may miss local cultural context. Rather than simply deleting flagged content, Mod-Guide gives feedback intended to address the insensitivity itself. The work is situated in social computing research, with attention to how affected groups experience harmful speech.

The system uses a language model to analyse flagged text and respond with guidance, helping users understand why their words may wound minority readers. The authors frame moderation as a learning opportunity rather than only enforcement. Their study examines how such feedback can be designed for groups whose languages and norms are poorly served by mainstream moderation tools. The paper contributes to research on computing for societies.
arxiv-2606-13497:
Blank and colleagues present SPARC in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that labels robot demonstration data automatically and honestly. Structured annotations, such as object bounding boxes, trajectories, and phase labels, are valuable for training robot policies and planning systems. Automated pipelines can generate them at scale, but they offer no trustworthy quality signal. A detector's confidence turns out to be poorly calibrated for whether an annotation is actually correct. Users are forced to accept noisy labels wholesale or discard useful data.

SPARC exploits the spatio-temporal structure built into robot tasks to derive a reliability score for each annotation. Consistency across time and space exposes labels that a single-frame detector would pass silently. The framework is risk-aware: downstream users can keep high-reliability annotations and treat the rest with caution, instead of guessing. The authors argue that calibrated reliability, not just volume, is what demonstration datasets need.
arxiv-2606-13697:
Deng, Gao, and Wang improve a classic investing method that must cope with faulty forecasts. Mean-variance portfolio choice balances expected return against risk, but suffers when estimates of returns and their spread are wrong. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the multiperiod version, where holdings are adjusted over time. They add reference regulation, a penalty that keeps the chosen portfolio from straying too far from a trusted reference policy.

The authors derive how the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, a reward-per-risk score, behaves when assets are many relative to the data. They show how penalty strength and investment horizon jointly shape performance. A new effect appears: reference weights can correct errors in risk estimates, while the risk matrix corrects errors in return estimates. Simulations and real market data confirm the approach. Portfolios grow more stable, and Sharpe ratios improve markedly.
arxiv-2606-13897:
El Haskouki and Gernandt ask when energy-based models of physical systems stay well behaved after delays are added. Port-Hamiltonian systems describe machines and networks by stored energy, losses, and connection ports. Transport delays are natural here, but they can destroy passivity, the property that a system never creates energy at its ports. Their 2026 arXiv paper derives passivity conditions for linear versions with several constant delays.

The conditions use a chosen storage function with Wirtinger-based inequalities, ending as linear matrix inequalities a computer can check. Passivity also survives negative feedback interconnection, a key structural benefit. The authors recall stability conditions under both delay-dependent and delay-independent assumptions. Two applications ground the theory: district heating networks and an oscillator with delayed damping.
arxiv-2606-13997:
Aranda's team defines polarization as resistance to consensus, measured as the cheapest way to end disagreement. Existing measures compute a number from an opinion spread but never say where agreement could be reached. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines Minimum Effort to Consensus: the least cost of transforming a spread into a consensus one, minimized over all consensus points. The measure outputs the optimal consensus point itself, the cheapest meeting place.

In the basic case it equals the one-Wasserstein distance to the nearest consensus distribution. Special cases recover mean absolute deviation about the median, and variance-like dispersion. Two parameters weight masses and movement costs: group identification and the cost of revising beliefs. The optimal point anchors a Minority Principle and a closed-form Tipping Point method, which finds the critical mass where moving opinions away stops reducing it and starts increasing it. It is not monotone in extremism.
arxiv-2606-14097:
Czygrinow and Parvatikar sharpen the color threshold forcing a rainbow four-cycle in triangle-free graphs. A rainbow cycle uses a different color per edge; color-degree counts distinct colors at a vertex. Ding and others had forced such a cycle once the minimum color-degree passed n over five plus three root n. Their 2026 arXiv paper cuts the additive term to a constant.

The theorem: for large n, if every vertex of a triangle-free edge-colored graph on n vertices sees at least n plus seven over five distinct colors, a rainbow four-cycle must exist. The bound is provably best possible. A second result gives rainbow cycles of length four k under a weaker condition, color-degree above n over five plus three. Regularity and stability methods drive the proof. The threshold had fallen from n over three toward n over five; this pins it.
arxiv-2606-14597:
de Villeroché and co-authors test whether neural PDE solvers can scale to bigger domains in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neural operators learn to map inputs to full PDE solutions. Transformer versions excel on complex geometries. But they silently assume the domain size seen in training. So they fail on larger regions.

The authors argue this zero-shot task needs two traits. It needs spatial locality. It also needs translation equivariance, where shifting the input shifts the output equally. They build locality through a bias added to attention scores. The bias stays decomposable, so fast attention kernels still work. They pair it with rotary positional embeddings. Across two PDE benchmarks and a 3D industrial flow case, the approach helped a lot. Zero-shot generalization to much larger domains improved sharply. The transformer design itself stayed unchanged.
arxiv-2606-14797:
Watanabe models self-copying chemistry in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system has three layers. Raw molecules feed catalytic proteins. Large RNA-like chains act as genes. The chains fold, and their folded shapes set how active each protein is. A small noise term keeps the system out of balance, as real living chemistry is.

The model was searched for settings where the chemistry sustains itself. Two trends appeared together, as theory predicts. Disorder in the surroundings rose while the gene layer grew more ordered. The cost was steep: about five hundred eighty-nine nats of outside disorder per nat of gene order. Standard bounds on speed and precision sat far below the model's values. A stripped one-cycle version behaved far better. Its precision product fell to about five, near what ribosomes show.
arxiv-2606-14997:
Kwon and coauthors hunt for memory traces inside neural networks, modeled on brain engrams, in a 2026 study. Neuroscience defines an engram by four tests: specificity, reactivation, sufficiency, and necessity. Whether trained networks hold such identifiable units has been unclear, since parameters serve many behaviors at once. The team turns the four tests into a constrained inverse problem.

Solving that problem gives a closed-form estimator that isolates one memory trace from entangled weights. The solution also matches a natural gradient step on the parameter manifold, tying biology to information geometry. With a trace in hand, memories can be composed or erased by plain linear arithmetic, with no retraining loop. Experiments range from small multilayer perceptrons to billion-parameter language models. Traces show a condensed localization pattern even in large models. The authors frame the method as a structural route to machine unlearning, replacing slow gradient search with direct identification.
arxiv-2606-15497:
Yamada and colleagues present The AI Scientist in 2026, the strongest demonstration yet of end-to-end automation of machine learning research. The system creates research ideas, writes code, runs experiments, plots and analyses data, writes the full manuscript, and even performs peer review. Earlier tools automated single steps of science; none covered the whole cycle from conception to publication.

The team tests the system in two modes: a focused mode seeded with human code templates, and an open-ended, template-free mode that searches more widely. Both modes produce diverse ideas and test, report, and evaluate them automatically. One AI-generated manuscript passed the first round of peer review at a workshop of a major machine learning conference, where about seventy percent of submissions are accepted. The authors flag risks, including strain on review systems and noise in the literature, but argue such systems could greatly speed discovery.
arxiv-2606-15697:
Matsuzaki and colleagues apply equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory to a tungsten antifluorite in 2026, to pin down how electrons and lattice vibrations entangle in Cs2WCl6. Its tungsten sites have degenerate spin-orbit states coupling to Jahn-Teller active vibrations, which should distort the lattice. Yet experiments see no symmetry lowering in the low-temperature ordered phases, a standing puzzle.

The team derives model Hamiltonians for the embedded tungsten sites, then computes the X-ray scattering spectra and effective magnetic moment. Vibronic coupling makes several spectral peaks asymmetric, and the calculated moment tracks the measured temperature dependence closely. The verdict: the Jahn-Teller effect here sits in the weak regime, too feeble to deform the lattice. Its dynamic form still reshapes the spectra and shifts the moment, which reconciles theory with the missing distortion. The study also showcases coupled-cluster methods for metal sites inside correlated insulators.
arxiv-2606-15897:
Wyrwal, Ceylan, and Tong introduce topological flow matching in 2026, a generative modelling framework for signals that live on structured spaces rather than flat Euclidean ones. Standard flow matching treats data such as brain activity on a brain graph as plain vectors, discarding the domain's topology. The authors reinterpret flow matching as solving a degenerate Schrödinger bridge problem, which opens a principled place to inject structure: the reference process.

They augment that process with a drift derived from the domain's Laplacian, a prior that smooths signal components which do not correspond to topological features. The modification provably keeps flow matching's attractions: a stable, simulation-free training objective and deterministic sample paths, so the method drops into existing pipelines. Across brain fMRI, ocean currents, seismic events, and traffic flows, it improves over standard flow matching and over topological Schrödinger bridge matching, with the largest advantage on the most complex structures.
arxiv-2606-16297:
Krolewski and the DESI Collaboration map where gamma rays come from in 2026 by cross-matching the gamma-ray sky with galaxy surveys. The Fermi-LAT satellite sees extragalactic gamma-ray emission, but much of it stays unresolved, its sources unknown. Cross-correlating that sky with maps of large-scale structure reveals the redshift distribution of the sources, layer by layer. The galaxy maps come from the DESI DR2 release and the unWISE catalog.

First, known gamma-ray point sources cross-correlate clearly with structure, with a clustering bias near 2, like the massive galaxies that host bright active galactic nuclei. The unresolved gamma-ray background then shows a cross-correlation detected at about 10 sigma in total, strongly in both surveys. Its redshift pattern fits a mix of known source classes. The fits also flag some Galactic contamination at low energies, which softens earlier claims about the background's energy spectrum.
arxiv-2606-16997:
McLean bounds the size of curve-counting invariants in a 2026 algebraic geometry paper. Gromov-Witten invariants count curves on a geometric space with marked points, anchoring much of enumerative geometry and mirror symmetry. Knowing they exist is one thing; bounding their growth is another.

For any smooth projective variety, McLean bounds each primary genus-zero invariant using only concrete data. The inputs are the maximum degree of the defining polynomials, the norms of the inserted forms, the number of marked points, and the curve degree. The bounds grow factorially in the marked points. One consequence is analytic: the Borel transform of the generating function converges absolutely on part of the ample cone. The proof starts from Siebert's formula, expressing the invariants through Segre and Chern classes, and routes through an intermediate curve count in projective space. Explicit growth control turns a formal series into a function with a genuine domain.
arxiv-2606-17497:
Nasser and Adcroft present a 2026 arXiv paper on design rules for data-driven numerical schemes that solve the linear advection equation, a basic transport law in fluid simulation. Neural schemes can drift unstable or fail on new data when built without numerical analysis principles. Working with finite-volume methods in one dimension, the authors vary normalisation, training data, and architecture to see which choices govern stability, accuracy, and shape preservation in the learned schemes they train.

Reconstruction from cell averages alone makes the learning problem multi-valued, which explains poor generalisation across curvature regimes. Enforcing a semilinear form through local stencil-scale normalisation restores stability and good generalisation in their tests. A new data-driven flux limiter beats a classical scheme at preserving shapes by adding mild antidiffusion in near-linear regions. Training on polynomial profiles also yields stable, high-order schemes, with degree setting the accuracy order.
arxiv-2606-17597:
Čap and Gover present a 2026 arXiv paper in differential geometry on how spaces that open out to infinity can be described near their boundary, with general relativity as the motivating case. Scattering theory and relativity both use metrics with specific asymptotic shapes near infinity, and projective compactness captures some of them. The authors weaken that notion to projective pre-compactness, defined for torsion-free connections and, through the Levi-Civita link, for the metrics physicists use near infinity.

Under mild conditions on Ricci curvature, such a structure appears on the boundary itself. Slightly stronger conditions make the standard tractor bundle and its connection arise there naturally, through a smooth extension in Melrose's b-calculus. The boundary then splits into curved orbits matching space-like, time-like, and light-like infinities. A new normal form for such metrics ties the theory back to relativity's usage.
arxiv-2606-17997:
Qiumu and colleagues simulate the radioactive glow of matter blasted off a magnetar, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, and their rare giant flares may eject neutron-rich material where the rapid neutron-capture process can forge heavy elements. Late gamma-ray emission seen from the flare of SGR 1806-20 hints that this really happens.

Running nuclear reaction networks, the team finds the synthesized nuclei cluster near the first and second r-process abundance peaks. Because of that mix, the ejecta block kiloelectronvolt gamma rays about a thousand times more strongly than megaelectronvolt ones. The escaping nuclear light is thus dominated by MeV photons in the first thousand seconds, giving future telescopes concrete line signatures to search for after the next nearby giant flare.
arxiv-2606-18797:
Lu and the team study whether language models can judge how much errors in radiology reports matter, in a 2026 medical AI paper. Report scoring matters, because an omitted critical finding can change patient care. Yet existing metrics collapse quality into a baseless score. Smart language models blur the line between errors that matter and harmless rephrasings.

Using the ReEvalMed benchmark, the authors score evaluators on discrimination, catching clinical errors, and robustness to small, harmless variation, across eight of them in one-pass and two-pass settings. They find a common discrimination bias. Models detect errors well, but over-punish benign variation. Building four thousand report pairs, they trained lightweight metrics on open models that sharpened the boundary. Those beat larger medical models and rivaled closed ones. The costlier two-pass setting did not help throughout, mainly trading discrimination for robustness. So the paper advises one-pass trained metrics for use.
arxiv-2606-18897:
Xia and the team build a recommender system whose user intents are discovered from text by sparse autoencoders, rather than imposed, in a 2026 information systems paper. Intent-based recommenders model what drives clicks and purchases, to improve accuracy and interpretability. But most derive intents by clustering behavior. That makes them sensitive to sequence quality, forces a preset intent count, and leaves the intents without meaning.

SAERec applies a sparse autoencoder to large language model embeddings of a textual corpus. It pulls human-interpretable intents out of noise. For each user, it retrieves two kinds of intent priors. Personal intents match interests. Public intents capture item patterns shared across users, such as quality or price sensitivity. SAERec injects them into sequence modeling, through a multi-branch attention mechanism with fusion. Experiments on public datasets showed gains over leading baselines. SAERec also produced human-understandable explanations of its recommendations.
arxiv-2606-18997:
Galeano and colleagues introduce DIPHINE in 2026, a neural estimator for breaking down how information flows in complex systems over time. The framework behind it splits information into sixteen distinct atoms. These atoms capture what parts store alone, what they share, and what they create only together. Past tools could compute this split only for Gaussian or discrete systems, which blocked use on many real continuous systems.

DIPHINE uses score-based diffusion models to gauge all the mutual information terms the split needs, from a single trained network. A Möbius inversion step then recovers the sixteen atoms. The authors study how errors spread through that inversion. They show the key mapping has whole-number entries, and that the synergy-to-synergy atom is provably the hardest to gauge. On synthetic tests, the method recovers atoms well and beats older tools on continuous non-Gaussian dynamics.
arxiv-2606-19197:
Haak and colleagues study ABox abduction under repair semantics in 2026, asking whether hypotheses can satisfy several desirable properties at once. Abduction explains a missing entailment by proposing facts that, if added, would make it true. Under repair semantics, recent work has mapped properties like signature limits and small size. Hypotheses meeting more than one property would be even better for applications, but they had not been studied.

This problem is considered for a lightweight logic under brave and AR semantics. Hypotheses must combine properties, or pair a property with a best-score rule. The main observation is encouraging. Requiring extra properties often does not raise cost at all. Combined requirements can thus be imposed in many cases for free. That finding widens the design space for explanation systems.
arxiv-2606-19297:
Kachaev and colleagues ask in 2026 whether vision-language-action models retain basic commonsense and world knowledge after robotics fine-tuning. Such models start from powerful pretrained vision-language models, then adapt to robot data. Failures on knowledge tasks are ambiguous, since missing knowledge and poor low-level control look alike. The team introduces Act2Answer, a protocol that adapts knowledge benchmarks so agents must answer through action, not text.

Each question becomes a short tabletop episode. The agent makes one object-placement action to pick among candidate answers, yielding an action-grounded success rate with reduced control confounds. A curated suite spans diverse commonsense and world-knowledge categories. Layerwise intent probing further localizes where answer-relevant information lives across the backbone and action head. The large-scale study measures how much knowledge survives embodied adaptation, and where it fades. That map helps builders protect knowledge during fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-19497:
Hamed Talebian and five colleagues tackle blocked radio paths in Bluetooth indoor positioning in 2026. Bluetooth Low Energy direction finding can locate gear inside factories, but walls and machines reflect the signal. Those reflections create non-line-of-sight paths that bend angle estimates and spoil the fix.

The team built a controlled test setup that records labelled clear and blocked signals in two distinct indoor settings. Signal features pass through robust scaling, then checks with principal component analysis and density estimates confirm the two classes separate. A Nyström kernel map feeds a light support vector classifier, lifting accuracy by about 7 to 14 percent over raw features. A neural network scores slightly higher, but the kernel route costs less memory and power. Tuned thresholds then let small devices flag bad paths in real time.
arxiv-2606-19697:
Yanhong Li, Anej Svete, Ashish Sabharwal, and William Merrill show in 2026 that chain-of-thought transformers can run standard algorithms efficiently. Reasoning models emit thought tokens before answering, and theory says they can simulate Turing machines. Turing machines, though, are a clumsy yardstick for how algorithms are really designed.

Algorithms live in the Word RAM model, with random-access memory and unit-cost word operations. The team ask whether chain-of-thought can simulate Word RAM at matching speed. Sorting and shortest-path routines set the test cases. The answer is yes, up to small poly-logarithmic overhead. Three settings support the result: finite-precision models, continuous vector-valued thought, and a hybrid with a recurrent base layer. Flat instruction sets shrink the overhead further, to log-square or even a single log factor. Older Turing machine simulations needed quadratic overhead, making the new bound far sharper.
arxiv-2606-20097:
Zhentao Tan and six colleagues redesign hybrid attention for language models around one observation: attention heads inside a layer do different jobs, even though they read the same input. Their 2026 paper, HydraHead, mixes full attention, accurate but costly as context grows, with linear attention, cheap but weaker, along the head axis rather than layer by layer. Earlier hybrids assigned whole layers to one type, ignoring the specialization that interpretability studies reveal among heads.

HydraHead keeps full attention only for heads proven critical to retrieval, picked by an interpretability-driven selection, and fuses both output types through a scale-normalized module. A three-stage pipeline reuses parameters and distills knowledge, so training stays light. At a seven-to-one ratio of linear to full heads, it matched a three-to-one layer-wise hybrid on long-context tasks. Training on only fifteen billion tokens still beat rival hybrids by wide margins.
arxiv-2606-20497:
Antonio Varagnolo and four colleagues bring readable meta-learning models to chemical search with several goals at once. Their 2026 paper tackles the vast space of molecules that can actually be made, where stand-in models must juggle competing aims. Deep learning struggles here under the cost limits of quantum-level chemistry.

A modular pipeline pairs linear meta-learning models, whose rules chemists can read, with uncertainty scores that adapt their confidence, inside an Efficient Global Optimization loop. Training across chemical aims and cheap side properties lets the linear models borrow strength between tasks. Meta-learning of this kind is used in a multi-goal chemical search for the first time. Chemists get stand-in models they can actually read, which matters when a model steers costly synthesis choices.
arxiv-2606-20597:
Nia George and Simeon Sayer chart six decades of U.S. juvenile justice with topic modeling and LLM-assisted analysis. Their 2026 paper applies the methods to 60,470 appellate opinions from 1970 to 2025. Juvenile courts handle both delinquency cases and child welfare cases, and both streams have changed dramatically.

The analysis identifies 182 legal topics organized into 10 themes across juvenile justice litigation. Child welfare litigation tripled its share of the corpus, and sex offender registration cases more than doubled. The shifts trace the system's move from punishment toward protection, the arc the title names. Computational tracking shows legal change at a scale no manual review could cover.
arxiv-2606-20797:
M Abumusabh and the Belle II Collaboration report in 2026 the first measurement of mixing-induced CP violation in a rare B meson decay to two neutral pions. CP violation is a difference between matter and antimatter behavior. Such tests probe the standard theory and search for new particles or interactions.
