The data come from 190 million events collected with Belle II at the SuperKEKB collider in Japan.

A new method uses quantum entanglement of the produced B meson pair. It enables a time-dependent analysis without reconstructing the decay position of the signal meson. The mixing-induced coefficient is measured with large uncertainty, centered at 0.61. Precision matches what a conventional analysis would need twenty times more data to reach. A direct CP coefficient is also measured. Rare decay channels like this one can expose effects that common channels hide.
arxiv-2606-20897:
Zeyuan Chen and four colleagues propose PeerCheck in 2026 to raise the quality of language model academic reviews toward human level. Submissions keep growing, and peer review struggles to keep pace. Models are increasingly used to assist. PeerCheck first compares model reviews with human reviews. It finds different emphases: models prioritize theory, while humans stress methods and experiments.

Two improvement routes are then tested. Prompt methods such as chain-of-thought reasoning are applied. Retrieval-augmented generation, which fetches source text, is also tried. Chain-of-thought improves review quality clearly. Retrieval gives mixed results, an effect called the RAG paradox. For some models it even lowers quality. Knowing which aid helps and which hurts matters as journals consider model help. A fluent review that misses methods may look strong while failing the core job of peer review.
arxiv-2606-21197:
Sergio Lanza, Jae Lee, and Stefan Wermter propose a framework in 2026 to extract multimodal concepts from vision-language models through sparse autoencoders. Such models caption images and answer visual questions well. Their internal processes remain poorly understood. Sparse autoencoders can surface interpretable concepts inside a model. Most earlier work treats text and visual concepts separately, missing concepts that join both.

For each neuron, a candidate human-interpretable concept is proposed. Alignment between the concept and dataset samples is scored by cosine similarity. Visual, textual, and multimodal concepts are all analyzed in one frame. Earlier visual methods often gave vague or incomplete descriptions, limiting their use. Joint concepts matter because a vision-language model may encode ideas like a pictured word's meaning that belong to neither modality alone, and interpretability tools must catch them to explain model behavior.
arxiv-2606-21397:
Sebastian Neef and four colleagues benchmark language models as web security auditors in 2026, testing whether they can find real flaws in WordPress plugin code. The flaws targeted are classic web vulnerabilities: SQL injection, stored cross-site scripting, path traversal, and remote code execution. Six frontier and open-weight models were run under five prompt designs of varying structure and scope, across three repeated rounds.

Every model found genuine issues, but rates ranged widely, from 63 percent for Claude Opus 4.6 down to 35 percent for a self-hosted Qwen model. Prompts that narrowed the vulnerability scope beat open-ended ones, while prompt complexity mattered little. No model reported consistently across rounds, with some near fifty percent, and one baseline flaw escaped every model, a sober limit for automated auditing.
arxiv-2606-21497:
Neeraj Mohan Sushma and six colleagues propose Hierarchical Block-Local Learning in 2026, a training method that breaks the sequential bottleneck of backpropagation. Backprop forces errors to travel through every layer before any update, locking layers together and demanding symmetric forward and backward paths. Their framework splits a deep network into hierarchically linked blocks, each trained on local objectives drawn from variational principles, so no full backward pass is needed.

The authors claim this is the first method able to train deep networks in logarithmic parallel time in the number of layers. The hierarchy also defines a family of subnetworks along different paths, letting inference use varying effective depths. Tests on vision and language tasks reach competitive accuracy, and an extension covers recurrent sequence models that normally rely on backpropagation through time.
arxiv-2606-21797:
O'Keeffe studies swarmalators in 2026, models of moving oscillators whose positions and internal phases influence each other. His one-dimensional ring model adds van Hemmen pair disorder, meaning the coupling strength between each pair is randomly signed rather than uniform. Disorder of this kind is known from spin-glass physics, and the paper asks how it reshapes the ring's collective states.

Disorder first splits the static states into four branches: sync, split, splay, and phase wave. New order parameters that track glass-like order organize them. Because the oscillators move, two active states appear that the immobile version lacks: a bursty asynchronous state and, for balanced sign patterns, a glassy phase wave with rotating glass order. O'Keeffe derives a six-field reduced model, the exact sync boundary at any population size, and an exact antiphase phase-wave branch. A nonlinear theory covering both active branches remains open.
arxiv-2606-21997:
Galloway and colleagues examine, in 2026, a technical step inside the proofs of the Lorentzian splitting theorems. Those theorems describe when a spacetime must split into a time line times a fixed space. Distance functions to points along a complete timelike line are known to be locally equi-Lipschitz, meaning the whole family shares one local slope bound. That fact is essential to the classical proofs, and the paper asks whether it survives a natural generalization.

The generalization replaces points with the level sets of a Cauchy temporal function, a time function whose slices cut across the whole spacetime. The authors show the equi-Lipschitz property fails in general for these families of Lorentz distances. They then formulate conjectures about when temporal functions with the good property exist in such spacetimes. Those conjectures turn out to be equivalent to Bartnik's cosmological splitting conjecture.
arxiv-2606-22197:
Wang and colleagues introduce Multi4D in 2026, a framework for dynamic Gaussian splatting that aims to keep both motion consistency and visual fidelity. Dynamic splatting renders moving 3D scenes from Gaussian primitives. Deformation-based methods preserve object identity but oversmooth fast detail, while 4D methods capture detail at heavy storage cost and break identity over time.

Multi4D instead spreads modelling capacity over three levels: static structure, dynamic geometry that persists, and short-lived appearance primitives. Through shared rendering and residual-driven optimization, the levels compete to explain image error and specialize without any pre-assigned split. The split preserves long-term motion consistency while still capturing fine dynamic detail. The authors report top rendering quality in real time, with significantly fewer dynamic primitives. Because compact persistent Gaussians are tracked over time, the system also reaches top 4D segmentation accuracy, with a tenfold speedup.
arxiv-2606-22397:
Chengnan Shentu and four colleagues, including Jessica Burgner-Kahrs, work on soft robotics in this 2026 paper. Their robots are tendon-driven continuum robots, flexible arms steered by pulling cables. Learning to manipulate objects with the whole body is hard because good simulators for soft robots lag behind those for rigid ones.

The team derives a discretization informed by continuum mechanics, a way of splitting the flexible body into pieces for computation. It places the soft robot natively inside MuJoCo, a physics simulator, uniting tendon forces, body contact, and motion in one pipeline. They validate the simulator against a Cosserat rod reference model and against real robot hardware. Policies trained by imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations then transferred, with no further training, to a physical three-segment robot mounted on a Franka arm. The authors report success on two contact-rich manipulation tasks, a first for continuum robots.
arxiv-2606-22497:
Tianqi Wei, Xin Yu, Zhi Chen, Scott Chapman, and Zi Huang present a benchmark for vision-language models in this 2026 paper. Such models answer questions about images, but existing tests focus on ordinary photographs. Microscopic plant images, which reveal cells and pathogens, remain largely untested even though plant biologists rely on them.

Their benchmark, PlantMicro, gathers more than five thousand images from diverse hosts, biological domains, and imaging methods. Over nine thousand visual question-answering pairs probe different aspects of understanding these images. When leading models were evaluated, they struggled with fine-grained recognition and biologically grounded reasoning. On pathogen classification, the strongest example given scored about thirty-five percent accuracy. That is only modestly above the random guessing baseline of about twenty-five percent. The authors offer PlantMicro as a standard foundation for improving microscopy-level plant understanding in future models.
arxiv-2606-22597:
Srinivas Venkatanarayanan and Clement Pakkam Isaac test whether vision-language models can make verifiable decisions from street maps in this 2026 paper. Models increasingly read maps to support logistics, delivery, and accessible navigation, where the result is an action that must respect the road network. Most benchmarks grade free text, which cannot be checked against the underlying street graph.

Their benchmark, MapReason-OSM, renders maps of ten US downtowns at two zoom scales, each panel paired with a hidden street graph and oracles. Six thousand instances span twelve tasks covering routing, facility location, and visual disambiguation. Model decisions are snapped back to the graph and scored for validity, legality, optimality, and consistency across zooms. Across seven models, the systems read maps and routed simply, but failed at graph-cost reasoning. Placing a single facility pin was near chance even for frontier reasoning models, and answers often changed with scale.
arxiv-2606-22797:
Tianjia Dong, Nadav Kunievsky, and James A. Evans ask whether a language model's behavior travels, in this 2026 paper. Two decision settings can share identical payoffs yet differ in surface presentation. A model that behaves one way in the first may act differently in the second, which makes suite-based evaluation fragile.

The authors define behavior portability formally. They fit an interpretable behavioral model on data pooled from several source environments, then test it on a held-out target environment. Performance is compared against an oracle trained directly on target data, and their measure gives worst-case bounds for the target setting. Across seven classic economic decision problems, they found substantial, systematic portability losses. Behavioral profiles measured in one setting, they conclude, cannot be assumed to transfer to an equivalent setting with different wording or framing. That warning applies to any benchmark that treats one phrasing as the model's true character.
arxiv-2606-22997:
Dakai Guo and colleagues settle a number theory conjecture about binomial coefficients in a 2026 paper. Binomial coefficients count how many ways items can be chosen from a set. The conjecture, recorded in a public sequence database, concerns the greatest common divisor of a certain family of these numbers. It predicts exactly when that shared divisor equals one. The condition involves the largest prime power piece of a related whole number.

Guo and colleagues prove the criterion holds in full. The proof is also formalized in Lean, a computer proof assistant that checks each logical step. The formal version was accepted into the Formal Conjectures project, a shared library of checked statements. The text states that an AI agent system built by the authors generated both the plain-language proof and the Lean version.
arxiv-2606-23197:
Sophie Corallo and colleagues present the EVerest dataset for secure software engineering in a 2026 paper. Checking security end to end means tracing a system from written requirements through architecture down to code. No existing dataset spans all three levels with fine-grained security labels. EVerest fills that gap using a real open-source stack of software for charging electric vehicles, built with industry partners. The dataset holds eighty-four hand-elicited security requirements, each tagged with its security objectives.

Corallo and colleagues add over fourteen hundred fine-grained security elements, covering components, data, data flows, and states. Acceptance windows, cross-references, and trace links connect the requirements to the architecture model. Source code and documentation in natural language complete the package. The resource lets researchers test verification tools on one consistent, realistic system instead of toy examples.
arxiv-2606-23397:
Murtazo Nazarov builds a high-order finite element method that respects physical bounds in a 2026 paper. The method solves nonlinear scalar conservation laws, equations where a quantity is transported without being created or destroyed. A good scheme must keep the solution inside its invariant domain, never overshooting into impossible values. Nazarov combines a high-order scheme with a low-order bound-preserving scheme built on a fine submesh. The split avoids restrictions from lumped masses and wide stencils.

Nazarov links the two updates through a graph-Poisson flux reconstruction. Their difference becomes a set of conservative antisymmetric fluxes on a graph. Convex limiting coefficients then trim those fluxes, and a redistribution step restores exact conservation where room allows. Tests show high-order accuracy, convergence to the entropy solution, and robustness near discontinuities.
arxiv-2606-23497:
Talamini proves that solutions of certain wave-like systems have well-defined boundary values, in a 2026 paper on partial differential equations. The systems are two-by-two conservation laws, equations that track two quantities whose totals are preserved as they flow. Bounded entropy solutions can develop sharp features, so asking what value a solution takes exactly on a curve is delicate. For single scalar equations, strong traces have been known for years. For systems, the theory largely stalled.

Talamini shows that bounded entropy solutions of genuinely nonlinear, strictly hyperbolic systems do admit strong traces on Lipschitz curves, curves without sharp corners. The proof hinges on a new half-space theorem of Liouville type, for isentropic solutions whose normal trace stays constant. That theorem unlocks the first extension of scalar strong trace results to general genuinely nonlinear systems. Strong traces support boundary value problems and recent uniqueness arguments for rough solutions.
arxiv-2606-24697:
The Euclid Collaboration, with F. Passalacqua among the lead authors, tests how well the Euclid space telescope will measure galaxy redshifts. The test uses simulated data for NISP, the mission's near infrared spectrometer and photometer. Euclid relies on slitless spectroscopy, where spectra of nearby sources overlap on the detector. That overlap, cross contamination, is a main risk to redshift accuracy. The study runs pixel level simulations and pushes them through the Euclid spectroscopic pipeline.

First, an idealised case with no overlaps sets a baseline for accuracy against emission line flux and galaxy size. Realistic contamination is then added in stages. Adding ever fainter contaminants shows no clear harm from sources fainter than magnitude 20. The team therefore limits its main analysis to galaxies brighter than magnitude 24, to be safe. One early estimate says same redshift contaminants cause about 4 percent of the total degradation blamed on cross contamination.
arxiv-2606-24997:
Livia Betti and four colleagues open up location embeddings to ask what geographic knowledge they contain. Geographic neural models map any coordinate on Earth to a vector, absorbing geospatial data into their weights. Such embeddings are used off the shelf as general purpose features, yet users lacked a principled audit. The authors decompose the embeddings three ways. Sparse autoencoders yield latent concepts. Sparse linear concept embeddings over a geospatial dictionary recover natural language concepts. Saliency maps give visual features.

The decompositions keep high reconstruction ability while exposing readable structure. Forests, deserts, and urban features appear as distinct components. Sparse versions also reveal clear differences between encoders: some emphasise urban structures, others broader biome and climate signals. Saliency maps from the pretraining space highlight other features such as roads and landmarks. Betti and colleagues offer the analysis as an audit toolkit: check what the vectors encode before trusting them blind.
arxiv-2606-25097:
Speculative decoding speeds up language model inference: a small draft model proposes tokens and the target model checks them. Sahil Kadadekar asks whether draft side behaviour can leak into safety scored outputs when decoding runs at temperature zero. He builds a screen, the Typical Acceptance Invariance Screen, that runs target only and speculative decoding side by side on the same safety battery. The screen demands byte identity evidence, statistical equivalence within a tight margin, and effect sizes below a calibrated cutoff.

Across a confirmatory core and a large matched expansion, the tested stacks show no detectable safety divergence. The largest effect size on refusal behaviour is an order of magnitude below the trivial effect floor. An adversarially tuned draft produces byte identical output to the standard draft across thousands of samples. A change of numerical precision rewrites a large share of output bytes, yet no safety rate moves outside equivalence.
arxiv-2606-25197:
Choosing what to measure next is the core problem in adaptive data collection, from lab experiments to tuning models. Daolang Huang and colleagues present Polar in 2026, a method that separates learning a summary of past data from learning what to do next. The summary comes from a pretrained foundation model for tables, whose internal features act as a belief state, meaning a compact picture of what the data so far imply. A small policy head then learns choices on top of that summary.

Across Bayesian experimental design, Bayesian optimisation, and active learning tasks, Polar beat the leading purpose-built methods the team compared it with. It also needed far fewer training examples to reach that level. Because only the goal function changes between tasks, one simple framework covers all three settings instead of a separate design for each.
arxiv-2606-25697:
No polynomial surface can be exactly a sphere, so geometric designers approximate it with smooth patches. Ema Češek and Aleš Vavpetič construct such an approximation in 2026 from quadratic spline patches with geometric continuity, meaning the surface looks smooth across seams even where its parametrisation bends. Their building block covers a regular spherical polygon split into three times as many triangles as it has sides. Stacking those blocks over the faces of any uniform polyhedron, the Platonic and Archimedean solids included, tiles the whole sphere.

Only quadratic triangular patches are used, the lowest degree that can bend convincingly. Control points come out as explicit formulas depending on the polyhedron's geometry plus a single free parameter, which tunes the fit. The pair analyse how close the approximation sits to the true sphere and how its curvature behaves, a practical recipe for modelling pipelines that prefer polynomials over rational surfaces.
arxiv-2606-25797:
A Markov decision process mixes choice with chance, and checking its behaviour statistically usually assumes you may peek, sample, and peek again. Konstantin Kueffner, Tobias Meggendorfer, Maximilian Weininger, and Patrick Wienhöft supply the right statistics for that online rhythm in 2026. Classical workflows sample in rounds and widen bounds with blunt union bound corrections. Worse, existing implementations are often subtly incorrect, or wasteful, or both. The team's confidence sequences are built for continuous monitoring: valid at every moment, not just at preplanned checkpoints.

All variants are implemented in one efficient tool and tested for practical use. They beat the classical union bound style approaches head to head. Against the previous state of the art, the implementation needed fifty times fewer samples on average to reach its guarantees. For engineers verifying systems with unknown probabilities, that is the difference between a check that runs and one that merely exists.
arxiv-2606-26097:
Lukáš Gráf, Jenni Kotila, and Oliver Scholer study rare double-beta processes that emit positrons or capture electrons. The usual double-beta decay gets most attention as a probe of new physics. These sibling modes could complement it, especially for the proposed NuDoubt-plus-plus experiment. Three candidate isotopes are analysed: krypton-78, cadmium-106, and xenon-124. Matrix elements and phase-space factors are computed for both versions.

Standard Model channels split by reachability. The two-neutrino modes with electron capture look most accessible to experiment. The double positron mode stays strongly suppressed by phase space. For the neutrinoless channel, a projected half-life sensitivity is translated into new-physics reach. Lepton-number-violating scales from about one to one hundred tera-electronvolts come into view. Measurements across several isotopes can untangle competing operator effects. The modes thus earn a place beside conventional searches.
arxiv-2606-26297:
Ali Rajabi, Milad Hasanzadeh, and Amin Kargarian release a simulator that spreads quantum optimization across many processors. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm tackles QUBO problems, the yes-no optimization form behind much engineering design. Their distributed simulator runs inside the Qiskit ecosystem. One workflow handles everything: the problem is standardized, mapped to a cost Hamiltonian, split across quantum processors, and turned into circuits.

Single-processor and multi-processor modes share the tool. Processor counts and capacities are user settings, so problem size studies are easy to run. Reused parameterized circuits and batched evaluations trim repeated overhead. Parallel multi-start runs speed the search further. A browser interface built on Streamlit lets users upload problems and watch solution quality without touching code. General, reusable QUBO simulation was the gap; this package fills it openly.
arxiv-2606-26597:
Yiwei Bao, Jie-Shuang Wang, and Hao Zhou build a cleaner calculation tool for cosmic-ray electrons and positrons from pulsars. Pulsars, spinning neutron stars, can accelerate these particles. Their travel to Earth is modelled as diffusion through two zones. Diffusion is slow near the source and normal in interstellar space. Direct calculations in this setup suffer from cancelling oscillations and blurred cooling boundaries.

Their two-zone kernel solves the propagation in series form. Energy losses from magnetic fields and starlight are included along the way. The method keeps the sharp cooling boundary seen in detailed numerical checks. Applied to local fluxes, it shows distant pulsars matter collectively at moderate energies. Sources beyond a thousand light-years-scale distances can supply a large share of the mid-energy flux. Geminga-style slow-diffusion halos remain compatible with current positron and anisotropy data.
arxiv-2606-26797:
Hongyi Henry Jin and four colleagues show that the quality of reasoning training data reveals itself in its first few tokens. Fine-tuning on a small set of strong reasoning traces teaches language models to reason well. Curating that set usually needs expensive checks by stronger models. The first tokens of a trace, the authors find, already carry the signal.

Hard problems show up in the loss of the first hundred reasoning tokens at a slightly perturbed model checkpoint. Loss measures how surprised the model is. Examples with similar early loss patterns provoke similar learning gradients, a claim the authors prove. Fine-tuning two open models on medical and mathematics reasoning data followed. Their method beat existing curation baselines slightly while using far fewer tokens. The curation cost falls sharply as a result.
arxiv-2606-27097:
Podzolkova and Melnik model how the Milky Way's central bar stirs star orbits near a key resonance. Stars near the outer Lindblad resonance can fall into libration, a trapped swaying motion around a steady path. Their analytic bar model reproduces those radial velocity profiles seen in Gaia DR3 data. In their 2026 study, extra models that differ only in bar growth time let the team ask when the trapping begins.

Velocity curves from models with different growth times keep the same shape but slide sideways in time. The slide that best aligns them grows in direct proportion to the growth time, with a factor just over one half. Librations therefore start before the bar is fully grown. They begin once the bar reaches a little over half of its final strength. That timing gives a new handle on how quickly the galactic bar assembled.
arxiv-2606-27197:
Biswal and Polo build new pieces inside a doubled representation of a Kac-Moody algebra. These algebras generalise the symmetry algebras behind much of modern representation theory. The module named L of rho is the basic irreducible integrable module, built from the special weight rho. Tensoring it with itself splits it into components that are hard to enumerate directly. In the 2026 paper, rooted trees enter through a subgraph of the Dynkin diagram.

For each subset of that subgraph, the authors form a combined root sum and a candidate crystal element. Crystal elements are combinatorial shadows of module pieces, easier to track than the pieces themselves. Choices of a root vertex in each connected part fix the construction. Each candidate is proved rho-dominant, the key property certifying a genuine component. Whole new families of tensor product components thereby appear, tied explicitly to tree-shaped choices.
arxiv-2606-27397:
Feng, Chen, and He build a bargaining arena where language model agents trade, produce, and invest against each other. Static benchmarks miss the open-ended, mixed-motive character of real economic life. SidConArena formalises a multiplayer economy as a finite-horizon, partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases. Agents negotiate in natural language with binding trades, run deterministic converter-based production, and bid in sealed auctions for long-term assets. Structured observations and a neural-symbolic action interface keep free-form play rule-grounded in this benchmark paper from 2026.

Tournaments pit identical and mixed model lineups against each other. Stronger frontier models earn higher economic outcomes, as expected. Yet agents still misvalue resources, bargain passively, and plan poorly over long investment horizons. The arena exposes economic weaknesses that question-answering scores never touch. Negotiation skill, not just reasoning, becomes measurable.
arxiv-2606-27597:
Ocean internal gravity waves carry energy through layered water. The Garrett–Munk spectrum has long been the standard model of this wave field. It rests on hydrostatic assumptions and idealised layering, though. Those limits bite where dynamics turn non-hydrostatic or layering grows uneven. Leticia Fabre-Lima, Jeffrey Early, and Miles Sundermeyer build a broader framework in 2026.

Their version uses non-hydrostatic vertical modes. The modes live in horizontal wavenumber and mode space, not frequency space. That choice keeps wave modes energetically separate. Each mode has a deformation radius. The radius flags whether a mode behaves hydrostatically or not. Modes come from a numerical Sturm–Liouville problem, so any layering profile works. Worked examples show departures from the older theory near boundaries. Vertical variance and high-frequency vertical energy are represented better. Familiar features of measured wavenumber spectra are still reproduced.
arxiv-2606-27897:
Shopping catalogues let users filter watches by metadata. They poorly support open-ended browsing by look and feel, though. Kai Lawonn, Tobias Günther, and Monique Meuschke present a visual analysis system in 2026 for large wristwatch collections. Each watch is represented through separate attribute graphs. Dial colour and dial design get their own graphs. Watch type serves as an explicit semantic organiser.

The pipeline segments dials with a U-Net and predicts types with a vision transformer. Colours map to a shared perceptual palette, and dial structure is captured by a gradient-based descriptor. The authors extend the UMAP embedding method, merging attribute graphs under one objective. A class-aware layout term keeps global type structure apart, while local visual neighbourhoods stay intact. An interactive interface offers spatial navigation, filtering, detail inspection, and search by example. A pilot study with experts and novices suggests the system supports discovery and comparison.
arxiv-2606-27997:
Benchmarks with many datasets make model evaluation expensive. Selecting a small representative subset is the usual fix, but heuristics rarely check whether rankings survive. Rostislav Gusev and Alexey Zaytsev introduce a framework in 2026 for dataset selection judged by rank preservation. Bootstrap aggregation supplies valid confidence intervals, so methods can be compared on principle. Clustering, design criteria, random baselines, and greedy farthest-first selection are all tested.

Three domains supply the evidence, with 112 time series datasets, 57 language tasks, and 30 recommender datasets. In time series, the best strategy reaches a Spearman correlation of zero point nine five with full-benchmark rankings using only five datasets. Several methods beat random subsets there and in the language benchmark. In recommender systems, gains over random are small and usually insignificant. How well a method works depends on representation quality and benchmark size.
arxiv-2606-28197:
Yusuke Tsukamoto, writing alone, tackles a numerical headache in smoothed particle magnetohydrodynamics, a method that simulates magnetized fluids as moving particles. Simulations must keep the magnetic field free of divergence, a quantity that physics requires to be exactly zero but that computer errors keep making nonzero.

Tsukamoto corrects the field after each update by solving a projection problem built from the very operator that measures the error. Choosing the adjoint gradient, matched to a volume-weighted measure, makes the correction shrink magnetic energy rather than add to it, and yields a system solvable by a standard iterative method. In collapse calculations the projection pushed the normalized error far below a rival cleaning method, while costing only a small share of the update time.
arxiv-2606-28397:
Shaoxuan Li, Xiangyu Dong, Xiaoguang Ma, Junfeng Chen, Haoran Zhao, and Yaoming Zhou make aerial navigation agents check their own work. Drones following spoken instructions usually act in open loop. A big model proposes actions and the drone executes them unverified, so small early errors snowball into losing the target entirely.

Li's team built CLOSER-VLN around a closed loop of reasoning, verification, targeted retrieval, and correction before any action flies. A hierarchical reasoner drafts candidate actions, a multidimensional verifier grades their reliability, and only failed checks trigger a search of a memory bank for helpful examples. On the CityNav benchmark's unseen split, the system reached a success rate of about thirty-two percent, with path efficiency to match, supporting the value of self-verification in the air.
arxiv-2606-28497:
Taras Panamarev, Xiang Zou, and Bence Kocsis ask whether a hidden black hole tore apart the young stars at our galaxy's center. Those stars show several orbital planes and a spread of eccentricities, odd if they were born together in one flat, spinning gas disc. An intermediate-mass black hole orbiting the central supermassive one could have done the damage.

The authors first derive a criterion for where the intruder's torque beats the disc's own self-torque, then test it with direct N-body simulations. Orbit and mass decide everything. A prograde intruder quickly aligns with the disc and does little harm. A massive retrograde one anti-aligns and fragments the disc into three angular-momentum components, an inner disc, a misaligned overlap, and an untouched outer disc, while pumping eccentricities up. At two thousand solar masses the wreckage forms within the population's known age.
arxiv-2606-28597:
Davide Benussi, Ioannis Kosmidis, Alessandra Salvan, and Nicola Sartori make a statistical fix practical in daily use. Median bias reduction improves maximum likelihood estimates a lot, but the general methods are implicit. They require solving nonlinear systems, demand a fully spelled-out nuisance parameterization, and turn into algebra slogs whenever the target is a transformation of the fitted ones.

Their focused version is direct. For a smooth scalar transformation of a reference fit, they solve an equation built from the Cornish-Fisher expansion of the estimator. It needs only the original estimate, the change's gradient and Hessian, and values that the literature or Monte Carlo can supply. The result is third-order median unbiased and matches one-step versions of the indirect methods. Examples span post-selection inference, distances, and quantiles across regression, circular, and layered models.
arxiv-2606-28897:
Zhang settles a conjecture about special metrics, ways of measuring distance, on complete geometric spaces of five to nine dimensions. The metrics in question are critical points of a functional that integrates the square of scalar curvature, a summary of how space bends at each point. Earlier work by Catino, Mastrolia and Monticelli proved that in dimensions ten and above, every complete noncompact critical metric with finite energy must be scalar-flat, meaning its scalar curvature vanishes everywhere.

Those authors conjectured the same from five upward, but their methods left the lower range open. Zhang closes the gap. He verifies scalar-flatness for the remaining dimensions, five through nine. Together with the earlier result, the theorem now covers every dimension from five onward. Critical metrics of this functional there are forced to be scalar-flat.
arxiv-2606-29097:
Tu, Niu and Zhang present TrafficAlign, a framework that teaches language models to generate realistic traffic scenarios for testing self-driving systems. Pretrained models often produce scenarios that do not match real-world traffic distributions, limiting their value for finding dangerous cases. TrafficAlign instead synthesises scenarios from real driving videos, validates the data, and aligns the model with the validated scenarios.

The results cut both ways in a useful direction. Scenarios from TrafficAlign revealed up to about eleven percent more collisions, on average across three self-driving models, than rival methods produced. The scenarios are thus better at exposing weaknesses. Fine-tuning the driving models on them then cut collision rates by about thirty-six percent. A qualitative study across six diverse regions showed the scenarios matched local traffic well.
arxiv-2606-29697:
Liu, Plotegher, Roura, and He present MF-UAVPose6D, a framework that estimates the full pose of a fixed-wing drone from a single camera image. Six-degree-of-freedom pose supports airspace awareness, tracking, and counter-drone work. Non-cooperative targets usually lack CAD models and keypoint priors, the reference information that model-based or keypoint-matching methods rely on.

The method is model-free and monocular: at inference it needs only one RGB image and the camera intrinsics. A heatmap-guided step first finds a stable target anchor. A Perspective-Aware Module models observation-ray priors, while Dynamic Topological Sampling draws out weak structural cues from wings, fuselage, and tail. A decoupled translation-rotation decoder then estimates the pose. The team also builds a synthetic dataset. Experiments show accurate estimation without CAD models.
arxiv-2606-29897:
Tushar, Miao, and Tong study voice anonymization for children. Anonymization hides who is speaking while keeping the words usable, but most systems are built on adult speech and work worse on children's voices.

The team adapts a pipeline based on self-supervised learning, where a model learns speech structure from unlabelled audio, using child speech from the MyST corpus. They test single speakers and mixtures of two speakers. Child-domain adaptation improves how intelligible and natural the anonymized speech sounds while keeping privacy protection strong. For two-speaker recordings, first extracting the target speaker and then anonymizing protects privacy while keeping the conversational structure of the exchange.
arxiv-2606-30297:
Mahan Vaz Silva and Daniel Skurt build neighborhood semantics for modal logics with a deliberately weak negation. The base logic, CLoN, is a sublogic of the four-valued system FDE. Its negation lacks the usual axioms, making it both gappy and glutty. Modal extensions let the logic speak about necessity and possibility. Two neighborhood functions serve each modal operator here.

Careful definition of rejection sets does the heavy lifting. With them, non-trivial axioms involving weak negation become valid. The framework builds on earlier work on FDE-based non-normal modal logics. Its philosophical aim concerns deontic logic, the logic of obligation. A good deontic system must hold ordinary principles and admit moral dilemmas. It must do both without collapsing into triviality. This semantics is offered as groundwork for such systems. Weak negation, handled rightly, need not mean weak results.
arxiv-2606-30597:
Taixi Chen and Nancy Guo tackle a practical weakness of large multimodal models: they expect every input channel, such as image and text, to be present. In real use, channels often go missing, and performance drops sharply. Earlier fixes generated prompts from each input's own features. Those features grow unreliable as more data goes missing, so the prompts wobble too.

Chen and Guo flip the approach. Their learnable latent prompts are fixed anchors, trained once and independent of any single input. The prompts carry stable knowledge about each modality, meaning each kind of input, and can compensate when one kind is absent. Even with ninety percent of a modality missing, the method kept working. Across three benchmark datasets it reached state-of-the-art results over a wide range of missing-data settings.
arxiv-2606-30697:
Yogeswar Reddy Thota introduces LUMOS, a semantic layer that lets AI agents operate computers through meaning rather than screenshots. Today's operating systems are built for human eyes: pixels, icons and windows. Agents forced to read screenshots and guess coordinates pay high token costs and suffer ambiguity and delay. Yet systems already hold the needed facts in accessibility metadata, structured descriptions meant for assistive technology.

LUMOS converts that metadata, plus browser interface structures, into machine-readable blueprints. Each element gets a stable identifier, role, name, value, bounds and allowed actions. It can also ground a live pointer by asking the system which element sits under the cursor. The agent then works in an observe-act loop using only visible-interface primitives, not app-specific scripts. Thota stresses that LUMOS complements visual agents rather than replacing them, and points toward AI-native operating systems.
arxiv-2606-30897:
Antonella Fruscione, Kenny Glotfelty, William Joye and Jonathan McDowell describe SAOImageDS9, the image display and analysis tool built at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. DS9 began as a demonstration of reusable imaging components and grew into one of astronomy's most used viewing environments. It runs on all major operating systems as open-source software. Astronomers, observatory operators, instrument scientists and students reach for it across wavelengths, from ground and space telescopes alike.

The account traces DS9's development and explains its staying power. It reads many astronomical formats and coordinate systems, works directly with event lists and image cubes, and supports interactive analysis inside marked regions. It also talks to outside tools through command-line and messaging interfaces. An appendix lays out the internal architecture behind its long-term sustainability.
arxiv-2606-31397:
Nguyen and three colleagues present Mixture-of-Control, a cheap way to fine-tune transformers by editing states instead of weights. State-based tuning stores small control values rather than full weight copies, saving memory. Most such methods update each block alone, which blocks talk between blocks, while cross-block schemes cost too much.

Mixture-of-Control treats each block's control state as an expert in a sparse mixture-of-experts process. Local and global control signals then mix adaptively, so blocks share information at low cost. Across diverse transformer benchmarks the method beats other state-based approaches. Memory and compute stay close to the cheapest rivals, which makes the gain practical for teams adapting large models on modest hardware.
arxiv-2606-31597:
Schestag and Zeh speed up algorithms that orient unrooted phylogenetic networks, the graphs biologists use when evolution includes hybridization or gene transfer next to branching. Reconstruction often yields an undirected network, and choosing edge directions that form a valid rooted class, such as tree-child or orchard networks, is NP-hard in many cases. Their parameter is the network level, a measure of tangledness.

One framework enumerates directed spanning trees on the network's generator, its compressed core, then orients the rest of the edges fast, giving faster fixed-parameter algorithms for tree-based, orchard, tree-child and normal networks. A second framework guesses reticulation placements directly and covers temporal, reticulation-visible and tree-sibling classes. Even the task of making scanwidth, a layout cost, as small as possible stays single-exponential in the level under this approach.
arxiv-2606-31697:
Arifi and Suzuki bring exceptional points, the hallmark of non-Hermitian physics where two energy levels and their states merge into one, into hadron physics for the first time in a systematic way. Such points are well studied in photonics and atomic systems but barely touched in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons. Their proposed tuning knob is an imaginary magnetic field.

Computing neutral meson mass spectra with both a hadronic effective Lagrangian and a constituent quark model, the pair find exceptional points separating a real-spectrum regime from a complex-eigenvalue one. Weak fields produce level attraction between hadron states, in contrast to the repulsion seen with real fields, while stronger fields deconfine the hadrons, signaling an inverted potential. The mechanism opens a concrete route to non-Hermitian QCD studies.
arxiv-2606-31797:
Chaudhuri and four colleagues confirm, in simulation, that plasma double layers form at the edge of regions exposed to intense extreme ultraviolet light. A double layer is a thin structure of separated positive and negative charge that holds a sharp voltage drop. Whether one appears during fast, high-power EUV exposure matters for lithography plasmas.

Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations show the layer exists only while the EUV is on, for roughly 70 nanoseconds in their runs, and vanishes soon after switch-off. A threshold beam energy near 0.1 millijoules must be crossed first. Past that point the layer strengthens from weak to strong as power rises. The fingerprint could affect how EUV plasmas are modeled and controlled.
arxiv-2606-31897:
Joshi and his team report a long, wideband radio campaign on FRB 20240114A, a hyperactive repeating fast radio burst source. The Allen Telescope Array observed for 1,167 hours between January and October 2024. Coverage spanned about 900 megahertz to 7,620 megahertz of simultaneous bandwidth, a high-frequency regime still thinly sampled for repeaters.

Ninety-seven bursts were detected between roughly 900 megahertz and 5 gigahertz in the campaign, including a strong S-band episode. No bursts appeared in the highest tunings above about 5 gigahertz despite much exposure. Burst rates vary sharply with frequency and epoch. This confirms strongly chromatic, band-limited emission. Fractional bandwidth stays roughly the same at each scale, while sub-burst durations shrink and downward drift rates grow toward higher frequencies.
arxiv-2606-31997:
Yang and three colleagues explain why chromosome contact maps look multifractal. Hi-C experiments measure how often two DNA loci touch, and the contact probability falls off as a power law in genomic distance. Earlier studies reported multifractal scaling in these maps but explained it only through postulated models, leaving its origin unclear.

Starting from the measured power law alone, the authors derive the mass exponent that governs how moments of contact density scale with coarse-graining box size. The slope at large moment order is fixed directly by the contact exponent, switching value when that exponent crosses one. Results hold up under noise and across diverse organisms. Multifractality here is a direct shadow of polymer contact statistics, not an extra structure.
arxiv-2608-00297: How greedy is the Universe? arXiv 2608-00297. The entropy ledger. Researchers may consult the paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The library keeps the document safe.
audubon-journals-vol1-1897:
Maria R. Audubon, the naturalist's granddaughter, edited Audubon and His Journals for print in 1897. Volume one covers journals from 1820 to 1843. The Missouri, Labrador, and Florida expeditions supply its great journeys. Elliott Coues added notes that guide readers through names and places.

Day by day entries record birds seen, specimens taken, weather, and hardship. The journals show the rough fieldwork behind the polished pictures and biographies. Audubon's drive and charm both come through in his own words. The volume is a primary record of his working life. Two volumes hold the set. Historians of American nature rely on them.
audubon-journals-vol2-1897:
Volume two of Audubon and His Journals, also printed in 1897, completes the edited set. Maria R. Audubon prepared her grandfather's journals for the public, with help from Elliott Coues's notes. The entries continue the daily record of travel, collecting, and observation. Readers follow expeditions through wild country in Audubon's own hand.

Hunts, river trips, and meetings with settlers fill the pages alongside bird notes. The journals reveal the cost of the great picture work in money, health, and time. Together the two volumes form the primary record of his fieldwork. They let readers test the polished biographies against raw days. The set closes with his later journeys.
balzac-catherine-de-medici-wormeley-1897:
Balzac turned historian in Catherine de Medici, his study of the queen who ruled France through her sons. Katharine Prescott Wormeley's 1897 translation presents his defense of a woman history had painted as a monster. Balzac blends narrative with political theory, as the Philosophical Studies of his Human Comedy often do.

He reads Catherine as a state-builder trapped between faiths, parties, and foreign powers. Massacre and intrigue appear here as the grim tools of a weak crown, not mere cruelty. The book asks readers to judge a ruler by the state she held together, a bold claim then and now.
barruel-memoirs-jacobinism-vol1-1797:
Augustin Barruel was a French Jesuit priest who fled the Revolution and wrote his Memoirs Illustrating the History of Jacobinism in exile. Robert Clifford translated the work, whose first volume appeared in English in 1797. Volume one treats the antichristian conspiracy he saw behind the fall of the French altar and throne.

Barruel argues that the philosophers of the Enlightenment formed a sect sworn to destroy Christianity, with Voltaire at its head. He marshals letters, quotations, and lodge reports as his evidence, witness by witness. The volume is the French counterpart to Robison's Proofs, and the two books fed each other's fame.
barruel-memoirs-jacobinism-vol2-1797:
Volume two of Barruel's Memoirs, in Clifford's translation of 1797, turns to the Sophisters of impiety and the French academies. Sophisters is Barruel's name for the clever talkers he blames for poisoning French belief. The academies, in his telling, served as their general staff.

He traces how the learned societies of Paris rewarded works that mocked religion and softened morals before the Revolution. Names, prizes, and published letters build his case that unbelief was organized, not spontaneous. Readers who accept his first volume find here the machinery by which the plot was spread. Barruel writes as a prosecutor, and the academies are his second set of accused.
barruel-memoirs-jacobinism-vol3-1797:
Volume three of Barruel's Memoirs, in Clifford's 1797 translation, treats the Sophisters of rebellion and the Masonic lodges. Having charged the philosophers with killing faith, Barruel now charges the lodges with killing kingship. The two conspiracies, he argues, met and merged.

He describes grades, oaths, and secret signs as the training ground where men learned to plot against throne and altar together. His evidence mixes printed rituals, defectors' tales, and his own dark inferences from the Revolution's course. The volume carried his system from ideas into organization, where its influence on later conspiracy writing proved lasting.
barruel-memoirs-jacobinism-vol4-1797:
Volume four of Barruel's Memoirs, in Clifford's 1797 translation, completes the work with the Illuminati and the Germanic Union exposed. Here the plot goes underground and German, in the secret orders Barruel calls the conspiracy's deepest layer. Adam Weishaupt's Illuminati stand at the center of the charge.

Barruel prints the order's codes, grades, and plans for ruling its members' reading, writing, and friendships from the shadows. The Germanic Union, a reading network, becomes in his account the plot's recruiting arm. With this volume his system stood complete, and it haunted European politics for a century. Few readers finished the four volumes unshaken in the troubled 1790s.
beha-ed-din-life-saladin-pef-1897:
Beha ed-Din Ibn Shaddad knew Saladin as few men did, and his Life of Saladin, in the Palestine Exploration Fund edition of 1897, is an intimate portrait. Beha ed-Din served as judge and companion beside Salah ed-Din through the years of the Third Crusade. He watched the sultan at prayer, in council, and before Jerusalem.

The twelfth-century biography praises its subject, yet its closeness gives the praise weight. Saladin's justice, patience, and mercy appear in small acts recorded by a daily witness. For readers of the Crusades, no source brings the Muslim leader nearer than his own biographer's pages.
besant-ancient-wisdom-1897:
Annie Besant was a British reformer who became a leader of the Theosophical Society and its voice in India. Her Ancient Wisdom, published in 1897, outlines Theosophical teaching on the cosmos and human growth. The book served as the society's standard primer for new members.

Besant describes planes of existence above the physical, the long evolution of the soul through many lives, and the masters who guide mankind. Her scheme joins Hindu and Buddhist ideas to a Victorian faith in progress. Readers who wanted Theosophy whole, in one clear volume, started here for decades. Besant writes with a convert's zeal and a teacher's love of clear order.
borlase-dolmens-of-ireland-vol1-1897:
William Copeland Borlase made a full list of the stone tombs of Ireland. Book one of The Dolmens of Ireland came out in 1897. The set runs to three books in all. Dolmens are graves of great stones, with a cap stone on uprights.

County by county, Borlase gives the site, the shape, and the state of each tomb. Cuts and plans show the stones as they stood in his day. Folk names and tales cling to scores of the sites he lists. The book is the great list of its kind, still used by all in the field.
borlase-dolmens-of-ireland-vol2-1897:
Book two of Borlase's Dolmens of Ireland came out in 1897. William Copeland Borlase wrote the set as a full list of Irish stone tombs. This part runs on with the list by county. It also spreads the tombs out and weighs their shapes as a class.

Where the tombs cluster, and where they lack, forms one theme here. The build of chamber, cap, and mound shifts from place to place in his count. Tales and lore of the folk add life to the dry list of stones. The book is the mid part of the great list of its kind.
borlase-dolmens-of-ireland-vol3-1897:
Book three of Borlase's Dolmens of Ireland came out in 1897. William Copeland Borlase ends his three book list of the stone tombs here. The first books gave the tombs by county, one by one. This book takes the whole class in one wide view.

He sets the Irish tombs by the side of like tombs in Wales and France. Age, builders, and use all come in for a long, keen weigh up. A full list of all the sites ends the set for quick use. The three books form the great list of Irish dolmens to this day.
brinton-the-religions-of-primitive-peopl:
Daniel Garrison Brinton, one of America's first professional anthropologists, delivered these lectures on the religions of primitive peoples in 1897. He aimed to treat the beliefs of native peoples as true religions, worthy of the same respect given to the great faiths.

Brinton discusses animism, the belief that spirits live in things, and fetishism, along with myth, prayer, and priestcraft across early societies. He argues that a universal religious sentiment runs through all of them. His language belongs to his era, but his core claim was generous for its time. The lectures remain a readable statement of early American anthropology.
cheiro-language-of-the-hand-1897:
Cheiro, the stage name of Count Louis Hamon, published Cheiro's Language of the Hand in 1897. Cheiro read palms for famous clients in London and New York, and his book taught the art to the public. Palmistry, in his system, read character and fate from the shape and lines of the hand.

Lessons cover the mounts, fingers, and main lines, with drawings that show each mark and its claimed meaning. Cheiro also gave rules for judging health, talent, and likely turns in a life. The book made modern palm reading fashionable, and it remains a basic source for anyone who wants the classic system in full.
chopin-night-in-acadie-1897:
Kate Chopin published A Night in Acadie in 1897, her second collection of Louisiana stories. It continues the world of Bayou Folk, the Creole and Acadian country along the bayous and the Cane River. Chopin wrote these tales in St. Louis, working from the years she had lived in Louisiana.

The title story follows a young planter through one charged night of music, longing, and restraint. Other stories treat marriages cooling or kindling, old women remembering, and children watching the adult world. Chopin's women, especially, chafe against the narrow lives assigned them, in hints of the themes The Awakening would soon state openly. The collection is the essential companion to Bayou Folk.
cia-0000008697:
Case number 12,558 produced a set of photo comparison results dated January 1971. CIA specialists compared photographs as part of the search for missing American servicemen in Southeast Asia. A case number stood for a face, a name, and a family waiting for news.

Photo comparison meant matching features across images taken years and hardships apart. Analysts measured, judged likeness, and stated how sure they were. A match could confirm a prisoner alive; a mismatch closed a false lead. The file shows that careful craft at work on one numbered case. Hundreds of similar cases moved through the same process.
cia-0000009197:
German railway systems and their emergency capacity drew a CIA study in July 1949. West Germany had just become a state, and its railways were the new country's logistical backbone. Planners wanted to know how well the lines could serve in a crisis.

The study weighs track, rolling stock, and repair ability under emergency strain. Rail capacity mattered because any defense of Western Europe would move by train. Infrastructure papers like this one lack drama but carry strategy inside them. The file shows intelligence work at its most practical, counting bridges and freight cars in the early Cold War.
cia-0000009797:
Reported sightings of Caucasian and American prisoners in North Vietnam are collected, with a cover item, in an April 1977 paper. Caucasian was the era's file word for Western-looking men whose nationality was unknown. Sightings of such men kept arriving years after the war.

Gathering them in one paper let analysts compare dates, places, and descriptions across claims. Some likely described the same man twice; others described no prisoner at all. Sorting them was slow, doubtful work with high emotional stakes. This compilation preserves the claims together, as officials saw them, in the postwar debate's early years.
cia-0000010597:
Consequences of communist control over South Asia are weighed in a September 1952 CIA estimate. The paper works as a thought experiment: suppose the region fell, and what would the West lose? India, Pakistan, and their neighbors held the land bridge between the Middle East and Southeast Asia.

Worst-case papers clarify stakes rather than predict events. This one counts ports, airfields, manpower, and prestige in the loss column. Its fears belong to the domino thinking of the early Cold War. Read today, it shows how large South Asia loomed in Washington's map of a world split in two.
cia-0000012297:
Another November 1961 memo from Helms to the DIA director concerns a Military Thought article whose quoted title begins 'The Use O...' and trails off. The Soviet journal's pieces were mined in Washington for what they revealed about how Moscow's officers thought. Titles cut short in the file still mark the traffic: piece by piece, the enemy's professional press crossed the ocean.

The memo keeps the interagency channel warm through the busiest season of the Penkovsky case. Its very frequency tells a story of appetite at the top. For readers, it is one beat in the pipeline that fed the colonel's secrets to their users.
cia-0000012397:
Birmingham, in England's Midlands, hosts meeting number seven on April 27, 1961. The debriefing roadshow moved again, and the record follows it across the country. By the seventh session the questions were growing deeper each day. They moved from what Penkovsky knew by heart toward what he could fetch, copy, or measure on his next trips home.

The record preserves the session's place in the spring campaign. Handlers and source had found their method by then. For readers, the page shows the operation's craft at work: a great source questioned city by city, day by day.
cia-0000012997:
The Soviet space program gets a full CIA assessment in February 1967, ten years after Sputnik. Soviet cosmonauts had led the early race: first satellite, first man, first spacewalk. By 1967 the American program was surging ahead toward the Moon. The question in Washington was what Moscow would loft next. Analysts also asked whether the Soviet lead had truly passed, or merely paused between triumphs.

The paper tracks the cosmonauts' progress and plans from the evidence available. It reads launches, failures, and silences for signs of what came next. For readers, it shows the space race watched from the other side of the fence.
cia-0000013497:
What would the communists do if the United States acted in certain ways toward Laos? A CIA paper from April 1962 works through the probable reactions. Washington was then weighing moves in the little kingdom's civil war. Each option risked answers from Hanoi, Beijing, and Moscow, and the paper games out the branches: protest, pressure, escalation, or war by other means.

The scenarios range from the plausible to the paranoid, as war games do. Their value lies in showing what decision-makers feared before they chose. For readers, the paper is the what-ifs of the Laos crisis, weighed in advance.
cia-0000013597:
Panama's prospects for relations with the United States fill a CIA paper from July 1968. The canal stood at the center of every question between the two countries. Panamanian nationalism pressed against the American-held Canal Zone, and riots and treaty talks had already marked the decade. The isthmus's restless politics made the waterway's future the hemisphere's standing problem in miniature.

The paper weighs the canal question and the ties around it. It judges the governments, the guard, and the street together. For readers, it shows the canal's shadow falling across every line of a small country's file.
cia-0000013797:
South Vietnam's cabinet crisis and its wider meaning are weighed in a CIA paper from September 1966. Saigon's politics were the war's second front. Generals quarreled, cabinets rose and fell, and each turn in the capital shook the war effort in the field. The crisis of that season set the ruling junta's factions against each other while American troops fought under their flag.

The paper treats the cabinet's fall as a military fact, not gossip. It weighs what the quarrel meant for the war's direction. For readers, it shows Saigon being watched the way battlefields were watched: closely, and with worry.
cia-0000014697: David Keppel and espionage frame a short CIA file dated January 2, 1951. It is one of several files here that carry Keppel's name. Repetition itself is a clue: the same contacts drew paper again and again. The new year file kept the thread alive as the Rosenberg case moved toward trial that spring.
cia-0000014797: Masters of Deceit, the book by J. Edgar Hoover, is noted in a CIA file dated January 3, 1958. The file gives a sketch of Russian activity from the book. Hoover ran the FBI and wrote the era's best known anti Communist primer. That the CIA filed its rival chief's book shows the paper crossed desks across the river.
cia-0000015297: A letter to Lloyd Berkner from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated October 2, 1957. It takes up the release of a scientific item, the title says in clipped words. Berkner appears again and again in these science letters. The file comes from the very week the space age opened with a Soviet first.
cia-0000015397: The Air Force asked a man named Robertson for leave to declassify a record, in a CIA file dated September 6, 1957. The record's name is clipped in the title. Robertson had chaired the 1953 saucer panel, whose report stayed secret for years. A plea to open it shows the secrecy itself becoming the story.
cia-0000022397: Information on the Powers trial, tied to the U-2, is gathered in a CIA record dated in 1960. A gathering file like this served as a briefing pack on the case. It would have held facts staff needed when questions came from above. Such packs show the agency feeding its own leaders the same story it tracked in enemy print.
cia-0000040897: An untitled CIA item dated March 4, 1976 mentions a response to a letter of April 16, 1976, as the catalog title records it. The dates in the title sit oddly together, which is part of what the record shows. What can be grounded is modest: the agency answered a correspondent in writing, and the reply was kept on file. Brief items like this preserve the routine traffic between the agency and the public it served.
cia-0000044997:
The CIA's records disposition handbook, dated August 3, 1982, survives in a record filed July 2, 1982. A disposition handbook rules how long records are kept or destroyed. It is, in plain terms, a rulebook about the agency's own paperwork.

Inside, schedules set the life span of whole classes of files. Some papers were kept forever, and others were burned on schedule. Those dry choices shaped the archive that history would inherit. Every file in this very set exists because a schedule once said to keep it. The file shows the system describing its own memory, and deciding, page by page, what the future would be allowed to know.
cia-0000045197:
President Duarte held a news conference, in a CIA record dated September 5, 1985. The kidnapping of his daughter stood behind every question asked. A president who is also a father speaks under a double strain.

Inside, his public handling of the crisis is recorded for the file. News conferences let a leader steady a country in real time. They also expose him, in front of the whole country, when the answers he needs are simply not there to give. The record preserves Duarte before the cameras that September, balancing the state's dignity against a father's plain wish to bring his daughter home alive.
cia-0000048997: The People's Revolutionary Army, one of El Salvador's guerrilla groups, set out its position on blame for a violent act in 1980. A CIA item from that year holds the statement, kept with the Truth Commission records. Guerrilla statements like this one were claims in a war of words fought beside the shooting war.
cia-0000049097: A trace response on Colonel Jose Adolfo Medrano survives in a CIA item from 1984, filed with the Truth Commission records. A trace response was the system's reply when a name was queried: the file's contents, summarized for whoever asked. Officers' traces built the cast list from which the war's judgments were later drawn.
cia-0000049197: Army officers in El Salvador considered mounting an assassination attempt in 1990, and a CIA item preserves the chilling discussion. The target's name is cut off in the title, so the document itself carries who was meant to die. Talk of murder among officers, filed as routine paper, shows the war's deepest rot.
cia-0000049297: Unease grew inside El Salvador's military in 1989, and a CIA item records it, kept under the Truth Commission's eye. Unease in the officer corps could mean anything from lost confidence to a coup in embryo, and watchers weighed it carefully. The item preserves the mood in the war's hardest year.
cia-0000049397: The Jesuit Case: Claims of Colonel Guillermo Benavides is the title of declassified CIA document 0000049397, dated July 4, 1991. Noted for the Truth Commission, the item centers on claims tied to the named colonel in that case. It survives as a short declassified record focused on one officer, useful for tracing named figures through the Jesuit file.
cia-0000094997: Results of Nguyen Phong Thiep's visit to Saigon on October 21, 1968, are recorded in declassified CIA document 0000094997, dated September 5, 1968 in the catalog. The catalog date sits oddly before the visit date in its own heading. Readers get a short results record whose internal dating mismatch is itself worth flagging. Its catalog entry preserves the original heading word for word.
cia-0000096497: Progress report on the implementation of Recommendation number three of a report to the President is declassified CIA document 0000096497, dated March 2, 1957. The heading is cut short in the catalog. Readers find a short bureaucratic follow-up record, one of a numbered run of progress reports tracking single recommendations from a presidential board's report.
cia-0000107297: Officals Give ConcretT Proof of U.s. Pilot's Death is the heading, with officials and concrete misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000107297, dated June 5, 1991. The title reports officials offering proof of one American pilot's death. The pilot is not named in the heading itself. The brief record is a proof item, with both misspellings preserved as released.
cia-0000107497: Bloc Economic Activity in Cuba - 1960 Through June 1963 is the subject, its publication date an estimate, on CIA document 0000107497, dated September 2, 1963. The title sets its own span: three and a half years of bloc activity in Cuba. Bloc names the Soviet bloc in the heading's short form. The brief record is a dated survey item.
cia-0000109797: Weekly Situation Report: International Terrorism Article re Clifford Bevens Fou is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000109797, dated July 3, 1981. The title places a named article, on Clifford Bevens, inside a weekly terrorism report. What Bevens was found doing breaks off at Fou in the heading. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000119697:
This August 1951 paper is a National Intelligence Estimate on probable developments in the world situation through mid-1953. Estimates were the intelligence community's most formal forecasts, meant to give leaders a shared picture of what lay ahead. The Korean War was then in its second year, and Stalin still ruled the Soviet Union.

The estimate ranges across the globe, weighing war, politics, and the balance between the blocs. Forecasts on this scale show how the young CIA thought about the whole board at once. Reading it now lets one test the agency's judgment against what actually happened, a rare chance to grade the forecasters of the early Cold War.
cia-0000132097: An April 1961 CIA document is a history of the Clandestine Services, its subtitle breaking off in the heading. It was dated on the edge of the Bay of Pigs invasion, the agency's own account of its secret work, written from inside. The paper preserves that history as drafted. Internal histories were written for the institution itself, and an April 1961 draft stands just before the failure that would rewrite the service's story entirely.
cia-0000132497: Colombia possibly breaking relations with Cuba fills a CIA document dated January 2, 1961. Colombia did in fact cut ties with Havana later, joining a regional freeze-out of the Castro government. One by one, Cuba's neighbors were putting distance between themselves and the revolution. The short document weighs the chances of a Colombian break at the moment analysts were watching for it.
cia-0000135897: Dated 1 March 1954, this declassified CIA record carries a garbled catalog title: General — Political Action, Conversations; Specific — Debriefings Of, with a Deleted mark in between. What can be said from the record itself is limited: the subject headings concern political action, conversations, and debriefings, and part of the material was deleted before release. The v1 summary tied it to the Guatemala operation, but the title does not say that, so the link is not claimed here. The record is held as released through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135997: Filed on 3 February 1954, this CIA cable concerns the use of lawyers at the conference, legal cover weighed in a short cable from Lincoln. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136097: The record dated 1 March 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about training concerns for Calligeris, passed to Lugton while the recruit pipeline showed problems. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136197: Filed on 2 May 1954, this CIA cable concerns starting Operation A and an underground bulletin, fresh fronts opened for RAZMARA in May. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136297: One CIA cable dated 3 May 1954 handles a command message for CADICK revising unconventional tactics, the stock in trade rewritten. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136397: Rifle fabrication is pressed against a deadline in this January 1954 cable to LINCOLN. The makers will proceed with development and complete the maximum number of rifles, and can convert ten to folding steel stock; a hinged folding wooden stock would speed conversion, if acceptable. They ask whether the rifles must be single shot, noting supply has six new sterile .22 caliber rimfire rifles, single shot or box magazine, and the rest could be procured locally. The order's purpose is not stated here.
cia-0000136697: Dated 3 April 1961, this Spanish document is one of the latest-dated items in this slice of the 2506 Brigade files. Two weeks later the brigade landed at the Bay of Pigs. The catalog record names no subject for the document. It survives in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, a record from the operation's final days of preparation, when the plan was set and the force was waiting to sail.
cia-0000136897: Headquarters fires a list of planning questions at LINCOLN in this April 1954 cable. What operations are scheduled in the next two weeks, when will organizers move forward, when will black flights be completed, and when will hardware move from storage to forward staging? What tonnage goes into each destination under different scenarios, what total tonnage flies by black flight, and how many trained men are currently in place, especially those scheduled to enter Guatemala? The invasion timetable was being audited.
cia-0000136997: How the regime died is told in this June 1954 cable. An Iron Curtain shipment revelation shocked the army. Army leaders knew nothing of the weapons deal. They feared losing all power. Arbenz was arming the Reds, they believed. Word that the army was worried became a signal. It was the signal for the march. Work by an agent on the Swedish ship played a part too. It thus indirectly caused the regime's death, the cable claims.
cia-0000140397: Moral opposition to Artichoke work is recorded in this February 1952 interview. The man is a cleared agency employee with a responsible position. Interviewers first discussed random subjects with him. They established his competence and his interest in Artichoke-type work. They also established he appreciated the needed secrecy. He was then given a brief resume of the program. He said he was interested in the problem. But he felt morally opposed to applying these techniques himself. He could study the problem scientifically, though.
cia-06140497: AMENDMENT OF SOLICITATION/MODIFICATION OF CONTRACT - NO. 18, a CIA document. The contract amendment. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
comment-on-devient-alchimiste-traite-d-h: Comment on devient alchimiste, 1897. How to become an alchemist. This book preserves that treatise. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
conrad-nigger-narcissus-1897:
Conrad's 1897 sea novel follows the ship Narcissus home from Bombay with a crew of hard men and one dying sailor, James Wait. Wait's illness and death hang over the voyage, drawing out pity, resentment, and superstition in the men around him.

A great storm in the Cape gives the book its famous set piece of seamanship under terror. Conrad had sailed in such ships himself, and every rope and order rings true. The preface he added states his aim as an artist: to make the reader see. Many still call this the finest sea novel in English.
constitution-eritrea-1997:
Eritrea adopted this constitution in 1997, six years after winning its long war with Ethiopia. Chapter one gives general provisions for a single republic. Chapter two lists national goals and guiding principles, and chapter three protects basic rights, freedoms, and duties, including speech, worship, and fair treatment under law.

The National Assembly is the lawmaking body, and it chooses the president, who leads the executive. Later chapters cover the courts, elections, public finance, and local areas. At 59 articles the text is one of Africa's shortest charters. In practice the constitution was never fully put into force, and Eritrea has been ruled without it, a gap between paper and practice that critics cite often.
cournot-researches-fisher-1897:
Antoine Augustin Cournot was a French mathematician who applied calculus to markets half a century before it became normal. His Researches into the Mathematical Principles of the Theory of Wealth appeared in French in 1838, and in Bacon's English translation in 1897. Few read it at first, then economists found it everywhere ahead of them.

Cournot works out how a single seller sets price, then how two rival sellers settle into a balance called equilibrium. He treats demand as a curve that math can handle, demand falling as price rises. Marshall and later game theorists alike stand in his debt.
defoe-essay-upon-projects-1697:
Daniel Defoe published An Essay upon Projects in 1697, his first book, a prospectus for reform. The tract proposes banks, insurance, and academies for women, among many schemes for public good. It is the founding document of the projector literature of the Augustan age in England.

Defoe urges a national bank, highway repair, pensions, and friendly societies for widows and sailors. He backs insurance for merchants and houses, and schools that teach women real learning in earnest. Bankruptcy law, idiots' care, and seamen's wages all get brisk, practical plans in these pages. His tone is brisk and hopeful, sure that trade and reason can mend a kingdom's ills. Much that he sketched, from savings banks to female schooling, came true in time.
dionysius-areopagite-works-parker-1897:
John Parker gave the full works of Dionysius the Areopagite English dress in 1897. The scribe of these works claimed to be Paul's pupil of that name. Most now hold the works came from a Greek monk of a much later age. No set of texts did more to shape thought on God and the ranks of heaven.

The Divine Names and the Mystical Theology lead the set. Two works on the ranks of heaven and the Church come next, with ten letters at the close. God is past all names, the texts hold, yet each name tells some truth. The set lit the path of Christian thought on the dark side of God.
dnb-lionel-nathan-de-rothschild-1897:
The Dictionary of National Biography gave this life of Lionel Nathan de Rothschild in its 49th part, in 1897. Lionel was the son of Nathan and head of the London house in his turn. The DNB was the great standard life work of the Victorian age in Britain.
