The review gathers time-domain responses, whole-scalp power measures, and rhythm-based indices.

Early response parts such as N15 and P30 carry set meanings, global and local field power sum up spread of responses, and phase coherence indices capture rhythm resetting after each pulse. Work in Alzheimer's disease, depression, epilepsy, and stroke shows the promise, while artifacts, personal variation, and missing standards remain the brakes. Shared protocols would let clinics compare results fairly.
pmc-13328497:
Jiahui Li and co-authors explore a new cell death route in minimal change disease in a 2026 analysis. The disease is the top cause of primary nephrotic syndrome, and disulfidptosis, death from disulfide stress collapsing the cell skeleton, had never been mapped in it. Public gene datasets were mined with four learning methods.

Four hub genes, FLNC, GYS1, INF2, and MYH11, built a diagnostic chart reaching an AUC of 0.839 in exploratory testing, and clustering on them split patients into two molecular groups with distinct pathways and immune traits. Lab staining confirmed MYH11 runs high in patient tissue. The system is a starting map only, the authors stress, needing proof in larger groups.
pmc-13328897:
Kun Hwang reflects in a 2026 essay on a visit to the Chipyong-ni Battle Memorial and what its stories mean for military medicine. Chipyong-ni was a key Korean War battle for United Nations forces. Hwang focuses on three officers, most of all Ralph Monclar, who had been a three-star general in France yet served in Korea as a lieutenant colonel.

At age 58, Monclar led troops in harsh combat despite his former rank. Hwang links that choice to his own path: 38 months as a junior officer from 1983 to 1986, then training in plastic surgery and 30 years in academic medicine. Service past personal glory, and care for soldiers, form the core lesson Hwang draws.
pmc-13329797:
Diane Berry and team found signs that predict dementia in older people with essential tremor. Their 2026 prospective study tracked thinking skills in 350 cases, mean age 79.5 years, for up to 7.5 years, with mean follow-up of 4.7 years in all. Older people with essential tremor face a higher dementia risk, yet little was known about which traits raise that risk.

Older age and worse thinking at the start each predicted dementia. Weaker daily function, worse gait, lower balance confidence, and more low-mood signs at the start also predicted dementia, all with strong significance. Neither steady nor grouped tremor onset age predicted dementia, against the earlier view of older onset age as a risk factor. The team gives the fullest review to date by traits studied and cohort size, flagging low mood as a treatable factor that offers ways to cut dementia risk.
pmc-13329897:
Dinesh Baral and a large team study how film thickness affects germanium-tin layers for infrared devices in a 2026 report. Such alloys can be tuned for light sensing and can work with silicon, but high tin content brings strain and defects. Five samples with about 15 percent tin were grown by molecular beam methods at varied thickness.

X-ray maps tracked strain easing as thickness grew. Light output tests suggested fewer harmful defects as films thickened, up to a point. Near 150 nm thickness, tin began to separate out, marking a limit in the reported data. The authors define a useful growth window from 35 to 150 nm for relaxed, low-defect layers at this tin level. Thickness control is central, they argue.
pmc-13329997:
Evgeni S. Penev, Ksenia V. Bets, Jincheng Lei, and Boris I. Yakobson simulate how sulphur changes iron particle clumping in nanotube growth in a 2026 study. Large-scale nanotube making uses floating iron catalysts plus a sulphur helper, yet the helper's early role is poorly known. The team built a machine-learned atomic model and ran collision tests.

Sulphur cut sticking for small iron clusters but raised it strongly for larger ones, the simulations showed. The flip came from shape softness: sulphur on the surface lets clusters flex on impact, soaking up energy and holding together. That flex effect may explain mixed past lab reports on sulphur help, the authors suggest. Reactor design could use size-aware sulphur dosing.
pmc-13333097:
Prabhleen Brar and colleagues report a 2026 case of severe front-tooth injury caused during removal of an extra tooth, repaired by a mixed-field team. Injury during mesiodens extraction can badly damage neighboring teeth and their support, notably when imaging and surgical planning fall short. A 28-year-old woman presented with grade II looseness of four upper front teeth six months after mesiodens extraction. Clinical exams and cone-beam CT showed extensive root destruction and loss of supporting bone around those teeth.

The team chose a tooth-preserving course: root canal therapy with mineral trioxide aggregate filling, surgical apicectomy, fiber-reinforced composite splinting, and final zirconia prosthetic rebuilding. Follow-up at twelve months showed satisfactory healing and reduced looseness. The case stresses careful imaging and planning before mesiodens surgery, and it shows that even extensive iatrogenic damage can sometimes be salvaged without extraction.
pmc-13333597:
Hui Zheng and a large team of co-authors carried out a 2026 prospective cohort study of an integrated labor-delivery-recovery-postpartum unit at a busy tertiary hospital in China. They asked whether keeping low-risk mothers in one unit through birth improves outcomes.

A total of 542 low-risk women with full-term single pregnancies chose either the integrated unit or traditional delivery care. Groups were compared with matching, regression, Bayesian analysis, and machine learning. The integrated group had shorter labors, at 7.3 hours against 9.8 hours in traditional care, and far fewer cesarean births and newborn transfers. Mothers also reported feeling calm and relaxed more often, which supports wider use of this model for low-risk births.
pmc-13333697:
Giuseppe Scardina and co-authors examined how biological maturity relates to athletic performance in young soccer players in a 2026 study. Players of the same age can differ widely in physical development, and the team asked whether that gap shows across a full test battery.

Forty-four male players aged about 13, from under-13 to under-16 squads, completed jump, sprint, and endurance testing. Maturity status was estimated with the modified Mirwald equation, sorting players into pre, circa, and post peak height velocity groups. The post group beat both other groups on every measure, including jump height, 10 and 30 meter sprints, leg power, and VO2max, with large effect sizes throughout. The authors recommend that academies factor maturity into fitness profiling and training design.
pmc-13334397:
Börge Schmidt and co-authors asked whether selenium status explains lingering fatigue after COVID-19 in a 2026 community study. Inflammation during post-acute illness can suppress selenoprotein production, so the team tested selenium, selenoprotein P, and autoantibodies against it.

The cross-sectional study covered 750 adults checked about 21.9 months after a PCR-proven infection, and 23.1 percent reported lasting fatigue. Low serum selenium showed in 63.7 percent of participants and low selenoprotein P in 89.6 percent, while autoantibodies were rare at 3.9 percent. Taken singly, none of the three markers tied strongly to fatigue. The pairing of low selenium with raised autoantibodies, though rare, showed the notable signal, suggesting joint pathways deserve a closer look.
pmc-13334697:
Zhihua Zheng and co-authors asked why exercise links to lower depression in college students in a 2026 cross-sectional study guided by Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. They tested mindfulness and experiential avoidance as the steps in between.

Students came from 11 physical education classes at a single university in Jiangsu, China, and 308 valid questionnaires were kept from 320 invited. Scales scored activity, mindful attention, psychological inflexibility, and depressive symptoms, with gender accounted for. About 20.78 percent of students showed at least mild depressive symptoms. Exercise was tied to fewer symptoms and to higher mindfulness, and the serial pathway through mindfulness and then avoidance-related scores carried much of the association. The results suggest motion helps mood partly by training present-moment attention.
pmc-13336597:
Danielle Lee, Nicholas J. Norton, and Adam P. Dale assess newer microbe-finding tools in a 2026 review for patients with weak immune systems. Standard lab tests can miss odd or mixed infections in these hosts. Gene sequencing methods scan broadly without needing a guess first about which germ is present.

Case reports show sequencing caught unusual infections that routine tests missed at first. Larger studies found higher detection rates than standard methods, though fungi such as Aspergillus and some slow bacteria remain hard to spot. Gains for patients vary, and cost, complex workflows, and data skills limit wider use. The authors call for clearer proof of benefit and shared work standards.
pmc-13336897:
Marilyn Esclance DMello and colleagues match battery fluid to framework cathodes in a 2026 study of lithium batteries. Their cathodes are porous covalent frameworks decorated with TEMPO radicals, which store charge at high voltage near 3.6–3.7 V against lithium in cell tests. How the salt anion in the fluid shapes that storage was little known.

Five lithium salts were compared head to head. LiDFOB gave the best balance of capacity, speed, and cycle life, thanks to helpful anion-linked storage and surface behavior. Binder-free paper electrodes carried up to 80 wt.% active material at loadings of 40 mg per square centimeter while holding about 1.3 mAh per square centimeter in the reported cells. Matching parts, not just picking stars, lifts organic batteries.
pmc-13337097:
Zexuan Hong leads a 2026 team building a virus toolkit that homes to one neuron type in Parkinson's research. D1 receptor neurons of the striatum drive the direct movement pathway and fall quiet in Parkinson's disease. Selective tools to reach them were lacking.

Screening a capsid library found virus variants with far better backward access along D1 neuron axons from the substantia nigra. Engineered enhancers then drove strong, specific gene activity in those neurons in both mice and a macaque. Using the kit to modulate the direct pathway produced pathway-specific behaviors and rescued movement deficits in a Parkinson's mouse model. Precise access tools serve both basic circuit science and future therapy design.
pmc-13337397:
Hyuk Kim and co-authors compare death risks between two fatty liver definitions in a 2026 nationwide Korean study. MASLD ties liver fat to metabolic problems, while MetALD adds heavier alcohol intake. The sample held 7,783 adults aged 20–79 years from national surveys between 2007 and 2015, weighted to represent about 7.6 million adults, with deaths tracked to November 2023.

Both conditions raised overall mortality versus controls, significantly so for MetALD with a hazard ratio of 2.085 in the reported model. Cancer deaths rose in both groups, while heart deaths did not differ clearly. In MetALD, heavy drinking and smoking independently predicted death; for MASLD, being female and having higher income linked to lower death risk. Splitting the definitions reveals distinct risk profiles worth separate management.
pmc-13337497:
Xiaofeng Jing and co-authors build a gallstone risk model from health checks in Western China in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Among 17,768 subjects, 1,673 had gallstones and 16,095 formed the control group. The team picked factors with a selection method, then raced a logistic model against a random forest, checking separation, accuracy, and clinical benefit.

The random forest won, reaching an AUC of 0.747 with specificity of 0.91 and sensitivity of 0.86 in the validation check. Its risk estimates matched observed outcomes well, and benefit analysis favored it across useful thresholds. Confirmed risk factors included bile acid levels, smoking, diabetes, and blood lipid and protein measures named in the model. Moderate but usable separation could support earlier lifestyle counseling.
pmc-13337697:
Ce Gou and co-authors review treatments for oral lichen planus in a 2026 article. The condition causes long-lasting mouth inflammation with pain and burning, and it tends to return. Its causes are mixed, so no single clear treatment path exists.

Drawing on 46 articles from 2020 to 2025, the review covers drug options first. Those include steroids, calcineurin blockers, hydroxychloroquine, hyaluronic acid, and mTOR blockers. It also covers non-drug options such as platelet concentrates from the patient's own blood and light-based therapy. The authors propose combined drug plans and alternatives, aiming to guide trials toward care fitted to each patient.
pmc-13337897:
Tingjie Liu and a large team survey health literacy in model healthy communities in a 2026 study. Residents of two such communities in Xiaoshan District, Hangzhou, were sampled at random. The question was whether community building links to stronger skills for finding and using health information.

A total of 263 residents answered, and the overall literacy rate reached 65.78 percent as reported. That rate sat above the local 2024 figure of 53.18 percent cited for comparison. Gains appeared for lifestyle, skills, and disease prevention areas, while first aid and basic care areas slipped. Marriage, chronic illness, age, and self-rated health each linked to literacy level.
pmc-13340097:
Morgan De Kleine and colleagues lifted prenatal care in 2026 at Kijabe Hospital in Kenya, where death rates for mothers and babies rank among the world's highest. Most such deaths can be prevented by better prenatal care. A chart audit found large gaps at the first prenatal visit. The project aimed to lift good prenatal care for new patients to 75 percent within eight weeks.

Two tools drove four two week cycles of change. One was a standard intake form built from 32 World Health Organization and Kenya Ministry rules. The other was a risk calculator sorting patients into low, moderate, or high risk. Good care rose from 21 to 77 percent, and standard care scores rose from 42 to 83 percent. The cheap form can be adapted elsewhere, with birth outcome studies still needed.
pmc-13340197:
Maria Stefania Latrofa and colleagues test a dual Leishmania PCR assay across three machines in a 2026 study. Leishmania infantum causes dog and human disease widely, while a reptile-associated species now appears in mammals too. Samples came from sand flies, lizards, and dogs.

A portable chip device, a standard lab system, and droplet digital PCR each ran the same minicircle DNA assay. Detection limits and specificity were checked on cultures plus 120 sand fly guts, 29 lizards, and 101 dogs in the reported sample counts. Comparing platforms shows whether field-ready tools match lab accuracy for surveillance where both species overlap.
pmc-13340497:
Meral and colleagues check a Turkish tool that flags poor food intake risk in children with cancer. Poor intake can raise harm and slow care. The team ran the check in a children's cancer unit. They set it against two trusted checks. One was a scan tool for child cancer. One was a full hands-on review of each child. Close to half the children met the bar for poor nutrition.

The new tool matched both trusted checks well. At some cut points it caught all at-risk children. At others it missed some. Meral calls the tool simple and fit for daily use. More work should test how staff and families take to it.
pmc-13341497:
Where fat sits matters more than how much, argue Anke LiuLi and research partners in a 2026 review of adipose tissue distribution. Subcutaneous, visceral, brown, and beige depots differ in cell makeup, hormone output, and metabolic behavior, and fat lodged in organs adds further risk.

Visceral and ectopic fat track closely with insulin resistance, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, while lower-body subcutaneous fat can act as a safer storage buffer. Patterning reflects genes, development, sex, age, diet, activity, sleep, and stress. Treatments differ too: lifestyle change and GLP-1 drugs trim visceral fat, thiazolidinediones repartition lipids, and cold-based approaches stir heat-producing fat.
pmc-13342397:
Salomé Abdellaoui and colleagues tracked Janus kinase drugs in 2026 in rheumatoid arthritis in routine care, with prescribing shifts after October 2022 safety warnings. The look back study at one centre took in all consecutive patients starting a first Janus kinase drug, tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, or filgotinib, from April 2018 to November 2023.

Drug staying power by Kaplan Meier curves was the main endpoint. Disease scores at six and twelve months and reasons for stopping were secondary endpoints. Among 120 patients, 85 percent were women with mean age 57 and mean disease span 19 years. Pre versus post warning starters show how safety warnings reshaped prescribing.
pmc-13344097:
Yoram Wolf and co-authors link stomach acid drugs to trouble after tummy tuck surgery in a 2026 multi-institution cohort study. Proton pump inhibitors are common in patients with obesity, the group that most often seeks abdominoplasty. Their surgical risks in cosmetic care had gone unmeasured. The team mined a global records network.

After matching, 2,031 patients with a pre-surgery prescription faced 2,031 without any recorded use. Acid drug users suffered surgical-site infections at about two and a half times the rate, doubled wound opening risk, and needed opioids more often within 30 days. Gaps persisted at 60 and 90 days. The authors urge clearer guidance on managing these drugs around surgery.
pmc-13345797:
Chunru Chen and co-authors mapped in 2026 the research field on lymph node spread in ovarian cancer. Node spread is a key route by which this cancer grows. It shapes staging, treatment, and outlook. Despite rising clinical focus, no prior study had mapped how this field grew.

The team screened English papers from the Web of Science Core Collection from 2010 to mid-2025. They found 845 papers, with steady growth over time. Visual tools traced top themes, busy groups, and links between teams. The map shows where knowledge bunches, where gaps stay, and which paths look most hopeful. New researchers and funders gain a guide to a field that shapes survival.
pmc-13346597:
Dilek Yilmaz and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a Dutch decision aid improves shared decision making for patients facing implantable defibrillator implantation or replacement. The choice is nuanced, balancing protection from sudden death against device risks, lifestyle effects, and personal values.

Across six Dutch hospitals between early 2018 and late 2019, a stepped-wedge randomised trial rolled the aid out in stages, adding it to standard care. Patients and clinicians rated shared decision making with validated questionnaires, while decisional conflict scores captured whether choices felt settled. The trial asks whether a structured aid can make a high-stakes cardiac decision feel clearer, fairer, and more truly shared.
pmc-13348197:
Sbongile C. Jiane and colleagues explored in 2026 why men on antiretroviral treatment in Govan Mbeki, Mpumalanga, drop out of care. Staying on treatment is essential for viral suppression and for preventing HIV transmission, yet men in sub-Saharan Africa drop out of follow-up at higher rates.

Interviewing 21 men lost to follow-up at three primary health clinics between May and July 2024, the team used in-depth, semi-structured interviews analysed thematically to capture perceptions, experiences, and barriers. Work demands, clinic experiences, stigma, and side effects emerged as recurring themes. The findings point to male-friendly clinic hours, respectful care, and community support as levers for keeping men in treatment.
pmc-13349997:
Ying Zhang and co-authors probed in 2026 links between muscle and metabolic markers in metabolic syndrome, using photon-counting CT. This newer scan method measures muscle amount and quality with care. Metabolic syndrome shifts body build. Yet how muscle traits link to blood markers remains incompletely grasped.

Among 117 people, 38 with metabolic syndrome and 79 healthy controls, belly CT at the third lumbar level measured muscle area, density, and index. Fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin, and lipids were also taken. Correlation and regression maths, with interaction tests, mapped which muscle traits track with metabolic upset. The findings may turn routine CT muscle measures into early warnings for metabolic risk and targets for exercise and food plans.
pmc-13351697:
Liping He and Manli Zhuang review risk factors and prediction tools for kidney injury around surgery in children, in 2026. The injury affects 5 to 30 percent of children, and up to 40 percent of newborns after heart surgery. It raises the risk of death and lasting kidney disease, so early warning matters.

Four databases were searched to March 2024 for studies in patients aged 18 years or younger. Key risks include young age, congenital heart disease, kidney-harming drugs, and bypass surgery. Models range from standard statistics to machine learning with newer markers in blood and urine. The authors note a clear gap: few models are properly tested in children.
pmc-13351897:
Xavier Vaillo leads a 2026 registry study comparing drug treatment before surgery for stage III non-small cell lung cancer. Patients in the Spanish thoracic surgery registry had either chemotherapy alone or chemotherapy plus immune therapy, then anatomical lung removal, from January 2023 to April 2025. The full group held 114 patients, with 77 in the combined group.

After matching, 68 patients remained in 34 pairs. Full tumour clearance was higher with combined treatment, at 38 percent versus 12 percent. Downstaging and complete removal also favoured the combined group, though surgery took longer, at 240 versus 180 minutes at the median. Safety and complications around surgery were compared alongside cancer outcomes.
pmc-13352397:
Minkyeong Kim and colleagues use machine learning in 2026 to find what drives sarcopenia in Parkinson disease. Muscle loss and weak function are more common in Parkinson disease and link to worse outcomes. Clinical data were split into training and held-out groups in a 70 to 30 ratio, then screened before a shrinkage method picked six key predictors.

A logistic model built on those predictors gave an area under the curve of 0.793 on held-out data. Patients with sarcopenia had longer illness, higher disease stages, and heavier non-motor burden. Body mass index, body fat share, and non-motor traits such as thinking decline, autonomic problems, fatigue, and low mood weighed most. The authors stress non-motor care in muscle health.
pmc-13354197:
Sanjay Basu leads a 2026 transfer learning test of Medicaid risk prediction models across states. Models trained in one state face shifted populations, policies, and care patterns in another. Acute care use was predicted for high-risk care management enrollees in Washington, with 20,744 people, and Virginia, with 28,901 people. Outcome rates differed sharply, at 9.4 percent in Washington versus 25.6 percent in the Virginia group.

Nine approaches were compared, from plain logistic models to neural and ensemble methods. A meta-ensemble scored best on Virginia data, with discrimination of 0.728 and the best calibration of any method tested. Plain source transfer nearly matched it, at 0.725 on the same held-out Virginia data set. Target-only logistic lagged far behind, at 0.628 in the same head-to-head comparison test. Recalibration helped all models, and fairness gaps shrank with target adaptation though disparities persisted.
pmc-13354797:
Pavithra Venkataraman and Christian R Landry review in 2026 how gene changes that alter proteins interact with gene changes that alter how much protein is made. Either kind of change alone can shift fitness, but their joint effect is often a surprise. The review pulls most of its examples from studies in single-celled organisms.

Too little or too much of a protein can both cause harm, so the effect of a protein change depends on how much of it the cell makes. The authors sketch a way to join amount and action in one fitness picture. They argue this view helps explain adaptation, disease, and why the same change can help in one strain and hurt in another.
pmc-13354997:
Eleftherios K Soleas and co-authors ran a 2025 national consensus study in Canada to define what counts as scholarship in continuing professional development for doctors. Accreditation rules require such work from each office, yet no shared list said which outputs qualify. A panel from across the country took part in a three-phase Delphi process.

Twenty-nine panel members finished all phases and endorsed 18 of 31 types of work put to them. Newer forms gained backing, among them community engagement, pilot testing work, and advocacy scholarship. The authors say the shared definition can guide accreditation and promotion, and should be revisited as scholarly work keeps changing.
pmc-13356797:
Francesco Paolo Prete and others tested human factors in safe hand-off of cold light during laparoscopic gallbladder removal, in 2026. Xenon light chains used in laparoscopy can generate extreme heat, risking patient burns and fire. Human factors in how surgeons handle the light source had received little research notice.

The study studied errors and work factors that could compromise safety when delivering light to the endoscope during planned cholecystectomy. Workflow, handling, and equipment links were tested for hazards. Op teams gain useful guidance for preventing a rare but serious burn and fire risk in routine laparoscopy.
pmc-13356897:
Rebecca J Rockett and co-authors sequenced respiratory viruses in 2026 from Australia's first big post-Covid winter flu season, in 2022. One test panel read flu and other viruses at once from patient samples. The team recovered full flu genomes from three-quarters of confirmed flu samples and also found nineteen genomes of other viruses in co-infected samples.

The co-infections included RSV, the Covid virus, and several cold viruses, and their timing matched national trends. In most mixed infections, one virus far outnumbered the other. The H3N2 flu type dominated, with a smaller H1N1 share all winter. The authors show how multi-virus sequencing can track overlapping epidemics in real time.
pmc-13358497:
Lin Chen and Yufu Ye wrote a 2026 commentary on spleen-saving surgery for tumors in the tail of the pancreas. Keeping the spleen helps the immune system, but the classic methods force a trade-off: one is hard to do, the other often starves the spleen of blood. The authors discuss a newer twist on the method.

The newer approach keeps the splenic artery but gives up the splenic vein. In the study they discuss, spleen damage and swollen stomach veins dropped sharply compared with the older method. Chen and Ye weigh the gains, the proof so far, and the open questions, such as which patients suit the method best.
pmc-13358997:
Hunter Scott reviews treatments for fatigue in sarcoidosis in a 2026 paper. Tiredness strikes between 30 and 90 percent of patients with this inflammatory disease and can linger even when scans improve. Past reviews covered only some drugs and skipped non-drug and newer options. Scott set out to gather the whole field and grade the strength of the proof.

Drawing on trials and guidelines from the last decade, the review covers disease drugs, stimulants, exercise, and coaching approaches. Some standard drugs ease inflammation yet worsen tiredness over time. The paper also explains how to rule out other causes of fatigue first, so treatment aims at the right target.
pmc-13360297:
Aya A Eltaibany led a 2026 lab study that built a tiny 3D model of the human blood-brain barrier. This barrier is the tight wall of cells that guards the brain from germs and toxins. The team grew organoids, small self-built balls of mixed brain cells, to copy that wall. They then stressed the models with inflammation signals and with a stop-and-restart of oxygen and sugar.

Both stresses made the barrier leakier and weakened the genes that seal cell joints. Immune cells crossed into the organoids in larger numbers under both kinds of stress. Drugs that block the sticky molecules immune cells use to cross cut that movement back down. The model gives drug makers a human-like test bed for studying brain swelling, stroke harm, and new treatments.
pmc-13361397:
Sarah Rebeca Teixeira de Sousa and co-authors present the plan for a 2026 trial on thinking skills in women with breast cancer. Cancer treatment often dulls memory, attention, and planning, hurting daily life and mood. The trial tests ALMA, a playful program of attention and memory training. It will run at one hospital complex in Salamanca, Spain, with 63 women in active treatment.

The women will be split by chance into three groups. One gets health education, one gets standard solo brain training, and one gets the full ALMA group program. Sessions are face to face and last two hours. As a protocol, the paper sets out the design before results exist. It gives other teams a clear template for testing ways to protect the mind during cancer care.
pmc-13362397:
Fatma Al-Zahraa Sayed and a large team report a 2026 rat study on tiny selenium particles coated with EGCG, a green tea compound. Rats fed a high-fat diet gained blood fat problems, liver harm, and heart stress marks. The team tested the new particles against plain EGCG, plain selenium, and a standard lipid drug in 42 rats split into six groups.

The coated particles gave the best overall gains: better blood fats, lower liver and heart harm marks, and stronger defenses against cell damage. Swelling signals fell and liver tissue looked healthier. The work is early and in rats, but it backs more tests of tea-based nano treatments for fatty liver harm.
pmc-13363497:
Zilong Tang and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study on a new set of benzamide compounds tested against crop fungi. Fungal diseases cut harvests worldwide, and older fungicides are losing ground to resistance. The team built a series of 2-acyloxybenzamides, confirmed their structures with standard spectra, and screened them on several plant pathogens in the lab.

One compound wiped out the rice blast fungus fully in the screen, and another strongly held back a Phytophthora species. Dose tests set the strength of both leads. Computer docking pointed to an enzyme in the fungi's melanin pathway as the likely target, a path that neither plants nor animals carry, which hints at safe selectivity. Field and safety tests remain ahead.
pmc-13364097:
Liang Zong, Yun Cheng, and Yi Yao present a 2026 study on congestion control for networks that join satellites, drones, and ground links into one path. Satellite hops add long delays and many bit errors, while drone hops shift shape constantly, so classic control mistakes channel errors for true congestion and throttles needlessly. Their scheme tunes the opening data push for slow-start and adds a sharp test that tells error losses from queue overflow losses.

Simulations showed shorter queues at drone nodes, faster delivery across multi-hop ends, and higher throughput in high-delay setups than with standard control. The authors offer the design as groundwork for the space-air-ground networks planned for sixth-generation mobile service.
pmc-13368397:
Cristian Hardaman and others asked whether seizures causes amygdalar growth or follows from it, in 2026. The amygdala is central to the limbic system, and size gaps were long linked to mental illnesses. In seizures, amygdala growth has been told of mainly on scans, yet its medical, brain-wave, and tissue pattern was unstudied.

Reading issued papers and the authors' experience, the work argues that growth reflects a defined pattern beyond imaging, with characteristic medical and brain-wave traits that respond to given care. The review reframes growth as a medical entity, not only a scan finding. Epileptologists gain a fuller picture for recognising and treating this distinctive presentation.
pmc-13371197:
Mario Saia and colleagues track malpractice claims linked to hospital-acquired infections in Italy's Veneto region in a 2026 study. Such infections raise illness, death, and costs, and severe cases can lead to claims over failed prevention or care. Claims from 2010 to 2024 in the regional error monitoring system were classed by outcome, infection site, and care setting.

Of 19,380 malpractice claims over fifteen years, 1,106 concerned hospital-acquired infections. Overall claims fell over time, yet infection claims rose in both number and share. Most infection claims involved non-fatal harm, while a smaller share involved death. The trend warns hospitals and insurers that infection prevention is also a legal risk, and it points to where stronger controls could cut both harm and claims.
pmc-13372197:
Nnaemeka H Ugwuchukwu reports a grave immune flare in a 2026 case report. A woman with a rare, fast type of breast cancer got a drug that frees the immune system to fight tumors. She came in with fever and low blood counts, and was first treated as if she had a blood germ.

Germ care did not help, so the team checked for an immune storm that eats blood cells. Lab and tissue tests fit that rare ill, with five of the set signs met. High-dose steroid drugs calmed the storm. The case warns teams that new cancer drugs can spark this storm, which looks much like a plain infection.
pmc-13373797:
José Luis Coyac-Rodríguez and colleagues map the genetics of leaf vein density in maize in a 2026 study. Dense leaf veins help plants move water and sustain photosynthesis, and flowering plants, especially C4 species, evolved denser veins than early land plants. Using native Mexican maize varieties adapted to varied climates, the team tracked vein traits and photosynthetic rates.

Higher vein density tracked with higher photosynthesis, but only for small intermediate veins. Varieties from drier places raised vein density sharply in heat, suggesting a role in water efficiency. Twelve genetic regions linked to vein patterning were found. The work gives breeders genetic handles for maize that photosynthesises well while using water wisely in hot, dry conditions.
pmc-13375697:
Alan Calder and colleagues test whether a harmless mouth bacterium uses a secretion weapon to compete with neighbours in a 2026 study. Neisseria subflava, a commensal, carries a Type VI secretion system, a molecular syringe that injects toxins into rivals. The team knocked out the core gene TssM in strain KU1003-01 and ran competition assays against gonorrhoea bacteria, a second subflava strain, and the yeast Candida albicans.

Recoverable target cells differed clearly between the parent strain and the knockout, showing that the secretion system contributes to competition with all three targets. The work establishes that even a non-pathogenic Neisseria wields a functional weapon, shaping which microbes share its niche. That insight matters for understanding how commensals hold ground against pathogens.
pmc-13377397:
Puteri Nur Athirah Megat Mohamad Aminuddin and co-authors tell of brain TB with a nerve palsy in a 2026 case report. A man aged 22 from Bangladesh had fever, head pain, mind shifts, and a droop of one eye with a wide pupil. Scans showed fluid on the brain and small dead zones.

Spinal fluid held high protein but plain sugar, and all germ tests came back blank. The team still called it brain TB, on tale, scans, and risk, and began germ drugs plus high steroids. His signs got much better on drugs alone, with no need for a brain drain. The case backs bold calls when tests lag.
pmc-13377697:
Jia-chun Tao and colleagues survey neuromuscular reversal and monitoring practice among anaesthesiologists in China in a 2026 study. Residual muscle blockade after surgery raises lung complications, yet monitoring and reversal use were poorly mapped. An online questionnaire with 25 questions, distributed through an anaesthesia forum and WeChat for 30 days with one response per IP address, yielded 3,168 valid responses.

Rocuronium and cisatracurium were the most used blockers. Only about 40 percent routinely gave reversal drugs, mostly neostigmine, with sugammadex used by only about 19 percent. Quantitative monitoring was routine for only 1.6 percent, while 98 percent relied on clinical signs alone. Higher education and senior rank predicted better practice. The survey exposes a wide gap between guidelines and routine practice.
pmc-13379397:
Gokulkumar Sivanantham and co-authors describe a 2026 study turning jackfruit seed peel, a waste material, into a useful plant-based filler. The peel comes from the fruit of Artocarpus heterophyllus. The team extracted microcrystalline cellulose, a fine powder widely used in medicines and materials, from that peel.

Extraction used alkali treatment, acid breakdown, and bleaching to strip away lignin and other plant parts. A battery of tests then checked the product's structure, purity, heat stability, and particle size. The cellulose proved highly ordered in structure, with a crystallinity measure above seventy percent in the results reported. The work suggests farm waste can supply a renewable filler for greener materials.
pmc-13380797:
Huanchang Yan and a large team present a 2026 analysis of a giant cluster in an HIV transmission network in Guangzhou, China. Large clusters hold a large share of people living with HIV, but their size makes targeted action hard. The team developed a way to split a giant cluster into smaller communities for precise intervention.

Using network data from 2008 to 2020, they split one component of 681 members into 34 communities with dense links inside and few outside. Every link between communities ran through central members of one community, which family-tree analysis identified as the likely source of the whole component. People with similar traits tended to cluster, flagging possible outbreak pockets.
pmc-13381997:
Eusebi Chiner and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of how older patients stick with airway pressure treatment for sleep apnea, where the airway collapses repeatedly during sleep. The condition becomes much more common with age. The standard treatment blows air gently to keep the airway open, but only works if patients keep using it.

Good use is usually defined as at least four hours on most nights, with best results at six to eight hours. Many patients stop early, and long-term abandonment is common. Among older adults who start, though, use can match or beat younger patients. The review describes a pattern where use rises into the late seventies and then falls, and discusses the barriers involved.
pmc-13382697:
Genevieve Crotty and Wasim Awal describe a 2026 case of a dangerous bulge in a stomach artery treated by injecting clotting agent through the skin, guided by scans. Such pseudoaneurysms are a rare complication of long-standing pancreas inflammation, where digestive juices erode nearby artery walls. Their patient was a man of 65 with chronic pancreatitis.

The usual treatment threads a catheter through the arteries to block the bulge, but his vessel layout made that unsafe. Instead, doctors injected thrombin directly through the skin under scan guidance. The bulge clotted and resolved on follow-up imaging. The case offers an alternative route when standard access fails, with imaging central throughout.
pmc-13383197:
Fangman Chen's team built a nanozyme whose power switches on under sound waves for precise cancer therapy, in a 2026 study. Natural force-sensitive enzymes tune cell chemistry under force, but artificial nanozymes with strict time and place control were rare. The team embedded force-responsive ferrocene units in a flexible frame to create the MRNZ device.

Acoustic shear reshaped the units, lowering electron density and steric crowding at iron sites and boosting peroxide-like activity. Controlled low-dose oxygen signals then acted as messengers to rewire cell chemistry and toughen stem cells against oxidative stress. Loading glucose oxidase inside hollow MRNZ added a second enzyme layer, pointing toward sound-triggered paired therapy.
pmc-13386797:
Zhongnan Xiao's team tested AI-based retinal screening in teachers and a retinal density marker for myopia, in a 2026 prospective study. AI fundus imaging enables large-scale retinal screening, but use in worker groups was limited. The team screened 648 Beijing teachers with fundus photography and systemic exams, using AI to quantify fundus tessellated density and other retinal measures, then testing links with refractive error and work factors.

Mean refractive error sat near minus two and a half diopters. Density varied across the macula, highest in the nasal quadrant. Density, near work at 30 centimeters, and eye structure measures each linked independently with refractive error. Near work beyond one hour at 30 centimeters tracked with higher density. Density showed moderate power to flag high myopia, at about 78 percent area under the curve, and linked with immune-inflammatory indices. The marker is observational and needs longitudinal validation.
pmc-13388097:
Ashton Bailey, Ryan Gibson, and Kristine Griffett review clock-receptor drugs against inflammatory brain disease in dogs in a 2026 article. Meningoencephalitis of unknown origin is a presumed autoimmune condition and a major treatment challenge in veterinary neurology. Evidence ties helper T cells of the TH17 type and their messenger IL-17A to the inflammation.

Compounds that activate REV-ERB receptors suppressed TH17 growth and eased disease in autoimmune models, with favorable safety signs. Those receptors also steer circadian rhythm and metabolism, widening their immune footprint. The authors map a path for testing such drugs as add-ons to standard immune suppression in dogs.
pmc-13389897:
Hatem Mousa Taha and Khaled Hatem Taha present, in 2026, a 63-year-old Palestinian man with Morvan syndrome whose blood tests stayed negative for the usual antibodies. He showed the full pattern of the disease: constant muscle twitching, extreme sleeplessness, fast heart rate, heavy sweating, and major weight loss.

Muscle recordings across twelve muscles showed the characteristic rapid discharges of this condition, while brain imaging, spinal fluid tests, and cancer screening found nothing. Validated tests confirmed no CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies in blood or spinal fluid. Working in a resource-limited setting, the team built the diagnosis from the clinical pattern and electrical proof. Neurologists gain a worked example of treating a rare autoimmune condition without antibody confirmation.
pmc-13390197:
Runzi Yang's team tracked eight men with Kimura's disease of the eye socket, a rare chronic immune illness that usually strikes young Asian men in the head and neck. Orbital spread is rare and its long-term course was poorly mapped, so the team looked over cases at one centre from 2010 to 2025.

Patients averaged about twenty-one years old. Painless eyelid swelling was the top first sign, and eyelid and tear-gland tissue were most often hit, with dense eosinophil buildup on lab checks. Surgery plus body-wide steroids formed the main treatment, and the series maps return patterns that doctors can use to plan follow-up.
pmc-13390297:
Natalia E Jiménez's team compared seven automated tools for building draft genome-scale metabolism-linked models in multicellular eukaryotes, a task most tools were not designed for. They applied AuReMe, CarveMe, merlin, ModelSEED, Pathway Tools, RAVEN, and Reconstructor to a mosquito, a hamster ovary cell line, and a brown alga.

No tool excelled at both model functionality and eukaryotic traits such as compartmentalisation and organism-specific metabolism, with methods trading one strength against the other on network size, consistency, annotation, and speed. The comparison gives teams a practical guide for matching a reconstruction tool to their organism and goal.
pmc-13391697:
Trent Kite and colleagues systematically review, in 2026, artificial intelligence tools that predict recurrence in high-grade gliomas. These aggressive brain tumours almost always return, and no definitive treatment exists despite standard therapy.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science for studies using machine learning to forecast recurrence, then pooled key accuracy measures with a random-effects model. Neuro-oncology readers gain a combined verdict on how well algorithms currently predict return, which could support individualised therapy timing, plus a clear view of the variation between studies that tempers enthusiasm.
pmc-13394397:
Hagita, Murashima, and Ohkuma use, in 2026, united-atom molecular dynamics simulations to watch strain-induced crystallization in polyisoprene, the polymer in natural rubber. Stretching rubber past a threshold makes tiny crystals form inside it, and those nanocrystallites toughen the material like extra cross-links. Experiments confirm the crystals exist, but their birth and distribution at the molecular scale have stayed murky, which the simulations were built to clarify.

The simulations captured nanocrystallites forming spontaneously from an oriented, stretched melt, verified against computed two-dimensional scattering patterns. Small crystals born during rapid stretching then either grew or melted away during the following still period at constant temperature. Crucially, whether a crystallite survived correlated better with how aligned the polymer segments were at the start than with the overall strain level alone. The authors argue that designing tough soft materials should focus on controlling segment orientation, not just stretch.
pmc-13394697:
Philippe Genereux and a large team model, in 2026, the costs of early valve placement in symptom-free aortic stenosis. The valve narrows with age, and risk climbs once symptoms start. Their model compared a tube-placed valve, TAVI, with watchful waiting across nine European countries. Inputs came from the EARLY TAVR trial and past studies, tracked over a whole lifetime.

Early TAVI came out ahead in every country in the model. It saved money and added healthy years of life in each setting. Gains in quality-weighted years were modest but steady. The authors credit the timing of costs, since waiting still ends in valve work. They back early spotting and prompt care.
pmc-13394897:
Wang and team examine, in 2026, whether ovarian function and fertility recover after anti-NMDAR encephalitis. The disease is an autoimmune brain illness that mainly strikes women of reproductive age and often involves ovarian teratomas, a type of tumor. Their cohort covered 106 women treated at one hospital between 2015 and 2024, tracking hormone levels, menstrual function, and pregnancies, with a separate look at the 23 tumor cases.

Tumor-associated cases were sicker at presentation, needing intensive care and mechanical ventilation more often than other patients. During the acute illness, 38 percent of all patients showed suppression of the hormone axis controlling the ovaries, usually as missed periods. Recovery was the rule afterward: hormone levels improved significantly during convalescence in the followed patients. Pregnancy rates ended up comparable, at 80 percent in the teratoma group and 83.3 percent without tumors, reassuring data for counseling young survivors.
pmc-13395397:
Pengchao Yang and colleagues trace, in 2026, a stress path that drives bone loss during swelling diseases. A cell stress arm named IRE1-XBP1s ran hot in bone-eating cell precursors in inflamed mice. Blocking it cut the making of bone-eating cells and eased bone loss in dishes and animals. Gene reads showed the arm switches on a serotonin carrier gene.

Serotonin, the carrier's cargo, blocked a self-cleaning process that restrains those cells. A common antidepressant that blocks the carrier also slowed cell making. A compound named 3MA softened serotonin's effects. In cells from patients with inflamed bone disease, blocking the axis helped too. The authors name a new drug target.
pmc-13396097:
Emma Valima and others study cell-fate rewiring by chromatin SUMO tags in a 2026 paper. How this protein tag shapes cell give was unclear, so the team tracked CEBPA-led flip of blood cancer B cells into guard-cell-like cells.

Joined chromatin, access, RNA, and protein maps showed a live rise in SUMO2 and SUMO3 tags at CEBPA-bound spots in early rewiring. The helper NCOA3 showed a sharp rise in SUMO tie and shared CEBPA and SUMO-bound spots. The work bares a SUMO-backed control layer in cell fate flips, with hints for steering cell kinds on demand.
pmc-13396197:
Matos and team describe, in 2026, a newly found pegivirus causing encephalitis in red-legged partridges, a game bird farmed across Europe. Pegiviruses are usually seen as harmless, so brain disease linked to one is unexpected. Gene sequencing of brain tissue from outbreak flocks identified the virus, named ParPgV, and microscopy showed encephalitic lesions, dying neurons, and viral particles inside neurons.

Experimental infection of red-legged partridges, grey partridges, and lab chickens confirmed the virus targets the nervous system, and infected red-legged partridges developed cerebellar atrophy visible on MRI scans. Finding negative-strand RNA, the copying intermediate, proved the virus was actively copying itself in each host species tested.
pmc-13396297:
Roger Plaza-Clar and others weigh two seed-growth tests for Parkinson-type illness across labs in a 2026 multi-site study. This seed test spots Parkinson-type illness, and test brews may sort Lewy-body illness from glial-inclusion illness, but head-to-head test proof was thin.

In a tight two-by-two plan, two brew kinds each ran at two free labs. Spine fluid came from 60 people, with system atrophy cases plus Parkinson and Lewy dementia cases in the mix. The study scores match and illness sorting across brews and sites. Doctors gain a firm base for picking and reading these seed tests.
pmc-13396397:
Cai and team name, in 2026, the ion channel TMEM63B as a regulator of placental development acting through nucleocytoplasmic transport, the shuttling between nucleus and cytoplasm. The channel senses osmotic and mechanical cues. In trophoblast cells, the placenta's building blocks, it stabilizes transport machinery that moves cell cycle regulators in and out of the nucleus as conditions change.

Losing the channel weakened the Ran protein and its export complex with XPO1, trapping the cell cycle brake p21 inside the nucleus and stalling trophoblast growth. In mice, homozygous knockout pups survived at only 5 percent after birth, far below the 25 percent expected from Mendelian inheritance, and placenta-specific knockouts survived at 12 percent in the reported litters. The resulting placental dysfunction caused perinatal death. The authors frame TMEM63B as a pivotal link between mechanical sensing, nuclear transport, and healthy placental growth.
pmc-13396997:
Kshitiz Pandey and co-authors survey how artificial intelligence could personalize nerve-based treatments for heart disease, in a 2026 review. Cardiac neuromodulation covers techniques that rebalance the autonomic nerves, from stimulating the vagus nerve to silencing overactive kidney nerves, all aimed at hearts driven by faulty nerve balance.

Big trials of these methods have repeatedly missed their main goals, with many patients simply not responding. The authors blame blunt dosing, stimulation that spills onto the wrong fibers, and wide differences in nerve patterns between patients. Learning algorithms that read a patient's signals and tune stimulation to match are offered as the route from mixed trial history to clinic.
pmc-13397097:
Meihui Huang and co-authors gathered the meta-analyses on exercise for people on hemodialysis and graded the whole pile, in a 2026 umbrella review. Dialysis patients are often urged to exercise, yet the reviews behind that advice are scattered and of uneven quality.

Eleven meta-analyses, drawn from four databases through January 2026, were scored for method quality and evidence strength. Aerobic exercise improved dialysis adequacy, peak oxygen use, walking distance by about 65 meters, systolic pressure, inflammation, and depression scores. Resistance training helped walking and physical quality of life. Effects the reviews claimed for other outcomes, such as diastolic pressure, did not hold up.
pmc-13397197:
JaeWoo Park and co-authors printed microscopic OLED pixels in one inkjet pass, with each pixel walling itself off as it dries, in a 2026 paper. Inkjet printing promises large light-emitting displays without masks or vacuum steps, yet keeping micron-sized pixels even has been a stubborn problem.

Two solvents, chloroform-like trichloromethane and dichloroethane, were blended so that as the drop dries, the glowing material separates sideways from a displaced polymer underlayer and settles into its own compartment. Microscopy and chemical mapping confirmed the self-sorting. A single programmed solvent step replacing several lithography steps could cut the cost of fine-pitch display making.
pmc-13397597:
Augustin Murhabazi Bashombwa and others gauge hospital readiness for road crash care in Central Africa in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Well-ready hospitals with enough staff and supplies are vital for crash care, yet readiness along major road routes was uncharted.

Fifty-three hospitals along crash-prone routes in Cameroon and South Kivu province in DR Congo were surveyed face-to-face with managers on rules, staff and stuff, buildings, and training needs. Thirty hospitals were in Cameroon and 23 in South Kivu. The study bares gaps that ministries must close to save crash victims.
pmc-13397697:
Abdullah Al Habib and others name drivers of patient contentment in a Bangladesh primary health clinic in a 2026 study. Patient contentment signals health care quality and readiness, chiefly in low- and middle-income primary care, yet proof from Bangladesh public clinics was thin.

Among 508 patients visiting Savar Upazila Health Complex in April and May 2025, contentment was gauged with the short-form Patient Satisfaction Questionnaire, with social, patient, and clinic factors gathered by set interview. Stock and machine learning reads matched each other in finding telling patterns. Clinic chiefs gain locally grounded levers for lifting primary care.
pmc-13397897:

pmc-13398097:

Their 2026 pre-post study covers 175 adults with post-traumatic stress disorder, a condition that often travels with raised autism spectrum traits. Hard evidence on whether those traits change therapy response had been scarce.

The programme packed prolonged exposure, EMDR therapy, teaching sessions and physical activity into an intensive course. Based on a 50-item questionnaire, 70 patients fell into a high-trait group and 105 into a low-trait group. Clinician-rated symptom scores were taken before and after, and the analysis tested whether change over time differed by group, a result therapists can use when planning care for mixed presentations.
pmc-13398397:
Christopher Sparks and co-authors build and test an electronic phenotype, an algorithm that finds chronic kidney disease in hospital records at scale. Their 2026 study uses four years of encounter and laboratory data from a large Australian tertiary hospital, excluding transplant recipients and dialysis patients.

The algorithm flagged 17,908 likely cases from a hospital cohort of 342,146 people, about 5.2 percent, using diagnosis codes, reduced filtration rates, or protein in urine lasting at least three months. Blinded chart review of 200 records showed diagnosis codes were the most sensitive single route, while filtration and protein criteria were highly specific. Coding for kidney disease rose steeply with disease stage. The authors conclude that adding laboratory data finds new, often early, cases with high confidence, though overall sensitivity remains limited compared with codes alone.
pmc-13398497:
Guilin Wang and colleagues compare two ways of watching kidney risk during ureteroscopy, the scope procedure that clears urinary stones. Sheaths with pressure sensors and scopes with built-in gauges now give live pressure readings in theatre. The authors argue that watching one measure alone undersells risk, and sketch how paired monitoring could catch danger sooner.
pmc-13398697:
Kadeem A Knight and Cherian J Cherian present a teenager whose pancreas was cut in two by what looked like minor trauma. Their 2026 case report follows an 18-year-old woman who arrived ten days after a blunt blow to the belly, with worsening upper abdominal pain and vomiting. Pancreas injuries are rare, hidden deep in the body, and notorious for late discovery.

Surgeons removed the tail of the pancreas and the spleen, and she healed without complications or later hormone or enzyme failure. The authors back decisive surgery when high-grade injury tears the duct, rather than watchful waiting.
pmc-13399197:

Thirty patients were split between the two graft types, and the surgeons measured each graft before implantation. Hamstring grafts came out longer, averaging 28.8 centimeters against 25.8 for the peroneus longus grafts in the reported comparison. Peroneus grafts were thicker, at about 9.33 millimeters against 8.47 for the hamstring option. Body measurements did not reliably predict hamstring graft size, though younger and taller patients tended to yield longer peroneus grafts. The authors say such patterns can help surgeons plan which graft to harvest.
pmc-13399297:
Luise Longo Angeloni leads a large Brazilian team reporting whole-genome sequencing results for patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, in a 2026 paper. Whole-genome sequencing can also surface novel NF1 variants, incidental findings unrelated to the reason for testing, and occasional dual diagnoses. The authors present their cohort as evidence for what genome-wide testing adds beyond targeted panels in this disorder.
pmc-13400197:

They modeled the change with two-level regression.

Then the surprise: cynicism, burnout's detachment component, fell significantly during the pandemic rather than rising. Job satisfaction and physical health did not change significantly. Their practical conclusion targets workload management and mental health support for this workforce.
pmc-13400297:

Their 2026 phase 1 work addresses cancer that has spread to the membranes around brain and spinal cord, a stage with high unmet need. The primary safety endpoint was met, and 50 milligrams was chosen for the ongoing expansion phase. Median life span was 6.6 months, with quality of life stable. pmc-13400697:

Cancer-associated fibroblasts, which build matrix and modulate immunity, remain poorly defined in this tumor and blur with tumor cell programs. The authors weigh fibroblast states, from inflammatory to contractile, and their roles in growth, immune exclusion and treatment response.
pmc-13400997:

Papillary fibroelastomas usually sprout from valve surfaces. Although harmless under the microscope, they are mobile and can throw off clots that cause stroke or heart attack.

Surgeons removed it on bypass and pathology confirmed the diagnosis. The accompanying review found varied presentations and attachment sites in published cases, with a strong preference for surgical removal of mobile non-valve lesions.
pmc-13401297:
Oliver Chinonso Mbaoma, Stephanie Margarete Thomas, Andrew J Macdonald, and Carl Beierkuhnlein wrote a 2026 primer on Europe's native mosquito species that can transmit disease, a group often overshadowed by invasive species. They also discuss habitat shifts, hybridization across habitat gradients, and the finding of non-endemic pathogens in field-caught secondary vector species, all of which shape future risk.
pmc-13401397:
Chao Han, Yifei Wang, and Shuai Guo wrote a 2026 letter about a study by Zhang and colleagues on kidney injury linked to polymyxin B, a last-resort antibiotic, in 325 Chinese patients. pmc-13401597:

pmc-13401897:

Time to weight-bearing, X-ray healing, and complications completed the picture.
pmc-13402297:

pmc-13402497:

pmc-13402597:

pmc-13402797:

pmc-13402897:

pmc-13402997:

pmc-13404097:

pmc-13405097:

pmc-13405397:

pmc-13407597:

pmc-13408597:

pmc-13409097:

pmc-13410797:

pmc-13411097:

pmc-13411297:

pmc-13411897:

pmc-13413197:

pmc-13424297:

pmc-13425897:

pmc-13426097:

pmc-13426497:

pmc-13427097:
Catherine Varner asks how to keep Canada's emergency physicians from leaving in a 2026 commentary on new longitudinal survey findings. Varner argues system fixes, not resilience training, must answer attrition on this scale. Staff who feel they can not give safe care in time are the ones most apt to quit, and that link runs through each round of the poll.
pmc-13427497:
Elise C. Bixby, Christine Banks, Lauren H. Redler, and Jennifer J. Beck tackle billing codes for shoulder joint surgery in young athletes in a 2026 coding guide. Lower limb problems dominate pediatric sports practice. Adolescent upper limb injuries and overuse still fall squarely in scope. Worked hypothetical cases walk through posterior shoulder impingement in a 17-year-old pitcher and other scenarios across the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, and sternoclavicular joints.

Clarifications tie each code choice to what the operative report must document. Accurate coding protects reimbursement and audit standing for procedures surgeons perform less often.
pmc-13427997:
Sai Sanikommu and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, early trials of engineered immune cells against brain tumors in children and young adults. CAR-T therapy retrains a patient's own T cells to hunt a chosen target, and it works well in blood cancers. Solid brain tumors are a harder test. No deaths were caused by the therapy itself. Immune side effects were common yet reversible with steroids and related drugs. About two thirds of judged patients at least held their disease stable, while clear shrinkage stayed rare.
pmc-13428097:
Alberto Zambudio Munuera and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, cystinuria, an inherited condition that makes hard kidney stones return again and again. A gene fault stops the kidneys from reabsorbing cystine, an amino acid that then crystallizes. Fresh registry data from 269 European patients show how far real care falls short of targets. Only about 16 percent hit the goal range for urine acidity, and about 39 percent formed a new stone within a year.

It also weighs N-acetylcysteine, a familiar drug with a sound chemical rationale but no solid trial proof yet in this disease. Many patients stop the current sulfur drugs because of side effects, which keeps the search for add-on options active.
pmc-13429697:
ZuoJun Huang and colleagues quiet a gene called CLYBL to ease lung harm in sepsis, where wild inflammation and a upset body chemistry kill air-sac cells. In a mouse model of gut sepsis, CLYBL rose a lot in lung tissue and in gut macrophages, the clean-up cells of the immune system.

With CLYBL quiet, a calm-down chemical called itaconate built up, harsh macrophage action eased, and air-sac linings held firm, so fewer cells died. Lung doctors get a new gene target and a smart carrier aimed at septic lungs.
pmc-13429897:
Daniells Erazo leads a large French team reporting, in a 2026 study, real-world results for tofersen in a genetic form of ALS. Tofersen is an injected genetic drug for patients whose ALS stems from a faulty SOD1 gene. Nineteen centers in the national ALS network contributed 46 treated patients. Each patient's decline rate before treatment was compared with the year after starting, and blood levels of a nerve damage marker were tracked.

pmc-13430797:
Jennifer L. Ridgeway and colleagues study champions and early adopters of shared decision making for heart-disease prevention, a practice urged but rarely routine. Enthusiastic, skilled champions may pull peers along, yet their real influence was little described.

A conversation aid for cardiovascular risk reduction was built into electronic records in three United States health systems. Eight of fifteen affiliated clinics used a champion strategy, with adopters defined by at least two tool uses and superusers by at least twenty. Adoption and penetration were tracked across early, active, and maintenance phases. Implementers get a human map of how a decision tool spreads clinic by clinic.
pmc-13431497:
Peter K Vogt wrote a 2026 essay that traces where cancer genes came from and where the field now heads. Bird viruses form the root of the story. Work that began with the first found sarcoma virus grew into lab tests that could count cancer-driving strength in grown cells.

Work on mammal viruses soon joined in, and some genes found that way now anchor drugs that hit cancer with aim. pmc-13432797:
Li and colleagues test isobavachin, a plant flavonoid, as a guard for the kidney and heart against high uric acid, the state behind gout. Uric acid lowers with the compound in past work, but organ protection needed proof. Their 2026 study combines network pharmacology, which predicts drug targets from databases, with docking models. It adds tests in kidney and heart cells bathed in uric acid, and a mouse model of long term high uric acid.

The screens pointed to NF-κB, an inflammation switch, and cell tests confirmed the compound calmed that pathway and protected cell types. In mice, treatment improved kidney tissue damage and cut collagen scarring by blocking a cell shape shift that drives fibrosis, meaning scar buildup. Heart injury, thickening, and scarring also eased. The anti inflammatory effect ran through two gates at once: quieting NF-κB and stopping assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome, an inflammation trigger complex.
pmc-13432897:
Sidra Ghafoor and co-authors sprayed a building-block amino acid on maize leaves in 2026 to test whether the spray shields the crop from salt strain. Salt cuts growth and yield for maize across wide farm belts. Pots split by salt load and by spray strength, with plain water and no-spray sets for fair checks.

Salt slashed shoot and root weight and drained leaf greens. The strongest spray clawed back much of the loss, lifting weights and greens past the plain sets. Salt also raised two harm marks in leaves, while the strong spray cut both back down. Guard enzymes and a guard compound all ran hotter under the strong spray. The authors pitch leaf sprays of this kind as a cheap, scale-ready shield for salt-hit fields.
pmc-13433597:
Fatemah I Ammar and co-authors looked back in 2026 at 133 patients at a Saudi center. Each patient had blood plasma swapped as care for nerve diseases. The team asked whether daily function rose after the swaps. The swap clears antibodies and like plasma freight that drive harm. Charts spanned care from 2015 to 2022 across a wide disease list.

A standard daily-life scale read each patient before care and three months after the last swap. Scores rose with firm proof for six named diseases, from joint-nerve and muscle-nerve faults to brain swelling of immune kind. A mixed tail group showed no firm gain. Deaths ran under seven in a hundred, with none laid on the swaps. The authors back swaps for picked diseases, with the chart base as the cap.
pmc-13433997:
Ján Bíňovský and co-authors froze a tail-gripping virus of staph germs in 2026 to watch its base plate flex and fire the tail's squeeze. Such viruses punch germ walls with a spring tail to pour their genes in. Cold frames show the plate as core, wedges, and arms that bear grip proteins and tripod stacks.

On host touch, grip proteins swing and reshape. Tripod shifts free the core spike and weld parts, which bare wall-chewing zones of hub proteins. Arm moves run through wedges to the tail's starter ring. The ring swells, the sheath snaps to half length, and the tube drives a short span into the cell. Kin viruses of thick-wall germs likely share the play, the authors say.
pmc-13434797:
Ruikang Yan and a large team blend ranking math with machine learning to firm up transport safety choices in 2026. Multi factor choices for policy often wobble when judges weigh factors by feel. Their model pairs a refined ranking method with a learning step that cuts noise.

The learning step squeezes data onto axes that best split groups apart. Cleaner data then lets a grouping method find crisp patterns. A case study across Asia Pacific economies shows steady, scalable results. Planners get a tool that shows its work while it ranks. Resource choices gain a firmer footing.
pmc-13436097:
Jivraj and colleagues investigate Britain's coastal health puzzle in this 2026 study: seaside towns record some of England's worst health outcomes, yet living near the sea is also claimed to protect health. Using two national birth cohorts, people born in 1958 and 1970 and followed into midlife, they tested whether coastal residence itself predicts multimorbidity, meaning two or more chronic conditions.

The analysis covered 13,691 respondents from the earlier cohort and 14,683 from the later one. Growing up on the coast showed no link to midlife multimorbidity, but living coastally in midlife carried 1.21 times higher odds of later multimorbidity in the 1958 cohort, an association that faded once neighborhood deprivation entered the model. People who moved away from the coast were healthier than those who moved in, pointing to selective migration concentrating disadvantage in coastal towns.
pmc-13438397:
Olufisayo Olakotan and colleagues evaluated STORK, a parent education program built to cut infant death risks in England's Midlands, a region with high rates and stark ethnic gaps. The program teaches parents of early-born babies, backed by a phone app holding the lessons. Their 2026 study interviewed sixteen parents and three facilitators at a Leicester hospital group between June and December 2024.

Parents said the training left them surer and readier, above all on emergency response, safe sleep, and infection control. They asked for teaching that is hands-on, early, and flexible around fragile babies. Facilitators agreed on the program's value and named its strains: thin resources, and content needing shaping for the region's many cultures. The authors argue parent education earns its place only when it fits family life and language. Their findings sketch how to spread such programs without losing families most at risk.
pmc-13439697:
Bauer and colleagues engineer mice that produce mostly daughters or mostly sons. Their 2026 paper borrows machinery from the t-haplotype, a selfish genetic element in mice that rigs its own inheritance. The team built a selfless version of its central responder element that disables the sperm carrying it, and placed it on the X or Y chromosome.

When the element sits on one sex chromosome, the sperm carrying that chromosome are knocked out, so offspring are predominantly the other sex and mostly non-transgenic. The authors stress what the design avoids: earlier sex-ratio methods compromised animal health, cut fertility, or required fully transgenic breeding stock. Because undesired-sex offspring in livestock are often culled, a cleaner genetic route could matter commercially. The authors describe the mouse results as a groundbreaking proof of principle for animal breeding.
pmc-13439997:
Pierre-Luc Fournier and colleagues ask whether rules and paperwork help or hinder nurses' agility at work, surveying Canadian nurses in 2026. Agile staff adapt quickly in a shifting system, and patients benefit when they can. Standardised processes might support adaptation by clarifying work, or choke it like red tape does. Survey answers from 2,173 nurses fed a statistical model linking standardisation, administrative burden, agility, and judged quality of care.

Care quality rose with nurses' agility, both inward-facing and outward-facing kinds. Standardisation fed agility rather than blocking it. Administrative burden did the opposite, dragging agility down. Cutting pointless paperwork is their practical takeaway for managers.
pmc-13442397:
Bartłomiej Ptaszek and colleagues ask whether whole-body cold sessions change balance in a 2026 study of 12 healthy young women. Each woman stood on a force plate before and after ten cold chamber sessions. Tests used one leg or both legs, with eyes open or shut, to vary how hard balance had to work.

Some sway measures shifted after the cold series, most clearly path length and sway speed in the hardest stance, one leg with eyes shut. Load spread across the feet also changed in a few tests. The authors read the shifts as a sign that cold can tune the sense of body place, yet they stress the small group and lack of a control arm. Firm claims must wait for larger trials with random group splits.
pmc-13442597:
Choi and colleagues compare exercise patterns and high blood pressure across social groups in South Korea. Weekend warriors pack their weekly activity into one or two days, while regular exercisers spread it out. Their 2026 study analyzes 28,039 adults from a national health survey run from 2018 to 2023. It sorts people as inactive, partly active, weekend warriors, or regularly active, and splits results by schooling and household income.

Every active pattern tied to lower odds of high blood pressure than inactivity, and weekend warriors showed the lowest odds of the active groups in adjusted models. Schooling did not change the weekend warrior link. Income did: the tie between weekend activity and lower pressure ran stronger in lower income adults. The authors note the survey is a snapshot, so long term studies should test whether packed weekend exercise truly protects across income levels.
pmc-13442897:
María Estefanía Peña Giraldo and colleagues report brain vein clot removal with a stent tool in a 2026 case paper. Scans showed wide clots in the top brain vein and in side veins on both sides.

Six passes left the top vein near-fully open, with flow restored and no harm from the work. She left after 12 days with strong limb marks. At 34 days her function score sat at zero, which marks no lasting deficit.
pmc-13442997:
Tiantian Pan and colleagues test a growth-versus-safety trade in 22 Eucalyptus species in a 2026 study. Trees must move water fast to grow, yet wide pipes risk air blocks in drought. No study in that count showed fast growth and strong safety together.
pmc-13443097:
Ashleigh Iwikau and colleagues show how migrant fish carry the seeds of fast form change in Galaxias fishes in a 2026 study. Some lines gave up sea trips and settled in fresh water, a shift that remakes salt handling, muscle, motion, and breeding. Most strong shift genes sat clumped on one chromosome, a packed kit of co-adapted parts. Migrant groups held jackpot fish that carry the whole kit intact, at high shares. Fresh splits cut off by landslides in New Zealand shifted form fast, fed by those carriers. The authors call the kit a clear case of modular change, where one packed gene block lets whole trait sets flip in a few generations.
pmc-13443197:
Itziar Cenzano and colleagues track marrow wall and stem cells as a blood state slides toward myeloma in a 2026 study. The early state, MGUS, can sit quiet for years before cancer blooms. Mouse models that copy the slide gave single-cell reads for vessel lining cells and marrow stem cells.

A joint interferon program marked one model but missed its fiercer twin. A three-drug mix hushed that program, helped lining cells adapt, and revived bone power in stem cells. Patient checks found the same mark enriched across stages.
pmc-13443797:
Tingting Wen and coauthors propose a 2026 diagnostic framework linking three-dimensional city form to urban vitality, a link that simple density measures capture poorly. Using building footprints and heights for central Jinan, China, the team built multifractal metrics and a vitality index from population, venues, and road data. The link was then modeled with XGBoost and SHAP explanations.

The heterogeneity index emerged as a top predictor of vitality and stayed highly ranked across alternative settings, adding signal beyond standard shape measures. A segmented analysis found a stable sensitive zone near an index value of 1.82. The mismatch gauge flags places where built form and lived activity diverge, giving regeneration planners a quantitative triage tool rather than a causal claim.
pmc-13444497:
Capucine Habay and colleagues compare clot makeup in cancer-linked strokes against twin stroke types in a 2026 study. Cancer can spark strokes and can hide behind a first stroke. Their pool held nine cancer stroke patients, three with heart valve clot growths, plus matched peers with heart-source or artery-source strokes, 16 in each peer arm.

Pulled clots faced lab melt tests with a standard clot drug. Cancer clots held their weight at a median mark of 92 percent after the drug bath, against 9 percent for artery clots. Melt resistance rose with platelet and von Willebrand marks and fell as red cell share rose. A white clot subgroup, pale and red-cell poor, held all three valve cases. The authors tie clot build to drug failure risk.
pmc-13445197:
Xin Cheng and colleagues present a lab protocol that makes fear memories spread to safe settings in mice without making the core memory stronger, published in 2026. Training in two distinct settings, rather than the same one twice, brings lasting stress-like behavior along with the broadened fear. The protocol then lays out memory tests and behavior checks, giving labs a shared way to probe how sharp fear turns wide and heavy.
pmc-13445497:
Lisa Schoof and colleagues ask how much yearly MRI scanning adds for people with multiple sclerosis who take the drug ocrelizumab, in a 2026 cohort study from Amsterdam. Guidelines urge a scan each year, yet disease activity on this drug runs low, and scans burden patients and clinics alike. The team counted how often follow-up scans showed fresh activity.

The group held 342 patients with at least two scans during treatment, giving 1,639 scans in all. Activity appeared in under two in a hundred scans, touching fewer than seven in a hundred patients, over a median of about four years on the drug. The number of scans needed to find one active case climbed steeply after two years. Yearly scans in patients without symptoms never led to a change in treatment.
pmc-13445697:
You-Tong Lin and colleagues test whether a chemical mark on RNA, carried in tiny blood particles, can flag colorectal cancer and its stage, in a 2026 study. pmc-13446297:

Those proteins drive inflammation across the body and can reach the brain. The team reads the gap as a first clue that immune processes may take part in how stuttering arises, and they call for deeper study of the link.
pmc-13446597:

The review maps where its gene copies sit across species, what switches the RNA itself on, and how crops might gain from fine edits to the module. The prize is plants that hold yield while standing stress, a balance breeders chase.
pmc-13448197:

pmc-13448897:
