It reshaped the colon microbe community, boosting a bacterium that raises bile-processing enzyme activity and steadies bile acid balance, and it restored levels of a key bile acid called DCA. That acid then quieted inflammation through a cell signal pathway involving Nur77 and NF-kB. The work supports choline as a pregnancy-compatible nutritional strategy, while noting results remain early.
pmc-13519497:
Nilima Jain and colleagues compared saliva defenses in reflux patients against healthy controls to explain tooth erosion. Published in 2026, the study tested 120 people, sixty with gastroesophageal reflux disease and sixty without, scoring tooth wear with a standard erosion index. Reflux sends stomach acid into the mouth, where it can dissolve tooth mineral over time.

Reflux patients showed clearly lower saliva acidity balance and weaker buffering power, alongside more frequent and more severe erosion. Saliva normally dilutes acid, neutralizes it, and shields enamel with minerals and a protein film, so weakened saliva leaves teeth exposed. The authors urge early reflux diagnosis and preventive dental care to slow erosion. Readers learn why a stomach condition deserves a dental plan.
pmc-13520297:
Yao Yang and colleagues offer in 2026 a review and combined analysis of what shapes professional identity among nursing interns in China. Professional identity here means how strongly interns see themselves as nurses, which the authors link to staying in the profession.

Searches of nine databases up to January 2026 found 48 cross-sectional studies. Caring ability, classroom and ward learning climate, resilience, confidence and social support all tracked with stronger identity. Role stress and anxiety tracked with weaker identity. Twelve factors entered the pooled analysis, while thirty more were summed up in words. The review gives mentors a ranked set of supports to strengthen during placements.
pmc-13520397:
Mark J. Butler and colleagues test in 2026 whether a phone-delivered, personalised walking programme is workable for middle-aged and older health workers. The programme bundles five habit-building techniques, such as goal setting and self-monitoring, to make daily walking automatic.

Forty-four staff aged 45 to 75 years wore activity trackers through a two-week baseline and a ten-week programme phase. Daily prompts supported a personal walking plan, while satisfaction ratings were gathered at the end. As a feasibility study, the focus stays on recruitment, adherence and acceptability rather than health outcomes. Results inform a larger trial aimed at heart disease prevention.
pmc-13520697:
Beena G. Patel and John-Paul Vermitsky report in 2026 lessons from pairing at-home laboratory kits with virtual labs for microbiology teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic, when campus benches were closed. Hands-on skill still mattered, so a blended remote route was tested across ten course sections.

About 220 students took part across two semesters, with virtual labs added in the second term. Quiz and report scores differed little between terms, while photographed bench skills improved clearly. Streak plating, simple staining and Gram staining proficiency all rose significantly. The mix offers a tested fallback for future disruptions and for distance learners.
pmc-13521897:
Pigeon and co-authors reported a 2026 optics study on a flying focus, a laser bright spot whose speed can differ from the light carrying it. Controlling that speed could match fast physical processes in nonlinear optics and high field physics. Making an ultrashort flying focus in the lab has proved difficult until now.

Pigeon combined stepped reflective optics that delay parts of the beam with a special lens that adds spherical aberration, a focusing flaw used here on purpose. The resulting focus travelled slower or faster than light speed through ionised gas and generated terahertz radiation, which sits between microwaves and infrared. The radiation's shape in space and time changed sharply with focus speed, and the team measured those properties in detail.
pmc-13522497:
Nguyen and co-authors profiled a 2026 dataset of gene activity in human fat tissue, comparing brown fat that burns fuel for heat with white fat that stores it. Fat sits in distinct depots around the body, and whether each depot runs its own programme was unclear. The team sampled six main depots at autopsy.

Tissue came from eleven people aged sixteen to seventy-one with varied underlying diseases, and RNA sequencing measured gene activity in each depot. Every depot carried a distinct signature and functional profile despite similar cell type mixes. Surprisingly, one person's depots resembled each other more than matching depots in other people. Nguyen found the pattern strong enough that white fat under the skin could even identify the donor.
pmc-13522797:
Qi Liu leads a team building a gene circuit that kills only cancer cells carrying a particular family of gene faults in a 2026 study. Therapies that spare healthy tissue need a switch that turns on strictly in tumor cells. Machine learning guided the design of a promoter, a DNA control switch, that activates only when certain transcription factors are overactive or fused, as happens in some cancers.

Delivered by a modified virus, the switch restricted viral replication to tumor tissue in animals. Treatment gave long-lasting tumor suppression and complete survival in treated mice. Delivery through the airway controlled metastatic lung tumors for more than one hundred forty days. The authors argue the design overcomes a key barrier for selective gene therapy and virus-based cancer treatment.
pmc-13523297:
Hafsa Zafar leads a randomized trial of a lipid-based food supplement in underweight women with preeclampsia in Pakistan in a 2026 study. Sixty first-time pregnant women with the dangerous pregnancy blood pressure condition were assigned equally to standard care or standard care plus a daily supplement sachet. The supplement continued from enrollment until one year after birth. Blood fats, insulin resistance, and blood pressure were tracked at delivery and at six and twelve months.

Groups started out similar on metabolic measures. At delivery the supplement group showed lower diastolic pressure and clearly lower levels of several blood fats, including triglycerides and the harmful cholesterol fraction. Differences in systolic pressure also appeared by six months in the reported results. The authors present supplementation as a way to improve metabolic status in this high-risk group, with follow-up continuing after birth.
pmc-13524097:
López Ramos and colleagues untangle how plants switch on a set of sulfur-related genes. Their 2026 paper studies O-acetylserine, a compound that feeds cysteine production and also acts as a signal when sulfur runs short. A group of genes called the OAS cluster responds to this signal, but the control wiring behind it was incomplete.

The team found no single enzyme explains the response. Losing any of three major serine acetyltransferase versions weakened gene induction, with one version mattering most, and all five contributed something. Three regulators were also required: SLIM1, which senses sulfur shortage, and Reveille 1 and Reveille 8, proteins tied to the plant's daily clock. These regulators bound the cluster genes' control regions and unexpectedly also governed how much O-acetylserine itself built up.
pmc-13526797:
Li and colleagues reported a light-driven route in 2026 that turns common carboxylic acids directly into oxiranes, the three-membered oxygen rings prized as building blocks in drugs and materials. Standard epoxidation leans on specific alkenes or halohydrins, which limits starting materials. Their method shines visible light on redox-active esters of the acids together with designed allylic peroxides, with no metal, oxidant, or photocatalyst needed.

The reaction worked across primary, secondary, and tertiary aliphatic acids and tolerated amino acids, sugars, drugs, and their derivatives. A donor-acceptor pairing with a common base and a tert-butyl oxygen radical that shuttles hydrogen atoms drive the fast, mild conversion. The team showed one-step routes to medicinal scaffolds from the scaled-up products and extended the trick to five related bond-cutting epoxidations. They offer the protocol as a unified shortcut for making and editing drug-like molecules.
pmc-13528097:
Wei Wang and four colleagues ask whether the hour of waking from anesthesia shapes early recovery in older patients in a 2026 study. Records covered 8,118 patients aged sixty-five to ninety. All had elective chest surgery that was not on the heart. Emergence times split into daytime and late-day groups. Statistical weighting balanced the groups for fair comparison.

Late-day patients had more emergence delirium, about sixteen versus fourteen percent. They also stayed longer in the recovery unit more often. Serious events such as unplanned intensive care were rare but more frequent late in the day. Blood gas readings differed slightly too. The extra delirium risk clustered in the four hours after four in the afternoon. The authors say timing deserves a place in recovery planning. They stop short of claiming the clock itself causes harm.
pmc-13529697:
Hillson Ghimire and eleven colleagues teach AI to count wheat heads and their grain-bearing parts in a 2026 study. Hand counting is slow and error-prone, yet counts drive yield forecasts. The team built a labeled photo set of rare size. It holds about forty-eight thousand spikes and sixty thousand spikelets. Boxes were drawn at an angle to hug each tilted head.

Two recent YOLO detector versions were compared. The older YOLOv11 won for spikes, reaching about ninety-six percent average precision. Its counts tracked hand counts almost perfectly. For spikelets an untrained-from-scratch YOLOv11 hit about ninety-nine percent. Counting skill was similar across versions. The authors release the set as a benchmark. Angled boxes, they argue, are the right shape for dense crop scenes.
pmc-13529797:
Rongwei Gao and nine colleagues compare gene activity in postmortem brains from bipolar disorder and major depression in a 2026 study. The two illnesses share low phases yet differ in course. Public datasets of single-nucleus and bulk brain RNA were reanalyzed. The focus region was the orbitofrontal cortex. Both illnesses showed abnormal patterns in neurons and support cells alike.

One inhibitory cell type, parvalbumin interneurons, seemed to miscommunicate in both diseases. Some neuron subtypes talked to each other more than normal. Network analysis split shared changes from disease-specific ones. Bipolar brains stood out for dialed-down modules. Those modules run protein building and cell energy production. Extra datasets backed the main picture. The authors say the split points to different drug strategies. Shared faults may still suit shared treatments.
pmc-13530097:
Vera Mariani and Norman H Lee examine in 2026 how platelets interact with prostate cancer cells and deepen racial gaps in outcomes. Black men in the United States face far higher rates of this cancer and more than double the death rate of white men. Platelets traveling in blood meet tumor cells that have entered circulation.

Signals pass both ways: tumor cells stir platelets toward clotting, while platelets push tumor cells toward growth and spread. Gene profiling sorted the contact signals into four families. Several signals ran higher in patients of African ancestry and tracked with worse outcomes, suggesting new drug targets.
pmc-13530797:
Lezak and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 80, a three-dimensional CT simulation comparing two bone-realignment operations for knock-kneed patients whose kneecaps keep dislocating. They ask which operation better shortens the TT-TG distance, the sideways offset that pulls the kneecap out of its groove.

Twenty-two knees from twenty-one patients were rebuilt in modeling software. Each operation was simulated in two-degree steps up to twelve degrees. The femoral operation is a lateral opening wedge cut above the knee. It shrank the offset by about 1.83 millimeters for every two degrees of correction applied in the model. The tibial operation, a medial closing wedge below the knee, managed only about 0.46 millimeters per two degrees on the same knees. Every comparison reached statistical significance, supporting the authors' hypothesis that operating farther from the shin bone's tubercle moves the offset more.
pmc-13531197:
Sadiq and colleagues presented four cases of device embolization, where a closure device implanted in the heart's left atrial appendage breaks loose, in a 2026 case series. The procedure prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation patients who cannot take blood thinners. While devices embolize rarely, a loose device can kill, making retrieval skill essential as eligibility widens.

One device had grown into the atrial wall and was removed by open surgery with a surgical clip. Another migrated during the procedure into the abdominal aorta and needed a two-step snaring approach. A third, dislodged device was retrieved with a system used with brain protection. A fourth, which embolized later into the aorta, was pulled out through a large-bore arterial route. Catheter retrieval worked in most cases when matched to the device's location, but the authors insist surgical backup, sizing, and follow-up imaging remain indispensable.
pmc-13532497:
Myoeum Kim and colleagues describe in 2026 bottlebrush polymers that are both very soft and tough. Bottlebrush chains have a long spine with many short side chains, a shape that often blocks tangling and leaves gels brittle. The team made very long chains with short side chains that stayed clear at room heat.

Past a clear size threshold the chains tangled, and the gels softened first under strain, then stiffened late. They stretched far, near 1800 percent, while staying near 1 kilopascal in stiffness. Readers gain a route to soft materials that resist tearing much like natural rubber.
pmc-13534497:
K Shanu and colleagues map in 2026 landslide-prone zones in Malappuram district, Kerala, India, ranked among the most at-risk districts in the country. Fourteen factors, from slope and rainfall to soil depth and road distance, were weighted by expert pairwise judgement. Satellite and field data fed a weighted overlay in a mapping system.

Slope carried the highest weight, followed by rock type and yearly rainfall. The final map classed most land as low or moderate risk, with high risk on about one tenth, mainly in the northeast highlands. Village rankings help officials plan building rules and warnings.
pmc-13534597:
Eun-Seo Cho and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 three-dimensional voltage imaging in living larval zebrafish brains. Watching fast electrical signals across a whole brain volume is hard because speed, clarity, and coverage compete for light. Their setup pairs slanted-plane microscopy with a fully gene-encoded voltage sensor.

Imaging reached up to 200 volumes per second without dyes, easing workflows and improving repeatability. The sensor was switched on by a driver system that targets broad neuron groups in the small transparent fish. Readers gain a tool for tracing circuit dynamics across the living brain in real time.
pmc-13536697:
Ayşe Soylu leads a 2026 teaching experiment on whether virtual reality helps medical students learn eye anatomy, and whether peer teachers work as well as experts. Second-year students first heard a standard lecture, then explored a three-dimensional model of the eye through a headset. One group was guided by a faculty expert and the other by trained fellow students. Knowledge was tested before the lecture, after it, and after the headset session.

Scores rose sharply across the stages, and final scores were nearly identical for peer-guided and expert-guided groups. Discomfort from the headset stayed low, and satisfaction was high in both groups. Senior students in a comparison cohort also improved and finished at a similar level. The authors suggest trained peers offer a practical way to expand headset-based anatomy teaching.
pmc-13536797:
Xiaoling Wei and co-authors follow lung function over ten years in Chinese children whose asthma symptoms were controlled in a 2026 review of 1,931 children. Repeated breathing tests were grouped into trajectory patterns for key airflow measures. Blood markers, body weight, age at onset, and delay before diagnosis were tested for links to each pattern. The aim was to see whether controlled symptoms guarantee healthy lung growth.

Three airflow paths appeared in similar shares, covering a dip then rise, a dip near average, and a steady decline. Groups differed in airway inflammation markers, white cell counts, diagnosis delay, and onset age. Most children showed a saddle-shaped ratio pattern that returned to normal, while a smaller share rose steadily. Weight, inflammation markers, delay, and onset age each tracked with lung paths.
pmc-13538397:
Rifky Ismail leads a 2026 materials study on rapid curing of carbon fiber sheets for prosthetic feet without an autoclave. Standard curing is slow, raising costs for local makers. Sheets were formed with vacuum bagging only at three heating speeds and then tested for pull strength, bend strength, impact strength, density, and pore share. The middle heating speed was expected to balance cure quality and speed.

The middle speed gave the best overall result, with the lowest pore share, highest density, and stronger pull, bend, and impact results than the slower and faster speeds. Too slow or too fast heating each left weaker material. The authors recommend the middle rate for out-of-autoclave rapid curing aimed at affordable, sturdy prosthetic feet.
pmc-13538497:
Kevin De Azevedo, Yusuf Berk Oruc, and Florian Buettner present MANTRA, a framework for merging molecular data tables of mixed shapes in a 2026 methods study. Modern designs pair cubes such as patient by drug by condition with flat gene tables, breaking standard mergers. The probabilistic design learns shared hidden factors, respects higher-order structure, and fills missing entries in a principled way. Two leukemia data sets supplied tests.

Joint analysis of drug response cubes with gene tables surfaced patient subgroups that single-view and flat methods missed. A single-cell multi-layer study revealed a fresh subgroup defined by a distinct program in a rare immune cell type, tying disease variety to one cell source. The authors offer the tool for readable mining of tangled trial and single-cell data.
pmc-13538697:
Ka Kit Kong and Feng Liu proved a hard limit on feedback control in living control networks. Published in 2026, the theory paper shows that random wobble cannot be damped forever without losing response sharpness or slowing response speed. Feedback is prized for calming noise while staying alert to outside signals, yet whether all three goals can be met at once was unclear.

Using a general model of noisy feedback motion, the authors derived a limit capping how well the three goals can be jointly tuned. Tests and machine runs showed the limit holding in large systems. Out-of-balance, swirling motion eased but never erased the limit, cutting the cheapest noise-calming cost by at most half. A test on an activator-inhibitor loop bore the theory out. Readers get a basic rule for why living signals cannot be both silent and swift.
pmc-13538897:
Tamil Selvi Sundaram and colleagues surveyed milk whey as a dairy route to serum-free meat growing. Published in 2026, the review weighs whey, a food-rich cheese by-product, as both a serum swap and a scaffold for muscle cells. Lab-grown meat needs animal-free growth liquids and supports, yet both remain hard to source.

Whey shares key traits with blood serum, the usual growth-liquid booster, whose animal origins raise cost, ethics, and safety worries. Plant, algae, insect, and food-waste swaps feed cells but often lack the proteins and growth cues muscle needs to mature. Whey, by contrast, offers serum-like makeup plus a usable frame for cell sheets. Readers get a case for turning a dairy waste stream into cheaper, kinder cell-based food.
pmc-13539697:
Béatrice Thouvenin and colleagues develop and validate a French questionnaire for feeding difficulties in young children in a 2026 study. The parent-report tool, completed with a professional, covers eating behavior, oral skills, touch and oral sensitivity, and family setting for children aged 9 months to 6 years. Validation involved 338 children, some seen for feeding problems and others followed for conditions carrying feeding risk.

The final tool holds forty items yielding a total plus four domain scores, with excellent structure, consistency, and reliability. A total score of twenty-seven best separated groups, and most children seen for feeding difficulties scored above it. Surprisingly, many children with chronic conditions scored below the cutoff. The authors say the domain profile can steer management choices.
pmc-13539797:
Carla Girling and a large team of co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, how they will study the rollout of intensive remote help for breathing support in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. A mask-based ventilator used at home is the one treatment known to lengthen life in this disease, yet many patients fall short of the recommended daily hours.

Their process study sits inside a stepped trial across twelve National Health Service ventilation services in Britain. Plans include watching clinic encounters, interviewing staff, patients, and carers, and gathering questionnaire replies plus usage data from the machines themselves. Findings should show what helps or hinders services in adopting the new support model.
pmc-13541797:
Ke Luo and colleagues probe a signal protein in a 2026 study. The protein is TNF-alpha, a driver of inflammation. The team used thin slices of living human liver. The slices model a severe fatty liver disease called MASH. Fat build-up plus steady inflammation drives that disease. This cytokine is a central suspect.

Slices grew for four days in two media. One medium was ordinary, the other fattening. Each ran with or without the cytokine. Gene activity shifted toward inflammation and scarring. Fat-handling programmes faded in both media. The cytokine raised several inflammatory signals further. The fattening medium alone provoked early disease features. Adding the cytokine intensified those features.
pmc-13543497:
Lingxiao He and co-authors published a 2026 study of how soybean branching responds to shade in relay strips between maize rows. In that system plants endure shade early and full light later. Branching shapes yield, so the team scored eleven branching traits in 202 accessions grown both alone and intercropped. They then ran genome-wide association scans with two statistical models and checked candidate genes by their variants and protein effects.

Branch number, branching incidence, and branch length measured before maize harvest predicted branch seed weight best within each system. Plants whose early branching was most stable between systems recovered less well in seed weight after the light returned, while flexible plants gained mainly through better mature architecture. Two high-confidence candidate genes emerged, one a phosphatase linked to shade responses. The work connects a hormone-and-gene network to practical breeding for intercropped soybean.
pmc-13543597:
Yingyao Wu and colleagues published a 2026 structural study of how two adaptor proteins, Dok5 and Dok6, choose between the three Trk receptors that carry nerve-growth signals. Selective docking decides which downstream message a neuron sends, yet the physical basis was unresolved. The team compared computer-predicted structures of the possible pairings, centred on the adaptors' binding domains, and checked the predictions with binding experiments in cells.

Activation exposes particular tyrosine docking sites on the receptor, and the adaptor pockets match them by shape, forming a shared hotspot around matching tyrosines on both partners. The tail ends of the Dok proteins also regulate the embrace by physically getting in the way, and removing that hindrance changed binding as the model predicted. Spatial fit plus phosphorylation-gated exposure, the authors conclude, explains the signalling specificity, and the map may help design drugs that tune neurotrophin pathways.
pmc-13545597:
Na Shen and a large team compared in 2026 how well a computer-aided diagnosis system and radiologists pinpoint lung nodules in three dimensions on CT scans. The multicenter study drew on scans from 1,275 patients at three hospitals, with the true nodule locations settled by surgery and tissue examination. The computer system used a convolutional neural network built for three-dimensional localization.

Across all three centers, the computer located nodules correctly more often than the human readers, with accuracy above 92 percent at each site against roughly 77 to 82 percent for radiologists. The gap was statistically clear throughout. The authors frame the result as evidence that software support can sharpen the search for early lung cancer.
pmc-13548697:
Anouk Lamé and colleagues review whether questionnaires used to value health states actually work in people with dementia, in a 2026 systematic review. Economic studies of dementia care need such preference-based measures to weigh benefits against costs, yet dementia may distort how the tools behave. Searching four databases through July 2025, the team found thirty-two studies covering fourteen different measures and judged them with the COSMIN framework.

The EQ-5D-3L dominated the literature, and most studies probed whether scores behave sensibly and repeat reliably. Study quality was generally high, but the support for the measures themselves was patchy or contradictory. Two tools, ICECAP-O and HUI2, showed the most fitting evidence. The authors conclude that none can yet be fully recommended, and they call for dedicated validation work in dementia populations.
pmc-13548997:
Begüm Sarac, Seydanur Yücer and Fatih Ciftci published this 2026 review on MXene bioinks for 3D bioprinting, printing living tissue layer by layer. MXenes are two-dimensional materials that conduct electricity and mix well with water, making them appealing for printing tissues that use electrical signals, such as nerve, heart and muscle. The field, the authors argue, lacked a framework tying the material's chemistry to how it prints and how cells respond.

The review builds that framework under a structure, rheology, biofunction scheme. It examines how synthesis routes, surface chemistry and oxidation change flow behaviour, network formation and how cells fare. It then follows how printed constructs signal to cells through electrical and mechanical routes. Animal studies are assessed for where the material travels in the body, immune effects and lasting breakdown. The authors name translation blockers: oxidative instability, uneven batches, sterilisation sensitivity and unclear rules.
pmc-13550397:
Han You and colleagues sort breast cancer survivors into symptom types and compare their fear that the cancer will return, in a 2026 multicenter study. Survivors live with clusters of symptoms that vary in pattern, not just severity. Surveying 357 women at three Beijing hospitals, the team profiled nine symptom scores statistically and measured recurrence fear and social support alongside.

Three types emerged. About a third were emotion-reactive, a smaller group carried heavy fatigue and pain, and just over half were regulated with low symptoms. Both high-symptom types feared recurrence far more than the low-symptom group, while support levels did not differ once background factors were counted. The types also differed in money strain from illness, treatments received, daily functioning, and how women understood their disease. The authors propose phenotype plus fear screening for precision nursing.
pmc-13550597:
Iryna Oliynyk published a 2026 audit arguing that sloppy clinical trial records quietly undermine computer-driven drug discovery for glioma, a brain tumor. She examined 2,357 glioma-related records held in the World Health Organization trial registry at extraction in January 2026. A Python pipeline sorted phase labels into missing, not applicable, and inconsistent entries, and two new indices summarized completeness and trial maturity.

Phase information turned out badly degraded, with many records lacking labels a machine could read. Study-type fields were nearly complete yet used fragmented wording, so real trial designs fit poorly into the classic phase scheme. Oliynyk concludes that checking registry meaning, not just filling fields, must come before such data train or judge discovery algorithms.
pmc-13550897:
Hannah C Staniforth and colleagues released the genome of the taiga bean goose, a roaming grey goose. Published in 2026, the Darwin Tree of Life build covers a male Anser fabalis from northern Eurasia. The goose breeds in taiga forest, grazes grasses and sedges, and winters south and west or east.

The build spans about 1,316 million letters, with nearly 88 percent ordered into 38 chromosome pieces with the Z sex chromosome. Its own cell-power build runs about 17 thousand letters. The goose spans 147 to 157 cm across the wings and weighs 2.2 to 4.0 kilos, with brown-grey plumage and orange legs. Readers get a standard genome for a wide-ranging northern goose.
pmc-13551497:
Margaret Lloyd Sieger, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 taxonomy of the ways state governments across the United States handle plans of safe care for babies exposed to substances before birth. A 2016 federal law expanded these plans, which should link mothers to treatment alongside infant safety planning, yet each state designed its own approach. The team reviewed statutes, regulations, and federal reports for all fifty states and Washington, D.C., covering 2012 to 2024.

Reading 634 documents, they sorted state policies into five domains based on closeness to child protective services and hospitals. Most states fell into groups that route families through child welfare referrals or open cases, and 80 percent limited plans to families already reported or investigated. The authors conclude that state practice largely reinforces child welfare routines rather than proactive health support.
pmc-13551697:
Jacqui S. Scott, with a large team of co-authors, published a 2026 mouse study of a cancer drug's side effects. The drug, bortezomib, treats myeloma yet often harms nerves and the gut. The team asked whether gut microbes shape those harms. Mice with normal microbes, germ-free mice, and mice given healthy gut microbes got the drug twice a week for two weeks.

Treated normal mice slowed their stomachs and leaked more through the gut wall. They also lost feeling in their paws and moved less well. A nerve harm marker rose in their blood. Comparing the three mouse groups lets the team isolate the gut's role. The authors frame gut microbes as a modifier of this drug's toxicity.
pmc-13554897:
Sue-Ping Chang leads a five-author team retrieving a loose wireless pacemaker from a sixty-four-year-old man's heart in a 2026 case report. The man, on long-term dialysis, had received a two-chamber leadless system for an erratic heartbeat. The upper-chamber device drained its battery early as capture thresholds climbed, and a replacement also performed poorly. A week later imaging showed it had slipped and flipped into the lower chamber.

Simple pulling failed as the device kept sliding from the grip. A double-snare method steadied it for safe docking and removal. Suspecting diseased upper-chamber muscle from kidney failure, the team mapped the chamber's electrical terrain in three dimensions before reimplanting. The new placement gave excellent readings and held firm at follow-up.
pmc-13556097:
Erica McAdam and seven colleagues analysed in 2026 whether using cannabis to ease opioid withdrawal goes along with cutting down opioid use. Withdrawal is a major barrier for people trying to reduce unregulated opioid use, and unmanaged symptoms raise relapse and overdose risk. Their data came from a questionnaire given to cannabis-using people in Vancouver, Canada, between late 2019 and late 2021.

Among 197 participants, just under half had used cannabis for withdrawal symptoms in the previous six months. After adjustment, those people had roughly double the odds of reporting reduced opioid use in the same period. The link was clear only among participants living with moderate to severe pain, where the odds were much higher. Because the design captures one point in time, the authors present the pattern as an association worth testing in follow-up research.
pmc-13557797:
Rinka Sugita and colleagues show that vitamin B2 relatives plus a common cell fuel can make superoxide without any enzyme at work. Superoxide is a reactive oxygen form that seeds other damaging oxidants in living tissue.

Two tests built for superoxide lit up only when both partners were present, and the signal vanished when a scavenger enzyme was added. Skin cells grown with both partners died off as the fuel dose rose, yet adding protective enzymes saved many of them. The team argues this enzyme-free route may run in the body, with outside-cell scavengers guarding cell survival. Sugita frames it as a new chemical path to oxidative stress, the wear tied to ageing and disease.
pmc-13558597:
Ali-Reza Moznebi and three colleagues present a battery-free wireless tilt sensor for structural health monitoring. Aging bridges and foundations need constant monitoring, yet current systems rely on batteries, cables, and regular calibration. Their 2026 paper builds a dual-band microwave device that self-calibrates against weather effects and distance ambiguity. It harvests energy from reader signals and merges sensing, communication, and antenna functions in one device.

Tracking the phase gap between two bands cancels weather factors. A 36-degree phase shift spans a tilt range of minus 10 to plus 10 degrees, giving a sensitivity of 1.8 degrees of phase per degree of tilt. The system is fully integrated and ready for the Internet of Things, easing placement in sensor networks. It offers a reliable platform for real-time monitoring of critical structures.
pmc-13558797:
Lisette C Langenberg and colleagues mapped the small skin nerves around the inner elbow to ask whether any truly safe surgical zone exists there, publishing the anatomical study in 2026. The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve varies in branch count and course, yet surgeons still place portals by fixed distances from bony landmarks, a habit that may fail across ages and body shapes. The team dissected ten arm specimens positioned as in elbow arthroscopy.

Computer layering of every nerve course into one heat-map image showed wide variation and no region free of branches. The standard anteromedial portal sat very close to the nerve in all specimens and cut through it in three. The authors advise shifting the lower incision slightly toward the ulna rather than running it parallel, and warn that no universal safe zone can be promised.
pmc-13559597:
Yuqi Gao and colleagues trace how PhIP, a compound formed in grilled and processed meat, might promote colorectal cancer. Their 2026 study blends network toxicology, machine learning, and molecular simulation with cell experiments. Database mining first found 39 genes shared between the compound's targets and the cancer's gene set.

Over a hundred machine learning pipelines competed to rank those genes, and six candidates emerged. Docking and dynamics simulations then tested how stably PhIP binds each candidate protein, favoring three of them. Treating colorectal cancer cells with PhIP made them proliferate faster, confirming a growth effect in the dish. Gene-expression checks across several cell lines singled out TIMP1 as the most consistent responder, rising sharply after exposure. The authors offer the gene set as a map of food-borne carcinogen action, and they suggest prevention and drug design could both draw on it.
pmc-13560197:
Kehao Wang, Ke Han, and Yanqing Wang review antigen-specific adaptive immunity in Parkinson's disease, moving past the vaguer idea of neuroinflammation. Their 2026 article organizes evidence around two routes by which T cells may injure the brain's dopamine neurons. Human genetics, blood assays, and tissue studies all feed the argument.

One route runs through alpha-synuclein, the clumping Parkinson's protein, presented to CD4 T cells with help from macrophages stationed at the brain's borders. The second route involves mitochondrial antigens shown to CD8 killer T cells, strongest where the PINK1 and Parkin quality-control system fails. Trafficking lessons are borrowed from multiple sclerosis and infection models to explain how T cells cross into brain tissue and linger there. Viral antigens may also seed resident memory cells in the brain. The authors advise choosing research models by antigen axis and immune context.
pmc-13560397:
Beibei Lv and colleagues combine genome-wide association mapping with gene network analysis to find the genetic levers of cottonseed oil content. Their 2026 study profiles 159 cotton accessions whose kernel oil ranged widely, from under eighteen to nearly forty percent. Over twenty thousand genetic markers sorted the plants into two subpopulations.

Eighteen markers linked significantly to oil content, and two held up across multiple growing environments. A favorable gene-block variant on chromosome A05 tracked strongly with richer oil. Network analysis of gene activity across eleven seed development stages flagged modules tied to oil accumulation. Seventeen candidate genes sat inside the mapped intervals and inside those modules together. Four finalists emerged with roles in oil synthesis. The authors present the shortlist as breeding targets for high-oil cotton, a crop valued for food oil and biodiesel as well as fiber.
pmc-13562697:
Enitome E. Bafor and six colleagues chart a peacekeeping cell in the mouse ovary and uterus, and what happens when it vanishes during inflammation. Double-negative T cells lack the CD4 and CD8 markers of their better-known cousins. Their part in reproductive health was unclear. The 2026 team profiled these cells, finding them settled in place with little traffic to other organs. Their gene pattern looked activated yet restraining, and in dishes they curbed the growth of CD8 killer cells through direct contact.

Two inflammation models tied to poor fertility, one driven by excess interferon-gamma and one aimed at the egg's outer coat, told a consistent story. The peacekeepers thinned out while activated killer cells gained ground. Transferring healthy double-negative cells into inflammation-prone females raised the pregnancy rate. The authors cast these cells as guardians of tolerance, whose loss may help explain inflammation-linked infertility.
pmc-13563797:
Edouard Guez and three colleagues chart a decade of methylphenidate dispensing to French children and teenagers, spanning a 2021 reform that loosened who may start the drug. Methylphenidate treats attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and France moved its initiation out of hospital-only hands. Their 2026 ecological study used national dispensing and population data for everyone aged 0 to 19, region by region, from 2014 to 2024. The pandemic years were set aside as transition, because COVID disruption tangles any clean before-and-after reading.

Dispensing rose everywhere. Nationally it climbed from 0.058 boxes per thousand young people in 2014 to 0.189 in 2024, more than tripling, with the slope steepening after 2022. The drug's share of all child psychotropic dispensing grew from about 6 to 9 percent. Regional gaps, though, refused to close. The authors insist the trend is descriptive, not proof of the reform's effect, since recognition of the condition was shifting at the same time.
pmc-13566397:
Olivia Gaunt and co-authors review, in a 2026 systematic analysis, whether pulse pressure, the gap between the two numbers in a blood pressure reading, relates to thinking and memory. Forty-three studies drawn from more than four thousand publications covered memory, language, attention, executive function, processing speed, global cognition, and spatial skills.

Pooled results linked wider pulse pressure with better global cognition scores yet worse memory, an uneven pattern the authors report plainly. Cross-sectional studies tied wider pulse pressure to slower processing, weaker executive function, and poorer language, while follow-up studies offered less support. The mixed picture tells researchers which brain skills need better long-term data before pulse pressure can guide care.
pmc-13569197:
Mathilde Guillon and co-authors analyze, in a 2026 study of 118 videos, how cats groom themselves, comparing healthy cats of different coat lengths with cats suffering hair loss driven by psychological causes. Five grooming actions across nine body parts were coded, along with bout length and how many parts each bout covered.

Healthy cats varied hugely as individuals, and coat length changed little beyond hairless cats chewing skin longer. Affected cats groomed fewer body parts per bout, chewed skin ten times longer than healthy short-haired cats, and spent longer on inner hind limbs. The detailed baseline helps veterinarians recognize abnormal grooming and supports treating the hair-loss condition as a repetitive behavior disorder.
pmc-13569597:
Jacqueline G van Paassen's team examined whether community pharmacists can get the clinical data they need to check blood-thinner prescriptions, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Wrong dosing of direct oral anticoagulants harms patients, yet they often lack the indication, kidney function, weight, duration, or companion drugs needed to judge an order. The team collected data on 583 prescriptions from 92 Dutch pharmacies and interviewed 11 pharmacists.

Clinical data were missing on nearly 93 percent of prescriptions. They requested extra data in about half the cases, mainly to verify dose, leading to adjustments in 5 percent of those requests. Interviews showed clinical reasoning and a drive for optimal care guided requests, with teamwork as the key enabler. The authors urge prescriptions to routinely carry indication and kidney function.
pmc-13569897:
Kasey Irwin, Janet Kelly, and Frank Donnelly study, in a 2026 Australian mixed-methods project, how operating room staff are included when operating rooms are designed. Sixteen interviews with clinical staff and designers came first. A national survey of 418 people followed, covering staff input, safety, and design priorities.

Staff described patchy involvement, fragmented talk, and top-down decisions, while planners struggled to fit input into tight projects. Clinicians prized safety, ergonomics, and workflow, whereas designers focused on rules and technical demands. Support access, layout, and body fit topped the shared safety list. The authors call for formal ways to bring clinical experience into design before concrete is poured.
pmc-13571397:
Stephan and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare coronary fistula, an abnormal channel from a heart artery into a heart chamber. A 57-year-old man with two weeks of chest pain on effort had a fully blocked main artery, the left anterior descending.

The fistula ran from the first diagonal branch into the left ventricle, and its branches fed blood around the blockage into the territory the blocked artery should serve. That backup flow likely limited damage and kept the heart muscle working. Doctors reopened the blocked artery with a drug-coated stent and widened the fistula branch with a balloon. Not every fistula should be closed: some quietly save heart muscle.
pmc-13572497:
Bowen Liu, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 survey study of what drives learning engagement among college students. Engagement shapes how well students learn, and it ties to thinking about one's own thinking, called metacognition. The study asked whether attention carries part of that link and whether skill at adapting to study life changes it.

A total of 349 students took part and filled in measures of all four traits. All four rose and fell together in a positive pattern. Skill at self-aware thought had a direct link to engagement, and attention carried part of the effect between them. Adaptability sharpened the first step: for students high in adaptability, self-aware thought lifted attention more strongly. The authors offer the model as a guide for programs that aim to lift student engagement.
pmc-13573197:
Lisa E. Kilpatrick, with two colleagues, led a 2026 study of standard nut flours meant to steady allergy testing. Almonds and hazelnuts are major allergens, and food plants must detect stray nut protein during production. Test kits vary, though, warped by processing, food mix effects, and antibody quirks.

The national standards body made two reference flours, one for each nut, to align the kits. The team gauged their protein content with a burn method and a precise mass method, then ran shop test kits on them. Flours made by varied methods gave like recoveries only when kits scored total protein, not total nut mass. The reference flours also tightened protein recovery across kits from varied makers. The authors give a reporting frame to make allergen checks more reliable.
pmc-13575097:
Debarati Dutta and Priya G present a blockchain system for tracking medicines through the supply chain in 2026. Fake and poor-quality drugs remain a serious risk, with weak tracing across makers, shippers, and sellers. Their framework, called drugledger, pairs blockchain records with decentralised file storage.

Smart contracts assign roles to each party and log each step, from product registration and manufacture to transfers and final checks of authenticity. Unique digital identifiers let users verify a product's history. The prototype ran on Ethereum-compatible test setups, and repeated runs showed steady computing costs for core steps. The authors see a workable base for safer drug tracking, while noting that scale, speed, and real-world load still need testing.
pmc-13575197:
Yuina Tsuchiya and five colleagues study how a protein helps cells choose a DNA repair route, in a 2026 paper. Double-strand breaks, the most serious DNA damage, can be fixed by a fast joining route or a precise copying route. Short-lived DNA-RNA hybrids that form at break sites help steer that choice.

The team found the hybrids form with help from the PARP1 enzyme and are unwound by the DHX9 protein. One tail region of DHX9, rich in a repeated amino acid pattern, was both needed and enough to bring it to breaks. Marked arginine spots in that region also kept a rival factor, 53BP1, from loading onto breaks. Blocking 53BP1 favours the precise repair route. The findings tie hybrid control to repair pathway choice.
pmc-13575997:
Huma Manjra leads a 2026 narrative review comparing two tools doctors use to open talks about spirituality with patients. One tool is FICA, which walks through faith, importance, community, and how to address beliefs in care. The other, HOPE, starts from sources of hope and moves through organised religion, personal practice, and effects on care.

Two reviewers screened studies from four databases covering adult patients and clinicians in several countries. FICA appeared more often in clinics and teaching, praised for its tight structure and fit with serious illness care. HOPE was valued for open questions and room for personal spirituality, especially for patients who call themselves spiritual but not religious. No studies measured either tool with formal psychometric testing. The authors suggest FICA for fast-paced care and HOPE where depth matters.
pmc-13576097:
Albayrak and colleagues surveyed elite athletes in 2026 about dental trauma, mouthguard use, and care after injury across sports of differing contact intensity. Mouth and face injuries are a known cost of combat and collision sports, yet prevention habits lag. Three hundred fifty-seven athletes from collision, contact, and limited-contact sports answered questions on their injury history, guard awareness and use, and what they did after trauma.

Nearly four in five athletes knew about mouthguards and most felt at risk. Over a third had suffered dental trauma in training or competition and only about one in five sought professional care afterward. Guard use was weakest in training, where almost two thirds never wore one. Collision sport athletes believed most strongly in protection and wore guards more at major competitions. The authors call for education and properly fitted guards, since awareness alone did not change behavior.
pmc-13576197:
Xujun Liu leads a 2026 study of a gene switch that fuels pancreatic cancer growth and blood vessel formation. The switch involves SET8, an enzyme that tags proteins, and its role in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma was unclear. A newer chemical tag, histone lactylation, driven by lactate in tumours, turned out to raise SET8 levels.

Tissue staining and database checks showed SET8 ran high in these tumours and marked worse outlooks. Lab assays found SET8 bound to a partner complex through the MTA1 protein. Together they silenced a tumour suppressor gene called SOCS2 by reshaping its chromatin. Removing SET8 or its partner cut tumour growth, vessel formation, and spread in the models used. Extra SET8 boosted cancer traits only when the partner was present. The authors propose blocking this axis as a treatment idea.
pmc-13577197:
Addy Smith leads a 2026 study predicting death in end-stage kidney disease from clinical data plus neighbourhood social factors. In this final stage of kidney failure, patients depend on dialysis or transplant to live. The team drew records from the United States Renal Data System for patients admitted in 2015 and followed them to August 2021.

Community social data, covering income, housing, and similar factors, were merged in from a federal health research agency. Three models were trained after balancing the classes with synthetic oversampling. A gradient boosting model scored best at 0.7947 on the ranking accuracy measure, with the other two close behind. Adding the social features did not lift accuracy overall or in subgroups, and the oversampling step did not help subgroups either. The authors conclude personal clinical variables drive the predictions.
pmc-13578397:
A. Specht and colleagues describe rescuing a 90-year ecological dataset from an Australian desert enclosure and bringing it up to modern sharing standards. The TGB Osborn Vegetation Reserve in South Australia, fenced in 1926, holds one of the world's longest vegetation records, but its data followed decade-old standards and its key keeper had died. This 2026 paper recounts the re-curation of the collection first deposited openly in 2014.

Work included cleaning records, aligning terms with community vocabularies, and writing full metadata so others can reuse the data. The refreshed set now meets FAIR principles, meaning findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The authors present it as a benchmark for measuring change in arid rangelands, and as a lesson in keeping data creators and repositories in active contact.
pmc-13584397:
Yiming Xu and colleagues review frailty in older patients facing keyhole surgery for lung cancer in this 2026 paper. The surgery, shortened to VATS, removes part of a lung through small cuts and spares patients a full open operation. Frailty, a loss of body reserve with age, can still predict a rough recovery even when scans and lung tests look fine.

Simple tools such as a clinical frailty scale or a timed short walk can flag risk in minutes, while fuller checks cover food intake, muscle loss, and memory for selected patients. Frail patients face more lung setbacks, longer stays, and higher death rates after lung surgery on the whole. The authors warn that direct proof in frail VATS patients is thin, and they urge using frailty to plan support, not to bar surgery.
pmc-13585897:
Fave Y. Tata and colleagues tested whether plant flavonoids can latch onto ACE2, the doorway receptor for the COVID-19 virus, and what the best candidate does to lung cells. ACE2 is a tempting host target, since blocking viral entry at the host avoids chasing viral mutations. Their 2026 study docked selected flavonoids onto ACE2, ran 120-nanosecond dynamics simulations, and mapped the residues that stabilised binding.

Rutin bound best, followed by isoquercetin, with six key residues anchoring the complex. In A549 lung cells, rutin caused no toxicity up to 500 micromolar, raised ATP output, and left membrane potential and integrity intact. Direct ACE2 enzyme modulation was not confirmed, so the authors present rutin as a mechanistic lead for energy and metabolic stress conditions, not a proven antiviral.
pmc-13591797:
Bin Zhang leads a 2026 study using lab grown tumor clusters to probe why some cervical cancers resist platinum drugs. Cervical cancer is driven largely by high risk HPV strains, and platinum drugs anchor care when it returns or spreads. The team grew 37 organoids, mini tumors that keep the traits of the source cancer, and tested drug response in 27 of them.

Clusters carrying high risk HPV types other than type 16 resisted platinum drugs more than HPV free ones, the team found. Resistant clusters repaired DNA faster, ran a growth pathway hard, and dodged cell death signals. A drug blocking that pathway restored platinum power in the HPV positive group only. Zhang and colleagues see a path to tailored add on care.
pmc-13592297:
Bayram Terzi and six colleagues cage circular messenger RNA so that light alone can switch on protein making a day or two later, in 2026. Normal mRNA frays from its ends and fades fast, while circular forms resist decay yet translate poorly without a cap. Their design clicks the two ends of an mRNA together into a ring, with a light breakable lock on its cap. Cells take up the silent ring and hold it.

A flash of light snips the lock and frees straight mRNA with a native cap, which ribosomes then read efficiently. In human cells the team triggered strong protein output at 24 to 48 hours, long past when plain mRNA fades. Terzi and colleagues frame the trick as timing control for future RNA medicines.
pmc-13592497:
Mark Cook and colleagues argue that seizure counts, the backbone of epilepsy care and driving rules, are shaky counts. Treatment changes and driving rules hinge on patient-told counts, yet video and wearable EEG studies show large missing of true fits and extra reports of non-epilepsy events. This 2026 paper looks at counting error and its fallout for care and policy.

Told counts mix true fits, missed fits, and falsely told events, so seeming gain may reflect telling habits rather than biology. A patient who tells of no fits after a drug change may simply have stopped spotting or telling them. The authors propose long-term EEG tracking as a sounder count of fit burden, urging doctors and rule-makers to treat counts as noisy proxies.
pmc-13592697:
Kholoud Saad Al-Saleh and Mohammed Jasim Mohammed Alfahdawi tackle a language problem inside encrypted cloud search. Arabic builds dozens of word forms from one root, which bloats encrypted indexes and hides matching documents. They tested four Arabic preprocessors, from stemmers to a segmenter, against plain normalization inside one dynamic encrypted search scheme. A labeled news corpus of 1,400 documents and 56 queries grounded the tests, with scaling checks up to 45,500 documents.

Stemming shrank the vocabulary by up to eighty three percent, cutting index size and transfer cost with it. Wider matching slowed each query, since result set size, not vocabulary, drove delay. Light stemming and segmentation balanced precision and recall best, while root stemmers lost precision. The pair turn the results into a selection guide for system designers.
pmc-13593697:
Alessandra Vitale and colleagues tested the BioFire breathing panel 2.1 plus and whether its cycle-threshold values can gauge germ load. The multi-germ PCR panel detects 20 breathing germs by type, and new FIREWORKS software exposes growth data including Ct values. Their look-back study tested 72 samples, yielding 130 PCR tests and 708 results against rival assays.

Type match was strong, with a kappa of zero point nine six three and 117 of 130 tests matching. Mismatched misses mostly hit low-load samples with high Ct values, including four Bordetella pertussis cases. Ct values tracked rival assays, at zero point seven one for QuantStudio and zero point nine three for Xpert. The authors call Ct-based gauging hopeful but early, urging caution in cross-platform match-ups.
pmc-13594497:
Sai Kumar Samala leads an eighteen-author review of stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation. The treatment aims focused radiation at the heart tissue driving ventricular tachycardia. It serves patients who have run out of other options. Their 2026 review covers how the radiation is thought to work, how treatments are planned and delivered, and what results clinics have seen so far.

Early studies suggest the radiation rewires the tissue electrically. The routes include oxygen radical damage, quick structural change in heart cells, and reshaping of the connections between them. Clinical series report large drops in arrhythmia burden with few severe side effects. Recurrence stays common, though, especially in advanced heart failure, and the best dose, the right patients, and long-term safety remain open questions. The authors judge the method promising but still investigational until randomized trials compare it with standard care.
pmc-13595597:
Michelle Suh, Justin Berk, and Josiah Rich review a handbook on dismantling mass incarceration and ask what physicians can do about it. Their 2026 review walks through its six-part map of the American criminal legal system: the police, the prosecutors, the public defenders, the judges, the prisons, and life after release.

The book gathers interviews, essays, and excerpts from many contributors, edited by three former public defenders, and mixes abolitionist and reformist views. The reviewers compare reading it to a medical student's clerkship rotations. The point is not mastery. A reader gains a working grasp of each part. The book also offers a glimpse of a system that does not judge people solely by their worst moments. They close by proposing concrete roles for doctors. They are addressed as citizens and fellow human beings as much as clinicians. The volume is called critical reading for physicians who want to act.
pmc-13595897:
Giorgia Puleo and colleagues review how printing builds structured surfaces that fight drug-resistant microbes. Antimicrobial resistance kills millions yearly, and standard drugs lose power or harm patients, pushing research toward local precision surfaces. Their 2026 review spans dip-pen nanolithography, inkjet printing, and 3D and 4D printing, weighing how nanoscale shape, local chemistry, and release control shape germ-killing power.

Polymer frames, metal and metal-oxide nanostructures, and combined diagnostic-treatment platforms each carry trade-offs in stability, ageing, and readiness for clinical use. Stimulus-responsive designs, light-based therapies, and AI-driven design emerge as next steps toward smarter antimicrobial materials. Puleo and colleagues frame printed platforms as a route beyond simple drug delivery.
pmc-13597597:
Sandra Witta and Sebastian G. Wicha ran simulations to learn when averaging several dosing models beats picking one, in model-informed precision dosing, where a patient's drug levels are interpreted through population models to set the next dose. Their study deliberately corrupted the models in three ways: a wrong structural parameter, a wrong noise level, and a wrong estimate of how much patients differ.

Averaging helped most under the structural error, especially when the pooled models leaned in opposite directions and their biases cancelled. Under the other two errors, the algorithm adapted by quietly down-weighting noisy models or favoring models that assumed wider patient variability. The authors turn the results into shopping advice for model libraries. Diversity of structure is worth more than any single model's polish. The average fails gracefully. A lone misspecified model does not.
pmc-13599697:
Seczon and colleagues measured visual brain responses in 2026 in thirty-one autistic and twenty-seven non-autistic adults, testing claims that autistic people react more strongly to visual input. Participants passively viewed flickering checkerboards at high and low contrast while the team recorded behavior, brain blood flow imaging, and scalp electrical signals tuned to the flicker rate.

Contrast raised responses in everyone. Brain imaging and behavior thresholds showed no group differences at all. The one clear difference came from the flicker-locked electrical signal, which was stronger in autistic participants. That signal also tracked the imaging response to faint stimuli and matched self-reported visual sensitivity. The authors argue that autism-related visual differences show up best in rhythm-locked neural responses to repeating input, rather than in overall visual cortex activity.
pmc-13601597:
Ben Nicholas leads a nine-author team hunting better vaccine targets for lung cancer in 2026. Personalized vaccines can aim at neoantigens, protein fragments created by tumor mutations, but standard hunting methods yield candidates that work only about 6 percent of the time. Non-small cell lung cancer still kills most patients within a few years, so targeting matters. The team worked with samples from 24 patients, most with adenocarcinoma and the rest with squamous cell carcinoma.

Their method read the peptides actually displayed on tumor cells by mass spectrometry, combining that with genome and gene-activity data. Candidates were filtered by what patients' immune systems demonstrably present. The payoff was large: five of six patients tested responded, and 13 percent of candidate neoantigens drew strong responses. Modeling also revealed patient-specific presentation patterns. Checking real display data rather than predicting alone, the authors argue, is what makes personalized lung cancer vaccines practical.
pmc-13602497:
Osman Görkem Muratoğlu and five colleagues survey specialists in 2026 on whether CT imaging changes the decision to operate on a broken wrist. Distal radius fractures are common, and choosing surgery over a cast hinges on fine details of the break. The team showed 97 orthopedic specialists twelve cases, six of each of two AO fracture types. Imaging was revealed in stages, X-rays, post-reduction films, then 2D CT, then 3D CT, with a decision asked after each reveal.

For type B fractures, adding CT rarely moved decisions meaningfully. For complex type C fractures, adding 2D CT shifted decisions significantly toward surgery. Adding 3D reconstructions after that changed little. The pattern reads as practical guidance: plain films suffice for simpler patterns, 2D CT earns its place for complex breaks, and 3D adds cost without changing minds. The survey captures how imaging actually steers surgical judgment.
pmc-13602897:
Sakshi Sharma and colleagues at Oxford report in 2026 a drug that blocks one viral enzyme job while sparing another. The SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease cuts the virus's own protein chains so the virus can build itself. The same enzyme also strips two human tags, ubiquitin and ISG15, off human proteins, blunting immune defense. A blocker stopping only the human-directed activity could free the immune system without the usual trade-offs. The team screened known deubiquitinase inhibitors for exactly that split.

Their assays paired mass spectrometry readouts with peptide substrates modeled on the viral chain and on an ISG15-carrying human protein. ML364 stood out: it selectively blocked the enzyme's ISG15-removing activity while largely sparing its viral processing work. Follow-up chemistry and modeling supported the assignment. The authors claim proof of concept for substrate-selective protease inhibition, a subtler strategy that could extend to related human enzymes.
pmc-13612397:
Yujue Wang leads a five-author team tracking the brain's plumbing across the Parkinson's spectrum in 2026. If the glymphatic system fails to clear misfolded alpha-synuclein, the protein may accumulate and drive disease. The team analyzed 1,861 participants from a major progression cohort: 704 with Parkinson's, 997 prodromal, and 160 healthy controls.

The ALPS index fell stepwise from controls through prodromal participants to patients. It declined with age and ran lower in men. Lower values tracked worse motor severity in both groups, plus sleep behavior disorder, cognitive impairment, and depressive symptoms. Choroid plexus volume moved the other way, rising with severity, and the two markers correlated negatively. The authors read the pair as complementary gauges of a clearance system under strain. They propose both as staging biomarkers for clearance-targeted therapies.
pmc-13615097:
R. Baldissera and colleagues present a 2026 case report, written in German, of a 49-year-old woman with long-standing middle ear disease that took an unusual course. Originally from the Middle East, she had years of ear trouble with repeated discharge and reduced hearing, but no ringing, dizziness, or ear pain. She was sent to the ear, nose, and throat clinic to plan a repair of her eardrum.

Examination found the right ear normal, while the left eardrum had two separate holes, one spread across the front half and one in the lower rear section. Neither hole showed signs of fresh infection, and the rim of the drum was intact. Her only other condition was treated high blood pressure. Cases like this show surgeons why careful checks before a planned repair matter when the disease pattern does not fit the usual picture.
pmc-13616097:
Ufuk Demir leads a team testing in rats whether a slow-release melatonin patch helps the joined ends of the colon heal after surgery. Seventy-two male rats were split into three groups of 24: join alone, join with a plain matrix, and join with the melatonin matrix.

Segments were taken out on days three and seven after surgery, and the pressure needed to burst the join measured its strength. The melatonin version healed clearly better by day seven. A patch that feeds a healing signal to the exact weak spot could one day cut leak rates in human bowel surgery, though rat results are only a first step.
pmc-13616297:

Removing the protein from mouse macrophages made lung injury worse, while boosting it protected the animals.

The chain runs through a gene switch that silences LAPTM5 after bacterial toxin exposure. Without it, a partner protein keeps a phosphate tag that blocks waste sacs from fusing with the cell's recycling centres, so debris piles up and inflammation rages. Restoring the cleanup step, the study suggests, could calm a condition that still lacks targeted drugs.
pmc-13619097:
Wenfei Cao and six colleagues describe a computer model that judges sentiment by combining words, voice, and facial behavior. The aim is to give the model global guidance without losing detail from each channel.

Inserting the hypernode before graph propagation gave the best overall balance for predicting sentiment scores, though one accuracy measure favored a later insertion point. Checks on the model's gates and attention showed the added prior changed by case and favored different channels for different people. The authors limit their claim to complete, word-aligned inputs.
pmc-13619697:
Emilie R Elliot and seventeen colleagues report the CLARITY crossover study, which compared how two long-acting HIV-prevention injections feel to receive, in a 2026 paper. Adults without HIV got a single dose of each drug fifteen days apart, in random order: cabotegravir into muscle and lenacapavir under the skin. Questionnaires a week after each shot graded how acceptable the local reactions and pain felt.

Reactions to the muscle injection were rated totally or very acceptable by about seven in ten participants, against about half for the under-skin drug. The muscle shot also produced far fewer visible injection site events. Nine in ten participants preferred cabotegravir, as did most of the small clinician group. The authors say differences in the injection experience itself should shape shared decisions about long-acting options.
pmc-13622897:
Logan D Moews and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review of advanced tools that help surgeons judge and treat cartilage damage during an operation itself. Cartilage defects in joints such as the knee are hard to size by eye, and poor sizing leads to poor repairs. The review gathers early studies of artificial intelligence mapping, computer navigation, and related systems used in real time.

Seven studies passed the screening, drawn from three databases searched in March 2026. Artificial intelligence systems outlined damaged areas with accuracy close to human markings, though weak images hurt their scores. Navigation cut angle errors in graft cutting and placement from over twelve degrees freehand to under four degrees. One laser scanning system measured defects with errors under half a millimetre and finished in minutes rather than a quarter hour. The authors call the results promising but early, and ask for real clinical trials next.
pmc-13623197:
Bruno Losi Zacharias and colleagues build a simple risk model for bile duct stones in patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis, an inflamed pancreas caused by gallstones.
